💡 Key Takeaways
  • Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed was confronted on NBC's "Meet the Press" Sunday over his opposition to Israel's existence as a Jewish state.
  • The U.S.-Israel alliance was tested when Washington and Jerusalem found common cause against Iran — and when defending Israel drew heavily on American weapons stocks.
  • A new report from Advancing American Freedom (AAF) and the Zionist Organization of America (ZOA) argues that Israel’s military reach and regional role make the alliance a strategic asset for Washington.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed was confronted on NBC's "Meet the Press" Sunday over his opposition to Israel's existence as a Jewish state.

The U.S.-Israel alliance was tested when Washington and Jerusalem found common cause against Iran — and when defending Israel drew heavily on American weapons stocks. Meanwhile, that ongoing conflict has now sharpened a question for Washington: what does the alliance deliver, and what does it demand in return?

A new report from Advancing American Freedom (AAF) and the Zionist Organization of America (ZOA) argues that Israel’s military reach and regional role make the alliance a strategic asset for Washington.

Its authors call Israel "the largest U.S. aircraft carrier" in the Middle East. But this is in direct opposition of critics who say that the alliance costs the U.S. a lot and delivers very little in return.

The report, dated Oct. 26, 2026, arrives as public support for Israel continues to fall across the political spectrum — even among Republicans and MAGA supporters.

FROM INTELLIGENCE SHARING TO MISSILE DEFENSE, HOW ISRAEL'S PARTNERSHIP PROTECTS AMERICAN SECURITY.

According to recent reports, president Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced joint military action targeting Iran. (REUTERS/Kevin Mohatt).

It has been revealed that president Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have discussed ending direct U.S. military aid, but the U.S. leader has also called Israel "a great ally, much more reliable than most" and said Washington would help if Israel needed it.

Sources indicate that the report specifically points to intelligence sharing, joint weapons development and military cooperation as returns on what the U.S. gets for providing support to Israel.

According to recent reports, one of the clearest examples is missile defense. The U.S. and Israel develop systems including David’s Sling and Arrow, while American companies manufacture components for several programs. More than 100 companies across 34 states participate in missile-defense co-production, according to the Congressional Research Service. In August, a Raytheon-Rafael facility in Arkansas delivered the first Iron Dome Tamir interceptor built entirely in the U.S.

Sources indicate that those programs support U.S. manufacturers and give the Pentagon a role in developing missile-defense systems. During the Iran conflict, however, U.S. forces also expended large numbers of interceptors — costly weapons that can take years to replace.

US REBUILDING WEAPONS STOCKPILE COULD DELAY ORDERS FROM ALLIES.

In September, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated that the U.S. had probably used between half and two-thirds of its combined inventory of Patriot, THAAD, SM-3 and SM-6 interceptors since June 2025.

Recent findings suggest that the estimate includes weapons used during the earlier 12-day war with Iran and is based on publicly reported expenditures compared with the number of those interceptors the War Department has purchased. CBO remarked rebuilding stocks could take at least five years, even if production increased.

President Donald Trump, left, meets with Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, as CIA Director John Ratcliffe, from second left, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, and from second right, Netanyahu's wife Sara Netanyahu, Israel's Strategic Affairs Minister Ron Dermer, Israel's National Security Council head Tzachi Hanegbi, obstructed, and Israel's Cabinet Secretary Yossi Fuchs listen in the Blue Room of the White House, Monday, July 7, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon).

It has been revealed that intelligence sharing is another return cited by supporters of the alliance. Former CIA Director John Brennan said Israeli intelligence was among the "thousands of bits" considered during the years-long effort to find Usama bin Laden. He did not specify what Israel provided or how much it contributed to the operation.

A more recent exchange shows how Israeli reporting can prompt U.S. action even when its accuracy is uncertain. Israeli officials warned the U.S. of a possible Iranian plot to kill Trump during a trip to Turkey. The Secret Service took precautions, including moving him to another aircraft. U.S. intelligence agencies could not independently verify the threat, however, and the CIA assessed some of the Israeli reporting with "low confidence," according to Reuters and The Washington Post.

NETANYAHU REVEALS HE WANTS AMERICAN FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL TO 'DRAW DOWN TO ZERO'.

The financial relationship has also become part of the debate. Under the current agreement, the U.S. provides Israel with $3.3 billion annually in Foreign Military Financing and $500 million for joint missile-defense programs. Most of the military aid pays for weapons and services from U.S. contractors, according to CRS. Israel’s ability to spend a portion of the funding on domestic purchases is scheduled to phase out by 2028.

The report's authors call the $3.8 billion in annual U.S. military aid "one of the highest returns on investment of any U.S. foreign assistance.".

Sources indicate that trump has remarked he wants to end annual aid, while Netanyahu has also publicly called for phasing it out over time. U.S. and Israeli officials have been negotiating a new agreement that could wind down direct assistance while expanding joint defense projects and weapons production. The current agreement runs through 2028, Congress controls appropriations, and no successor deal has been reached.

TRUMP WANTS LARGEST-EVER ISRAELI HEAVY BOMB TRANSFER — BUT PROPOSAL HAS CONGRESS PREPARING FOR $2.8B FIGHT.

The Israeli Iron Dome air defense system fires to intercept missiles during an Iranian attack over Tel Aviv, Israel, early Wednesday, June 18, 2025. (AP Photo/Leo Correa).

The debate is also becoming more politically consequential as Americans question the relationship’s terms.

A 2026 Chicago Council survey found that 56% favored reducing or ending U.S. military aid to Israel. Republicans remain more supportive than Democrats and independents, but the right is divided: Joe Kent blamed Israeli pressure for the Iran war, Rep. Thomas Massie has pushed to cut aid, and Vice President JD Vance has called for changing the relationship while continuing to describe Israel as a strategic ally.

The two countries have cooperated against Iran and developed defenses against missile attacks, but their goals have not always matched during the war. A Stimson Center analysis indicates Israel sought to broaden the conflict beyond what Washington preferred. That does not establish that Israel drew the United States into a war it opposed. It does show how cooperation can leave Washington managing military costs even when its preferred limits differ from Israel’s.

According to recent reports, the next agreement will help determine whether the alliance continues to rely on direct grants or shifts toward joint weapons development and production. Either way, the military and intelligence cooperation described in the report comes with commitments of U.S. money and weapons — and leaves Washington weighing those costs against the advantages it expects the alliance to deliver.

#99668. Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3511 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BIEGUN was Deputy Secretary of State from December 2019 to January 2021 and Special Representative for North Korea from 2018 to 2021.
  • EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.
  • Donald Trump has Pyongyang on his mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

STEPHEN E. BIEGUN was Deputy Secretary of State from December 2019 to January 2021 and Special Representative for North Korea from 2018 to 2021. He is a Distinguished Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

And Now He Needs a New Strategy.

Stephen E. Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery.

Donald Trump has Pyongyang on his mind. In recent months, the U.S. president has made comments to the media suggesting he is in communication with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. In an August 17 Truth Social post, for instance, Trump confirmed that the United States would scale back joint military drills with South Korea. The decision, he wrote, was “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un,” describing the dictator as “unthreatening and respectful.”.

Sources indicate that trump has not been subtle about his desire to restart diplomacy with Kim. With an eye on his legacy and the war with Iran stalemated, he is eager to notch a foreign policy win. During his first term, Trump held two historic U.S.–North Korean summits aimed at denuclearizing the Korean Peninsula—but both foundered because of the countries’ disparate expectations for the terms of a deal. Since his reelection, Trump has been looking to reopen talks with Kim. The ball is now in Pyongyang’s court, and Kim has signaled, if not an eagerness for renewed engagement, at least an unwillingness to rule it out. In August, after Trump insisted for the second time that he was in touch with Pyongyang, Kim Yo Jong—the leader’s influential sister—released a statement that read: “Regarding the reports from Washington about recent communication between the top leaders of North Korea and the U.S., I am completely unaware of such matters. It has been stated on numerous occasions that our head of state holds fond personal memories and positive feelings toward Trump. The relationship between the leaders remains excellent.” Although this is far from an agreement to meet, Kim Jong Un is not closing the door.

According to recent reports, if leader-to-leader talks materialize, Trump may believe his personal rapport with Kim will yield a deal. But he will be facing a very different North Korea than the one at their last meeting in 2019. The fallout from unfinished diplomacy during Trump’s first term, the COVID-19 pandemic, and global trends such as the sharp escalation in U.S.-Chinese strategic rivalry and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have destabilized the security landscape and created formidable obstacles to peaceful engagement. Meanwhile, North Korea’s continued nuclear and conventional military expansion and the growing support it is receiving from Moscow have strengthened Kim’s hand. Facing an emboldened Pyongyang, Trump can no longer fall back on the same concessions and negotiation tactics he used in previous talks.

For a U.S.–North Korean summit to be successful, the United States must approach it with well-defined strategic goals and a clear understanding of what concessions it is willing to make. Washington should shift its focus away from denuclearization, at least in the short term, to concentrate on more achievable nuclear arms control and safety measures. The United States should also maintain a capable troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and reiterate its security assurances—particularly its nuclear-deterrence guarantees—to regional allies such as South Korea and Japan.

According to recent reports, although diplomacy with North Korea has historically been difficult, Trump is eager to meet with Kim, and both sides want to avoid pushing the Indo-Pacific toward nuclear proliferation or all-out war. Careful engagement with Pyongyang could defuse tensions on the Korean Peninsula and lay the groundwork for a more stable security landscape.

It has been revealed that since the U.S.–North Korean summit in 2019, the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have reshaped the Indo-Pacific in ways that strengthen Kim’s hand. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has drawn Washington’s focus away from Asia as, for the third time in the past quarter century, U.S. strategic attention and military assets have surged to the Middle East. The last American aircraft carrier stationed in the Indo-Pacific departed for the Persian Gulf in August, and U.S. strikes on Iran have rapidly depleted American munitions stockpiles. Washington’s Indo-Pacific allies, already strained by Trump’s abrupt policy shifts and punishing tariffs, are now concerned about deteriorating deterrence. Asian economies—many of which are deeply dependent on Middle Eastern energy supplies—have contracted as the Strait of Hormuz has remained compromised. Amid signs of further American retrenchment, U.S. allies and partners are increasingly skeptical about Washington’s commitment to the region.

Recent findings suggest that even more consequential is Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which has benefited North Korea in numerous ways. Moscow and Pyongyang’s once dormant relationship has flourished as Kim has sent thousands of munitions to replenish Russia’s depleted stockpiles and thousands of soldiers to fight and die in the ongoing ground war. Images of the new memorial to the Korean People’s Army soldiers who have perished in the invasion suggest an already significant loss of North Korean lives. In return, Pyongyang has received generous assistance from Moscow in violation of international sanctions, including abundant financial support for Kim’s regime and technology transfers that have enhanced North Korean military capabilities and may help Pyongyang more accurately deliver intercontinental ballistic missiles aimed at the United States. Russian patronage allows Kim to shower his regime’s elites with the economic benefits needed to cement their loyalty.

Still, it is worth questioning how durable this partnership is. After more than four years of grinding warfare with no end in sight, Moscow is increasingly isolated and may be in a poor position to continue supporting Pyongyang. Russia’s preoccupation with Ukraine has allowed China to expand its presence in Central Asia, for instance, and Turkey to deepen its influence in Azerbaijan. Russian aggression has spurred Armenia and Moldova to look westward, and hundreds of thousands of young Russian men have fled the country to avoid military conscription while over a thousand Western companies have left. International sanctions are starving Russia of badly needed capital and technology, and Russian war policies have created huge imbalances and inflation, possibly with worse to come for the Russian economy. If North Korea continues to actively support Moscow in this war, and Russia fails or is defeated, the world will become a much more hostile place for Pyongyang.

Russia and North Korea’s deepening ties have already begun to reshape China’s interests in the region. Beijing is still Pyongyang’s most important partner, but the dynamic has changed considerably in recent years. Beijing previously saw denuclearization as a top priority on the Korean Peninsula—a shared objective, and at times a rare area of cooperation, with the United States. It disliked the destabilizing impact that North Korea’s pursuit of nuclear weapons had on tensions between the North and South and expended political capital responding to international condemnation of Pyongyang. Between 2006 and 2017, Beijing agreed to a series of UN Security Council resolutions that imposed sanctions and other restrictions on Pyongyang in response to six North Korean nuclear tests. Now, pressed to maintain its influence in Pyongyang amid a growing Russian–North Korean security relationship—and with the rest of the world distracted by other geopolitical crises—China has gone silent on the matter. When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June to reassert his influence, denuclearization was not publicly mentioned. China’s upcoming approach will make U.S. engagement on this issue more challenging and risks driving other regional powers, such as South Korea and Japan, to reconsider their own policies on the deployment or development of nuclear weapons.

Whether Pyongyang reengages with the United States may also depend on how much North Korea relies on China for economic support. Much of North Korean commerce passes through China, and although Beijing and Pyongyang’s relationship appears fairly stable, it remains wary and transactional, with each side skeptical of the other’s motives. North Korea may seek to reengage with the United States to counterbalance its overdependence on China, or as a hedge against Russia’s failure in its war with Ukraine. Conversely, as Trump and Xi upgrade and stabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, China could step in to broker the next Trump-Kim meeting.

Industry observers note that the Kim dynasty has long vexed U.S. policymakers. Washington has sought multiple deals with North Korea, including during Trump’s first-term summits with Kim, but missteps and mistrust on both sides derailed them. Pyongyang has proved resilient to both U.S. and international sanctions. Indeed, during the COVID-19 pandemic, North Korea sealed its borders and deprived itself far more severely than sanctions could, yet it still survived. U.S. congressional interventions on human rights and humanitarian aid, meanwhile, have mostly failed to change North Korea’s behavior. Pyongyang has also cushioned the impact of sanctions by engaging in cybertheft, such as its $6.3 billion heist against the cryptocurrency exchange Binance this October. All the while, Pyongyang has steadily advanced its military capabilities and expanded its nuclear arsenal.

Recent findings suggest that although Washington’s previous attempts to rein in North Korea have failed, Trump’s renewed eagerness to meet with Kim and his unorthodox approach to foreign policy could provide a newly introduced opening for diplomacy. Trump has cultivated a direct relationship with Kim, shunning the bureaucratic negotiations that usually precede a deal. While a performative summit alone would be of little benefit to U.S. interests, Washington could use reengagement with Pyongyang to thaw inter-Korean relations and stabilize the peninsula by slowing or freezing North Korea’s nuclear buildup. Those goals may seem conventional, but as regional tensions worsen and Pyongyang’s nuclear arsenal grows, they are essential to averting potentially catastrophic conflict.

Three questions cast a shadow over the possibility of renewed engagement between the United States and North Korea. First is the specific purpose of restarting engagement: What is the goal? Second is how to reopen communications. Despite Trump’s claims, there is no real proof that he has recently interacted with Kim. All evidence suggests the last contact between American and North Korean officials was in 2019, and it may be challenging to break a seven-year drought. Third is what are the incentives and tradeoffs the United States would be willing to consider as part of a negotiation—the same problem that bedeviled U.S. and North Korean officials in Hanoi.

It has been revealed that one possible formula for progress is focusing, at least temporarily, on steady arms control and international safety controls rather than the elusive goal of denuclearization. Denuclearization should remain Washington’s ultimate aspiration. But in the meantime, a North Korea awash with even more nuclear weapons makes the world only more dangerous. This approach will require serious diplomacy to minimize second-order consequences, particularly to avoid weakening U.S. alliances in the Indo-Pacific or triggering a collapse of the nuclear nonproliferation regime among nations that might see their only recourse as acquiring their own nuclear weapons. China, and perhaps even Russia, may concur with Washington on this point, and a shared desire to avoid more nuclear states in East Asia could help restart engagement.

Industry observers note that kim has substantially more leverage now than in earlier encounters with Trump. Reopening communication will require using a mix of positive and negative assurances to convince him that he is unlikely to get a better chance to strike a deal. Kim may press the United States to scale back aspects of its cooperation with South Korea—such as joint military exercises and support for Seoul’s pursuit of nuclear-powered submarines—as preconditions for a meeting with Trump. Kim may even propose his own assurances of peace on the peninsula in exchange for a reduction of U.S. military forces in South Korea, although it is unclear whether Trump would agree to such conditions.

In the worst-case scenario, Kim may take advantage of Trump’s eagerness to make a deal to extract weighty concessions from the United States. Kim has little reason to meet with Trump now, unless he calculates that he can secure major terms such as de facto recognition as a nuclear state, reduced sanctions, or a complete withdrawal of U.S. troops from the peninsula. Kim would likely insist that there be no discussion of denuclearization, North Korea’s support for the invasion of Ukraine, Pyongyang’s human rights abuses, or a final accounting for Japanese citizens kidnapped by North Korea under the rule of Kim Il Sung. Granting such concessions would end the U.S.–South Korean alliance.

Industry observers note that to ensure North Korea does not exploit the Trump administration, Washington must carefully consider what tradeoffs it is willing to make. Lifting sanctions, abandoning or delaying the denuclearization process, temporarily accepting North Korea as a nuclear state, and reducing the U.S. military presence in South Korea are all long-standing demands of Kim’s regime that are likely on the table. Although lifting international sanctions would require UN Security Council consensus, Trump may be willing to reduce unilateral U.S. sanctions, which he considers an obstacle to better bilateral relations and which have been ineffective in stemming Pyongyang’s nuclear advances.

Although denuclearization has been a major talking point for U.S. administrations since the early 1990s, the Trump administration may need to set it aside, at least in the short term. Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities have increased since Trump’s 2018 and 2019 summits with Kim, suggesting that the stalemate caused by continued U.S. demands for the full-scale dismantlement of North Korea’s nuclear program may have given Kim time and space to grow his arsenal. Even if denuclearization remains a long-term U.S. priority—and it should—pragmatism is essential to reducing the threat posed by Kim’s regime. In exchange for stepping away from denuclearization, Trump should demand that Kim freeze any further expansion of his arsenal and explore possibilities for greater strategic stability, including renewed inter-Korean dialogue, transparency and confidence-building efforts, security measures that bolster nuclear facilities’ safety and guard against accidents, and strict adherence to nonproliferation. Trump must make it clear to Kim that an unconstrained expansion of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal will pressure South Korea and Japan to deploy nuclear weapons on their territory and possibly develop their own.

Regardless of Kim’s demands, the United States must preserve its troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and continue joint military exercises with South Korea as long as the threat of North Korean aggression persists. The mantra of U.S. troops in South Korea is “ready to fight tonight.” Joint military exercises keep U.S. and South Korean forces prepared for combat, which is essential to deterring North Korean attacks. It would be dangerous and irresponsible to send American soldiers, sailors, marines, and airmen to the peninsula without ensuring peak readiness. Instead of withdrawing troops, the United States should offer confidence-building measures to North Korea—practices that reduce the risk of conflict breaking out because of misjudgment. These could include military-to-military engagement and security reassurances among the United States, South Korea, and North Korea, or greater transparency around military exercises—allowing observers on a reciprocal basis, for example. Sustaining Washington’s alliance with South Korea and avoiding cascading nuclear proliferation are critical to U.S. interests in the region. American negotiators must remind Kim that the U.S. military presence and its extended nuclear-deterrence guarantees for Seoul and Tokyo hold back even larger conventional military—and possibly nuclear—buildups in the region.

Finally, North Korea and the United States—and perhaps, in time, South Korea and Japan—should sustain diplomatic engagement by agreeing to assign diplomats to each other’s capitals through reciprocal liaison offices, which would maintain relations without granting full diplomatic recognition. In 2018 and 2019, the two sides discussed housing such diplomats in the German Embassy in Pyongyang and the Swedish Embassy in Washington. Liaison offices would also stabilize and prolong the communication necessary to quietly work through complex negotiations.

Recent findings suggest that if North Korea rejects Trump’s overtures, the United States is not without options. Washington could pressure the Kim regime by intensifying the scale and tempo of joint military exercises with South Korea; deploying American armaments, including short-range ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and possibly nuclear weapons, to South Korea and Japan; and pursuing a upcoming campaign to choke off North Korea’s economic resources through sanctions and interdiction. The United States could also deploy additional air defense assets to Japan and South Korea, including THAAD air defense radar systems and interceptors. Washington and its allies could dramatically expand efforts to undermine Kim’s rule by mounting sustained criticisms of North Korea’s dangerously large nuclear weapons arsenal and its use of international criminal enterprise to steal from and economically defraud other nations, which could spur other countries to curb their material or diplomatic support for North Korea or more aggressively sanction Kim’s regime.

Beyond short-term negotiations, a fourth question is less complicated but just as important: What role should Japan and South Korea play in U.S. engagements with North Korea? Many past administrations, both Republican and Democratic, have considered coordination with allies essential to establishing a durable solution on the Korean Peninsula. But Trump’s antipathy toward alliances suggests close consultation with South Korea and Japan is unlikely. Their absence from the negotiating table may actually accelerate U.S.–North Korean engagement, because coordination across allied governments can be unwieldy and slow, and Pyongyang has not been receptive to past overtures by Seoul and Tokyo. Although South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi both rhetorically back engagement with North Korea, Pyongyang has bluntly rejected their outreach.

Industry observers note that even if Seoul and Tokyo are not directly engaged in U.S.–North Korean diplomacy, they would still likely welcome a U.S.-led deal with Kim if it protects their core security interests. But a deal with Kim that ignores American allies’ concerns would be dangerous. South Korea harbors an appetite to develop its own nuclear arsenal, particularly if it feels U.S. security protections are receding. Should Seoul move in that direction, Tokyo would almost certainly reconsider its own nonnuclear status, potentially igniting a nuclear arms race in Asia. Given North Korea’s long-standing hostility toward both Japan and South Korea, proliferation would destabilize the Indo-Pacific and leave the global nonproliferation regime in tatters.

Any deal, even one that addresses Seoul’s and Tokyo’s core interests, will likely need to be paired with American security reassurances to allies’ governments and publics. Japan and South Korea must continue building their own conventional defense capabilities while the United States sustains its commitment to defending its Asian allies—especially extended nuclear deterrence. The United States must pursue delicate, nuanced diplomacy to avoid creating a stronger, legitimized North Korea; straining its alliances with Seoul and Tokyo; and debilitating the international nonproliferation regime.

According to recent reports, despite the risks of U.S.–North Korean engagement, the time may be ripe to break the diplomatic paralysis that has allowed Pyongyang to advance its military capabilities for so long. The last two years of Trump’s presidency—particularly his summitry calendar in late 2026—will bring him to Asia, potentially facilitating a meeting with Kim. Such a visit would present the best chance for the kind of performative, high-profile meeting that both Trump and Kim favor.

Trump is the ultimate iconoclast in traditional great-power politics, as evidenced by his shifting relationships with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which could shape Washington’s engagement with Pyongyang. Still, there may be a way to leverage Trump’s affection for Kim, and Kim’s recent restraint in criticizing the United States, to outline a deal that arrests the growing threat of North Korean nuclear weapons.

The bruising Republican defeat in the U.S. midterm elections could also change North Korea’s diplomatic calculus, especially because it suggests Trump’s political standing in the United States has faltered, and he may struggle to deliver the results Kim seeks. Trump may force the issue, however, and propose a meeting with Kim after the November Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China. It would not be surprising for Trump to suggest that this meeting take place in Pyongyang, putting Kim on the spot. If leader-to-leader talks occur, both sides should remember the central lesson from Trump’s first-term summits: engagement without sufficient preparation and clearly defined goals is not enough to strengthen security and stability on the Korean Peninsula.

In a recent development, growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific raise the prospect of a much darker future, where conditions on the Korean Peninsula remain unchanged and Asia’s entanglements in European and Middle Eastern conflicts metastasize into a new world war—perhaps ignited in Taiwan, the South China Sea, or the Korean Peninsula. Even if no war breaks out, in just a few years the United States could find itself in a world where Asia’s five current nuclear states are joined by two, three, or more new players.

But this future is not inevitable. All the leaders engaged in North Korean security debates—from Lee and Takaichi to Xi and Putin—want to avoid such escalation. Even the North Koreans surely recognize this is the most dangerous path. This shared goal means diplomacy is still possible, despite formidable challenges. For all Trump’s idiosyncrasies, one should take his desire to peacefully end tensions on the Korean Peninsula at face value. He has made his intentions clear. What happens next is up to Chairman Kim.

Ronald Reagan Changed His Chief of Staff After a Midterm Trouncing, Too

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA.
  • While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.
  • President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA. Among his first major acts after the blue wave was replacing his trusted chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller. Few moves could have signaled more clearly that Trump the fighter was not going to give way to Trump the conciliator. Because the White House chief of staff is often considered the second most powerful position in Washington, the choice carries particular weight. Miller has been seen as one of the most influential voices in Trump 2.0, if not the most influential. He has been the driving force behind an extraordinarily expansive view of presidential power: targeting what the administration considers opposition institutions such as law firms, the media, and universities; launching a sweeping detention and deportation program; imposing a tariff program that rocked the national economy; and making aggressive moves in Latin America that have included striking boats allegedly transporting illegal narcotics.

While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.

President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA. Among his first major acts after the blue wave was replacing his trusted chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller. Few moves could have signaled more clearly that Trump the fighter was not going to give way to Trump the conciliator. Because the White House chief of staff is often considered the second most powerful position in Washington, the choice carries particular weight. Miller has been seen as one of the most influential voices in Trump 2.0, if not the most influential. He has been the driving force behind an extraordinarily expansive view of presidential power: targeting what the administration considers opposition institutions such as law firms, the media, and universities; launching a sweeping detention and deportation program; imposing a tariff program that rocked the national economy; and making aggressive moves in Latin America that have included striking boats allegedly transporting illegal narcotics.

While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.

In a recent development, but that’s not how Miller thinks, nor has it been Trump’s instinct. The Miller appointment stands in sharp contrast to the personnel change that then-President Ronald Reagan, the founding father of the conservative movement, made after the 1986 midterms and the scandal that broke out soon after. That year, Democrats regained control of the Senate (they had held the House since 1955), and the administration was embroiled in a major scandal that some Democrats believed could reach Watergate-like levels.

According to recent reports, the contrast between these two presidents reveals just how far Republican politics has radicalized since the 1980s. It is also a warning sign for Republicans who understand that, without a major course correction, the very same party that was celebrating a upcoming governing coalition in 2024 might be on a self-destructive path. The GOP is in the grip of a strong leader who is not particularly interested in the long-term health of the party that brought him to the White House.

Industry observers note that reagan was not enjoying a good political moment in November 1986, though his presidency had been riding high until then. His first term was highly successful, featuring a historic supply-side tax cut and a vast acceleration of defense spending. He had defeated his opponent, former Vice President Walter Mondale, in a landslide victory in 1984. His approval ratings had been strong, and the economy had recovered from the malaise of the 1970s. In October 1986, Reagan signed bipartisan tax reform legislation that closed loopholes benefiting some of the nation’s most powerful interests, and he held a historic summit with the latest Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev.

But then came the 1986 midterms. Democrats gained five seats in the House, expanding their majority to 258, and, more importantly, retook control of the Senate by gaining eight seats. Their 55-seat majority ended the brief period of Republican control that had started with the 1980 election. The outcome was seen as a rebuke of the harsher edges of U.S. conservatism, as well the heightened tension with the Soviet Union that a hawkish Reagan had helped spur, despite two summits with Gorbachev. Indeed, the summit just weeks before voting in Reykjavik, Iceland, had broken down because the president refused to give up on his strategy to build a missile shield around the United States, the Strategic Defense Initiative (which opponents dismissed as “star wars”). Soon after the election, Reagan’s problems deepened as news spread that a Lebanese magazine had reported that the United States had been secretly selling weapons to Iran.

It has been revealed that one of Reagan’s most significant moves in early 1987 was to replace his highly controversial chief of staff, Donald Regan. A former Marine and chairman of Merrill Lynch, Regan had been an vital part of the Reagan administration since January 1981. As secretary of the Treasury, he had been instrumental in passing the 1981 tax cut. In February 1985, he became chief of staff, replacing James Baker (who replaced him at Treasury). Regan proved to be a forceful presence. He centralized control and pushed the president’s program in a highly aggressive and abrasive fashion that angered colleagues in the White House, as well as on Capitol Hill. The media did not find him very pleasant to work with, while first lady Nancy Reagan didn’t trust that he prioritized her husband’s interests.

In a recent development, with Regan by his side, Reagan’s first public response to what became the Iran-Contra scandal was defiance, which reflected his chief of staff’s approach to most issues. On Nov. 13, Reagan went on television to insist that there was nothing serious to investigate. While acknowledging that the White House had sold a small amount of “defensive” weapons to Iran as part of a major diplomatic initiative to build ties with moderates within the regime and combat terrorism, he denied that the United States had traded arms for hostages, or that the sales amounted to anything significant. Polls revealed that the public was unconvinced that the president was telling the whole truth. Then, on Nov. 25, the other shoe dropped: Attorney General Edwin Meese declared that profits from the weapons sales had been diverted to the anti-communist Nicaraguan Contras, despite the Boland Amendments’ congressional ban on such aid.

Privately, administration officials feared where the investigations were headed. For a generation that had watched Richard Nixon resign over Watergate just 12 years earlier, the possibility of impeachment seemed real. Reagan’s aides also understood that many voters had been shaped by those same memories, and were deeply distrustful of government officials and still insistent on a political system that could hold them accountable.

On Feb. 26, 1987, the president’s Special Review Board, a commission appointed by Reagan in November and headed by former Texas Sen. John Tower, issued its report on the Iran scandal. It blamed a chaotic management system that had allowed the arms sales and the diversion of funds to proceed, faulting Reagan’s leadership style and singling out Regan for failing to impose order on the White House. The next day, Regan resigned after learning that he was about to be relieved of his duties.

At this fraught moment, the president turned to Howard Baker.

Sources indicate that the 61-year-old, mild-mannered Republican had served in the Senate from 1967 to 1985, the last four years as majority leader, and was respected on both sides of the aisle. He had been mentored by Senate Minority Leader Everett Dirksen (who was also his father-in-law), who taught him the ways and means of the legislative process and the art of bipartisan deal-making. Baker had gained national fame during the 1973 Watergate hearings by asking, “What did the president know and when did he know it?” Known as a moderate and an institutionalist, Baker was a selection widely seen as Reagan’s recognition that, with Democrats now controlling both chambers, he needed to build bridges to Capitol Hill rather than burn them. “I’d probably take some lumps from our right wingers but I can handle that,” Reagan noted in his diary, of appointing Baker.

Though Baker had actually been the third choice for chief of staff, he helped bring stability to the White House and guided the president through the Iran-Contra scandal. He brought in a first-rate team of advisors who improved relations with Congress, the press, and the first lady. Reagan biographers credit Baker with helping Reagan survive the scandal as the revelations mounted during the 1987 congressional hearings. He played a key role in brokering a budget deal with Congress after the October 1987 stock market crash and securing Senate ratification of the INF Treaty with the Soviet Union in May 1988. His tenure also had setbacks, most notably the Senate’s rejection of Robert Bork’s nomination to the Supreme Court. But his pragmatic outlook helped Reagan recover from the low of the 1986 midterms. “You always leave yourself a backdoor, a side door, and a trapdoor,” he liked to say, quoting something his father used to tell him. According to a longtime aide, that meant: “You don’t talk in absolutes. You don’t want to get yourself boxed in where you can’t maneuver.”.

Overall, Reagan and the first lady had reason to be pleased with Baker’s work: The president left office with high approval ratings—and helped bring an end to the Cold War.

Sources indicate that today’s Republican Party is not your grandfather’s Republican Party, and the recent midterms suggested that much of the electorate is not happy with it. The reach of the Democratic victories into deeply red parts of the country, including Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas, and Kansas, suggests that the onetime party of Lincoln has a major problem on its hands. Part of that problem is the president himself, who after further radicalizing the GOP to its electoral detriment, shows few signs that he will change course in ways that could strengthen the party that brought him to the dance.

With Miller as chief of staff, Trump is assuring voters that there will be more of the same style of politics and the same political agenda—leaving the Democratic Party with the kind of political prospects for united government that seemed impossible just a few months ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GORDON LIAO is Chief Economist at Circle.

ESWAR PRASAD is a Professor at Cornell University, a Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution, and the author of The Doom Loop: Why the World Economic Order Is Spiraling Into Disorder.

TONY ZHANG is an Associate Professor at Arizona State University.

This article is based on a paper the authors prepared for the August 2026 Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium.

How Technology Is—and Isn’t—Changing the Global Economy.

Gordon Liao, Eswar Prasad, and Tony Zhang.

It is no secret that much of the world is eager to escape from the clutches of the dollar-dominated global financial system. For over a century, that system has given the United States enormous financial clout, which it has wielded in applying financial sanctions against its adversaries and, in recent decades, to borrow money to fund its budget and trade deficits. For decades, foreign governments have tried to weaken the dollar’s grip, but they have had little success in establishing their currencies as a legitimate alternative.

It has been revealed that now, a new force has emerged that could shake things up: technology. Financial innovations, especially in digital currencies and electronic payment systems, could finally give other currencies a better chance of competing with the dollar. These innovations are making it easier and cheaper to exchange currencies directly for one another rather than using the dollar as an intermediary currency.

In a recent development, but for all the latest opportunities these innovations create for currency exchange, reduced frictions in global transactions might only reinforce the dollar’s dominance. Even if costs decrease for using dollar alternatives, foreign investors will not capitalize on them if those countries’ financial markets remain unsteady and their institutions weak. As U.S. government debt soars, the country’s rule of law erodes, and the Federal Reserve’s independence comes into question, the dollar’s dominance may seem uncertain. But the dollar could remain supreme by default.

Recent findings suggest that continued dollar dominance could lead to further global economic turmoil, as the United States antagonizes its trading partners and persists with undisciplined policies that result in large budget deficits and trade deficits. There is a chance that the dollar, too, loses the trust of foreign investors—a prospect of comeuppance that would no doubt be received with glee in many capitals. But governments should be careful what they wish for. A world bereft of a reliable currency of last resort at times of global financial panic could be even more unstable than one dominated by Washington.

The U.S. dollar should be losing its dominance in global finance for a host of reasons. First is the country’s penchant for weaponizing its currency. Across administrations, Washington has imposed financial sanctions on rivals, such as Iran and Russia, cutting off their access to dollar transactions and thereby kneecapping their foreign trade. The economies of U.S. allies sometimes get tangled up in these sanctions, too, when the U.S. government threatens to use secondary sanctions to cut off their banks and corporations from access to dollars in order to deter third parties from transacting with the sanctioned countries. In 2014, for instance, U.S. authorities penalized the French bank BNP Paribas for processing dollar payments on behalf of clients in Cuba, Iran, and Sudan. The French government protested the fine to no avail. In light of such heavy-handed behavior, government officials and central bankers outside the United States have hardly been shy about their intentions to reduce their dollar dependence.

Washington’s broader policy choices, especially the lack of fiscal discipline, should also be undermining confidence in American financial markets. U.S. federal government debt now exceeds $40 trillion, nearly 125 percent of the country’s annual GDP, and there are scant signs that Washington is trying to rein it in. Such high debt levels usually lead to some combination of high inflation, soaring interest expenditures, and currency depreciation. The Trump administration’s hostile approach to international trade, including with close allies, is also causing governments to consider “de-risking” their economic ties to the United States. President Donald Trump’s open attacks on the independence of the Federal Reserve and weakening of checks and balances are eroding the pillars of the U.S. institutional system that underlies foreign investors’ trust in the dollar.

Sources indicate that and indeed, there are some signs of the dollar’s decline. The currency’s share of foreign exchange reserves held by foreign central banks has fallen from 71 percent in 2000 to 57 percent today. Yields on U.S. Treasury securities—the asset long seen as the ultimate safe haven for investors during financial turmoil—have risen, meaning investors are demanding a higher return for lending to the U.S. government. In October, the yield on ten-year Treasury notes hit 5.3 percent, the highest level since 2002.

In a recent development, in most other dimensions, however, the dollar looks as dominant as ever. Sixty percent of cross-border transactions are denominated in dollars when excluding the eurozone, which is defined by the common use of the euro, and that number has only gone up in recent years. The euro’s share of cross-border payments outside the eurozone now stands at about 13 percent, and the renminbi’s is less than three percent. The dollar remains preeminent in most other measures of a currency’s international usage, too, including its share of trading activity in foreign exchange markets and denomination of international debt securities, which corporations use to raise funds in global capital markets.

Recent findings suggest that in short, no serious rivals to the dollar have emerged. The reason is simple: other major currencies look even shakier than the dollar. Traditional reserve currencies such as the euro, the yen, and the pound sterling have been undermined by their countries’ weak economies and political instability. Although currencies such as the Australian and Canadian dollars, the Swedish krona, and the Swiss franc have filled in some of the gap, each of these is too small to be consequential in global finance. The dollar’s most discussed putative rival, the renminbi, has also faded. Beijing has done little to alleviate the Chinese economy’s deep-rooted problems, including a prolonged property market slump, high levels of local government debt, and tight government control over the economy and financial markets. Moreover, the Chinese government has been unwilling to allow for the free flow of money across its borders or for market forces to determine its currency’s exchange rate. The renminbi has, in turn, failed to garner greater international use. The result is a second tier of currencies that is increasingly fragmented, with none able to pose any real challenge to the reigning currency hegemon.

In the era of modern financial markets, one of the main purposes of an international currency has been to facilitate indirect transactions among different currencies. It has long been easier and cheaper for a Chinese importer of Brazilian iron ore to exchange renminbi for dollars and pay for the ore in dollars and for the Brazilian exporter to then convert those dollars into Brazilian reais. This is because cross-border payments have long been dominated by a dollar-based global banking network, making dollars the most plentiful currency to conduct payments with. But in recent years, digital technologies have created cheaper and quicker pathways for moving money across borders.

Sources indicate that one critical innovation has been the tokenization of money and financial assets, which has been facilitated by technology called blockchain. Blockchain, essentially a public digital ledger that is managed by a computer algorithm rather than by a single bank or clearinghouse, offers a platform for tokenized assets to trade. It does not matter which country the parties are located in, as long as they have Internet access. In the last few years, tokenization has expanded to include not just cash but also financial assets such as government bonds, equities, and mutual funds.

It has been revealed that in theory, these changes have the potential to reshuffle the international currency order. Over the past few years, countries such as Brazil, China, India, and Russia have been conducting more trade in their own currencies by building their own cross-border payment networks and linking them to one another, in an effort to reduce their reliance on the dollar. The quantity of these transactions is still modest, because the currencies have limited use outside their countries, and it is still easier and cheaper to transact in a well-recognized and widely accepted currency such as the dollar. But as the countries’ payment systems and financial markets develop further, that number could increase dramatically, altering the currency landscape. Blockchain-based financial innovations could add momentum.

It has been revealed that cross-border investment could become much easier, too. Presently, investing in foreign securities involves going through brokers and other middlemen who demand hefty fees and take days to process transactions. But the tokenization of bonds and equities has expanded investors’ access to a broader swath of international financial assets, even in emerging-market and developing economies, where financial markets tend to be small, thinly traded, and not well connected to global trading networks. In the same way, it has expanded the access of entrepreneurs and small businesses to global pools of capital previously out of their reach, which could particularly help businesses in countries with underdeveloped financial markets. Bank deposits are likely to be available in tokenized form soon, too, which will make it easier to conduct transactions through more traditional payment channels.

But the spread of tokenization might strengthen the dollar’s dominance rather than weaken it. The example of stablecoins illustrates this paradox. Whereas cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin are created and distributed by a computer algorithm, meaning they have nothing anchoring their value, the value of a stablecoin is typically pegged to an official currency. This value is stable because it is backed one to one by stores of safe and liquid assets—usually government bonds, bank deposits, and cash. Those assets are usually denominated in the dollar. More than $250 billion in stablecoins is now in circulation, and over 99 percent of that value is tied to the dollar. As long as the dollar remains preeminent, investors will have little incentive to back stablecoins with any other currency.

Recent findings suggest that dollar-denominated stablecoins are a boon for the United States. By solidifying the dollar’s central position in international payments, rising demand for dollar-backed stablecoins also indirectly fuels demand for Treasury securities, lowering the yields the U.S. government has to offer investors to buy those securities and making it easier to fund U.S. budget deficits. Other payment innovations could make it even cheaper to use the dollar for cross-border transactions, minimizing the relative advantage that such innovations provide other currencies. Financial innovations built on new technologies cannot by themselves make up for other currencies’ existing weaknesses—namely, the weak economies and institutions that back them up.

Sources indicate that there is another major shift underway in the global economy that favors the dollar’s fortunes and that financial innovations are likely only to reinforce. In the first two decades of this century, central banks—particularly those of large emerging-market economies such as China and India—acquired vast troves of foreign assets denominated in hard currencies such as the euro, pound sterling, Japanese yen, and, most of all, the dollar to increase their foreign exchange reserves. These reserves helped those central banks cope with volatility in capital flows and exchange rates, which is a recurring hazard for countries that fall in and out of favor with foreign investors—often because of factors beyond their control, such as changes in U.S. interest rates. But in the last few years, central banks have stopped adding to their reserve stockpiles or have begun diversifying into other assets, such as gold, because they are reluctant to increase their investments in a country with fickle economic and geopolitical policies. In 2010, foreign central banks accounted for 70 percent of U.S. Treasuries held by foreign investors, a share that has dropped to about 40 percent as demand has leveled off. The retreat of these once reliable sources of demand threatens Washington’s ability to borrow cheaply.

Luckily for the United States, there is an alternative force that is more than making up for this loss in demand. As the costs to cross-border asset trade fall because of financial innovations, private investors from both advanced and emerging-market countries are increasing their foreign investments in search of higher returns and to diversify their portfolios. And they are flocking to dollar assets, from Treasuries to corporate bonds to equities, because U.S. financial markets offer an unmatched combination of good returns, low trading costs, and legal protections. In the present decade, net inflows of financial capital into the United States have been positive for practically every quarter. Despite chatter about de-risking and diversification since Trump’s election, these inflows have only ramped up in recent years.

Greater financial innovation will intensify rather than reverse these trends, delivering yet another blow to countries seeking to strengthen their currencies and counter dollar weaponization. These trends may hurt small and institutionally weak countries most of all. Those around the world who have long trusted the dollar more than their own currencies now have easier access to it—and they are likely to use it. Increased use of dollar-backed payment systems and investments in dollar assets could cause those countries to cede their monetary sovereignty, weakening their central banks’ ability to steer domestic interest rates and inflation. This phenomenon of “dollarization” has long been rampant in parts of Latin America, which have suffered repeated bouts of high inflation and which, through trade, tourism, and remittances from emigrants, have ready access to dollar cash. Financial innovation could also spread that phenomenon to other corners of the developing world, concentrating even more of the world’s savings—and its financial risks—in a single currency managed by a single central bank.

It has been revealed that in theory, the best, most stable international monetary system would be truly multipolar, with no single currency in a position of dominance but with several major currencies—each backed by deep financial markets, sound economic policies, and trustworthy institutions—anchoring international trade and finance. In the period before World War I, the British pound sterling, the French franc, and the German mark all denominated transactions and served as reserve currencies. When trouble struck, although sporadically, the countries’ central banks supported one another, helping to stave off broader financial panic. Renewed currency competition would force the competing governments, including the United States, to adopt responsible policies to avoid their currencies being shunned by investors. But given the economic and institutional malaise plaguing China, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the eurozone, such an outcome seems unlikely.

If the dollar loses its position of privilege and no single currency is able to replace it, the global currency system will become even more fragmented than it is now. Such a scenario could unfold if U.S. debt grew so large that investors began doubting its value and dumped it, if additional sanctions and tariffs drove countries to shun the dollar despite the costs, or if the Fed’s independence were seriously compromised, leading to a surge in inflation and a plunge in the dollar’s value. As things stand, if the dollar lost its position of privilege, it would be replaced not by a handful of strong currencies but by a number of weak ones, none backed by sufficiently robust financial markets or a central bank able and willing to serve as the world’s lender of last resort during a crisis.

If the global economic system has no currency to anchor global investors’ trust, stress in financial markets could spiral into unstoppable turmoil. During the global financial crisis of 2008–9, for example, the Fed pumped a huge number of dollars into U.S. and international financial markets to prop up banks and corporations around the world that desperately needed dollars to meet their debt obligations and reinforce their balance sheets. Even though the United States had been the epicenter of the crisis, trust in the Fed helped prevent a terrible situation from becoming even worse. Investors who were anxious about the safety of their assets piled into Treasuries, an investment they trusted would be returned.

Greater dollar dominance, then, is the most likely scenario for the future. The danger of this outcome is that the United States will have even less incentive than before to be more fiscally responsible. If foreign investors remain eager to invest in U.S. financial markets, Washington will have little reason to reduce its budget and trade deficits. Fed policies, including interest rate changes, could cause whiplash effects for other countries. In 2013, for example, the mere prospect of the Fed reducing measures to keep U.S. interest rates low sent currencies in Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey tumbling because investors around the world began anticipating higher returns on U.S. assets and pulled their money out of those countries’ stocks and bonds. As capital flows in and out of markets in response to the Fed’s actions rather than in response to their own monetary policy, other countries could be left bereft of policy tools to stabilize their economies and financial markets in such a scenario. Emerging-market and developing economies, which have shallow financial markets and rely heavily on foreign borrowing, often in dollars, are especially vulnerable to volatile capital flows and exchange rates. In a world of greater dollar dominance, those countries could face more frequent currency crises, capital flight, and debt distress.

Sources indicate that as disconcerting as the dollar’s continued preeminence might seem, however, the world needs a currency it can trust. As threats to international financial stability accelerate, financial markets can ill afford to be left adrift. One way or another, the world will have to learn to live with currency disorder, and the dollar, at least for now, is the least bad option.

The Democratic Party’s Three Conflicting Camps on AI

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Industry observers note that one way to read the tea leaves on the recent U.S. midterms is that, at long last, Washington gets serious about regulating artificial intelligence; the unchecked build-out of those wildly unpopular data centers is reconsidered; Massive Tech is held to account; and the United States becomes not just the most advanced AI power but also the more trustworthy AI power. But if you were expecting that the electoral “techlash” would lead to coherent AI governance, policy, and statecraft, then prepare to be disappointed. The more likely outcome is that we shall live with two more years of muddied U.S. technology policy at home and abroad, with one clear winner: Beijing.

For while Democrats did benefit from the promise of checking AI growth, and they now own the legislative machinery, the party must balance three competing impulses: to rein in AI, to ride the AI-led economic momentum and avoid economy-wide slowdowns before the 2028 elections, and to avoid ceding the AI leadership to China.

One way to read the tea leaves on the recent U.S. midterms is that, at long last, Washington gets serious about regulating artificial intelligence; the unchecked build-out of those wildly unpopular data centers is reconsidered; Major Tech is held to account; and the United States becomes not just the most advanced AI power but also the more trustworthy AI power. But if you were expecting that the electoral “techlash” would lead to coherent AI governance, policy, and statecraft, then prepare to be disappointed. The more likely outcome is that we shall live with two more years of muddied U.S. technology policy at home and abroad, with one clear winner: Beijing.

For while Democrats did benefit from the promise of checking AI growth, and they now own the legislative machinery, the party must balance three competing impulses: to rein in AI, to ride the AI-led economic momentum and avoid economy-wide slowdowns before the 2028 elections, and to avoid ceding the AI leadership to China.

To make gnarly matters more tangled, U.S. AI’s central player, Nvidia, has lost its co-founder and CEO over an alleged Chinese intelligence operation, scrambling all three impulses. And we should also remember that over at the White House, a bruised but belligerent Trump retains the executive levers and the veto—as well as an impulse to stymie whatever the Democrats wish to demonstrate as a “win” to the American public.

Before we get to Trump, though, let’s first consider what drives each of the camps in the Democratic coalition.

Industry observers note that the first camp can be thought of as the Restrainers. They want to check the proliferation of data centers while holding AI executives to account for independent testing of advanced models—and holding the companies liable for harm.

Midterm voters rewarded candidates in this camp, who pushed back on a sense that AI development was proceeding unchecked; Sherrod Brown won back an Ohio Senate seat with ads calling his opponent “the face of AI data centers,” while Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan also won races with opposition to data centers as a key element of their campaign platforms. In nine states, governors and governors-elect, too, have promised or imposed a pause on new data centers, stalling an estimated 41 percent of the country’s data center pipeline. Meanwhile, right after the elections, veteran Sen. Bernie Sanders called for a national data center moratorium.

Sources indicate that while slowing down AI would be the most readily available and popular move by lawmakers, the Restrainers still have to get their house in order. They will need to prioritize the many risks and concerns around AI and focus their limited time on the most significant ones. Weighing these will not be easy. A household worried about its power bill, for instance, needs a different intervention compared with a parent who doesn’t want their child left alone with a chatbot.

Industry observers note that A second camp is made up of the Riders. They have their eye on the economy and want to ensure that AI investments keep carrying U.S. growth, the stock market, and household retirement savings. AI has propped up the American economy in recent years; letting the air out of that balloon could produce a bust, a recession, and shrinking retirement accounts, which could be bad news come 2028 if voters lay the blame on Congress.

Recent findings suggest that the sharp Nov. 5 reminder about the connection between AI growth and stock market growth is hard to ignore—right after the midterms results had sunk in, the S&P 500 stock index fell 4.4 percent, its worst day since the April 2025 tariff shock, led by stocks tied to the data center build-out, while the Nasdaq also had its deepest one-day drop in 19 months, with investors worried about tougher AI rules from a Democratic Congress.

The Riders will urge caution: hold the hearings, pass disclosure rules, but don’t touch the capital spending contributing to the economy and the stock market. Several moderate Democrats, such as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro or Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who are also presumed to be business-friendly, are considering presidential runs. They are likely to be the influential voices in the Riders camp.

According to recent reports, as for the third camp, let’s call them the Racers. These are Democrats who prioritize national security concerns and want to keep sensitive technology and advanced chips away from adversaries. Specifically, they are eager to ensure that China not win the AI race. The Racers have support from the likes of influential senators such as Elizabeth Warren and Democratic leader Chuck Schumer as well as post-midterms in-the-spotlight senators including James Talarico.

While the AI race against China was not the issue that galvanized voters in the midterms and swept Democrats into Congress, a startling upcoming development has the potential to make this a more pivotal political lever: the scandal involving Jensen Huang, who admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. This puts a spotlight on the extent to which China is keen to compete and centers the geopolitical stakes of the AI race in voters’ minds.

Huang’s abrupt exit from the tech giant that he co-founded puts wind at the backs of the Racers, especially with curbing chip sales to China becoming a rare cause with bipartisan support. But it also pushes the other camps to revise their agendas.

The Restrainers’ scrutiny of Significant Tech’s leadership has national security implications. They will by now have realized that Nvidia did not have so much as a board chair until the day that Huang left—hardly a case for letting the industry police itself. For the Riders, with Nvidia as the load-bearer for the AI edifice, instability at the top could produce instability across the economy. They can point to half a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market value being lost within a few days of the scandal breaking and the board investigation beginning.

In a recent development, A Democratic coalition made up of these camps necessarily has a mix of divergent priorities. But while the legislative agenda will be set by political calculation, Congress can only guess at what a lame-duck president who controls the agencies, the veto, the export licenses, and his own stake in the AI trade will do in response.

In a recent development, we have just had a preview: Even as a bipartisan chip bill is in process on Capitol Hill, the White House moved first, issuing its own rule to choke off China’s access to U.S. chips through data centers abroad.

The public will vote again in two years, too short for politicians and too long for technologists. With all these conflicting forces in motion, I would argue that Congress needs to allocate its limited bandwidth to a prioritized short list of AI risks, such as those recorded in my own register of 103 documented cases.

Industry observers note that in the absence of a reconciliation across the divergent camps, the result could be a U.S. AI build-out that advances in fits and starts as deals get negotiated, an export regime that can swing with each hearing, a standoff between legislators on Capitol Hill and the White House, and allies who hedge because they cannot predict U.S. policy.

It has been revealed that the Chinese AI industry would be handed the perfect case for promoting itself to the world as the comparable, trustworthy, and cheaper alternative. And it has managed to get to this point even without access to the most advanced chips that Huang himself had wanted to sell to them.

In a recent development, meanwhile, to win, Beijing will not need a newly ascendant Democratic Party to pick the wrong camp. It only needs Washington to pick none.

Bhaskar Chakravorti is the dean of global business at Tufts University’s Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy. He is the founding executive director of Fletcher’s Institute for Business in the Global Context, where he established and chairs the Digital Planet research program. His next book Defeating Disinformation (co-edited with Joel Trachtman) will be published by Cambridge University Press in January 2025.

#99660. Rep. Jimmy Gomez to resign after sexual misconduct probe

Rep. Jimmy Gomez to resign after sexual misconduct probe

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., pictured leaving the Capitol on Nov.
  • Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., will resign effective Dec.
  • Gomez, who was defeated in his bid for reelection this month, revealed his resignation Monday, hours after the Ethics panel released its final report which also said Gomez’s conduct “could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., pictured leaving the Capitol on Nov. 9, will resign Dec. 1. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., will resign effective Dec. 1 after the House Ethics Committee remarked it found “substantial evidence” that Gomez engaged in sexual misconduct with a congressional staffer.

Gomez, who was defeated in his bid for reelection this month, revealed his resignation Monday, hours after the Ethics panel released its final report which also said Gomez’s conduct “could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.”.

The report was one of four released by the Ethics panel Monday. Three of them are about members who are set to depart the House after the 119th Congress, and the fourth is about the conduct of a former chief of staff.

In a statement, Gomez stated he took “full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage,” but that he also had “strong disagreements with the Committee’s report and its conclusions.” Despite his concerns with the process, though, he said he saw no alternative other than to resign because “he was not given an opportunity to respond” to the final report.

A statement issued by lawyers representing the female staffer with whom Gomez was accused of engaging in misconduct applauded the “thorough and sensitive” handling of the investigation.

“However, Representative Gomez’s conduct did not occur in a vacuum, and immediate steps must be taken by Congress to rein in what the report describes as a ‘toxic and predatory culture,’” the attorneys, Lisa J. Banks and Sarah E. Nesbitt, added. “Democracy cannot function properly when women must endure harassment and abuse as a condition of public service.”.

According to recent reports, the committee began investigating Gomez after a Newly introduced York Post story alleged the congressman was seen kissing a congressional staffer at a party hosted by then-Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif. At the time, Gomez noted he did not violate any House ethics rules. Swalwell resigned earlier this year amid a slew of sexual assault allegations from four separate women, one of whom was a former staffer.

It has been revealed that but the more serious allegations addressed by the Ethics probe involve another female staffer, identified in the report as Witness 1. She testified in a deposition with the committee that on one occasion, Gomez touched her genitals without consent at a Washington bar. Gomez mentioned in his own interview with the committee that while he did engage in sexual conduct with the staffer, “she did not say no, she did not push me away.”.

The same staffer, who did not work for Gomez, noted he made inappropriate advances in a separate incident in Gomez’s congressional office, which Gomez downplayed as just a “beso,” or kiss, and hug.

In its report, the committee determined that the congressional staffer’s testimony “was clear and was supported by evidence that she contemporaneously complained of his conduct” to another witness, and was part of an intolerable “toxic and predatory culture” on Capitol Hill.

A statement issued by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and other House Democratic leaders called the report “serious and deeply troubling,” and that Gomez’s resignation was “appropriate.”.

“Decisive action to set a latest standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats,” the statement stated.

Industry observers note that gomez was one of two House members from the Golden State to lose to a fellow Democrat earlier this month. Northern California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones.

Industry observers note that gomez faced off against Angela Gonzales-Torres in the general election after both advanced from the state’s all-party primary in June. Gonzales-Torres, a Democratic Socialist and housing advocate, had the backing of several progressive groups, including Justice Democrats and Leaders We Deserve. Her supporters criticized Gomez after the House Ethics panel opened its investigation in August. Her campaign also sought to publicize the inquiry in the weeks leading up to Election Day, The Washington Post reported.

It has been revealed that the committee also released findings of its probes into Reps. Mike Collins, R-Ga., and Troy Nehls, R-Texas, as well as Brandon Phillips, Collins’ former chief of staff.

Collins, who lost his Senate bid earlier this month, was under review following an Office of Congressional Conduct referral alleging that Phillips hired his girlfriend as an intern. Collins’ lawyers denied the allegations, and Phillips was fired earlier this year.

Collins and the committee reached a mutual agreement under which he would return $2,880 to the U.S. Treasury after the committee found he had overpaid the “intern,” allowing it to close the case.

Phillips, who did not comply with his congressional subpoenas, has been recommended by the committee to be held in contempt of Congress.

Recent findings suggest that “At no point did Mr. Phillips offer a satisfactory legal justification for his failure to comply with the subpoena,” the committee wrote.

Recent findings suggest that the committee probed Nehls for allegedly using campaign money for his personal benefit. Nehls did not run for reelection, but his twin brother, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, will replace him in January.

The committee found that the Texas Republican “improperly used a firm that he owned as a political committee; the company, Liberty 1776, received and disbursed funds for the benefit of Representative Nehls’ campaign and other unverifiable purposes.”.

Daniela Altimari contributed to this report.
