China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that LYLE J.
  • NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.
  • Recent findings suggest that lyle J.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that LYLE J. GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.

NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.

How America Can Avert an Unnecessary Rivalry.

Recent findings suggest that lyle J. Goldstein and Nina Tannenwald.

Industry observers note that today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China. Policymakers point to China’s increasingly aggressive policies toward Taiwan, its massive military buildup, and its resistance to engaging in some arms control measures as evidence that Beijing has accepted the inevitability of such a race or is even pursuing one. Worried by intellectual frameworks that emphasize the likelihood of war between rival great powers, many U.S. leaders and analysts see little choice but for the United States to arm itself, too. But this thinking risks becoming a self-fulling prophecy. The major danger is that an unrestrained arms race increases the likelihood of war over Taiwan or even of a catastrophic nuclear exchange.

Recent findings suggest that but the pessimism about averting an arms race is misplaced. A nuclear arms race, in particular, is not a foregone conclusion—and the United States has real opportunities to curb one. Avoiding a nuclear arms race will require a broader approach than the two-pronged one Washington has recently favored: building up U.S. nuclear deterrence and seeking to force concessions from Beijing by imposing restrictions on trade and technology transfers. American leaders should instead look beyond traditional deterrence, which falls short because its threat-based approach tends to provoke competition over arms, and strive to establish a more fundamental strategic stability through a process of reciprocal de-escalation and compromise. China is likely to be amenable to reciprocal de-escalation: it has a long tradition of moderation in nuclear matters and, ultimately, Chinese leaders do not want a war over Taiwan.

It has been revealed that there are recent signs that even U.S. President Donald Trump, who has often boasted about his distaste for compromise, sees the value of engagement. After two U.S.-Chinese bilateral summits this year, in October he suggested that his November trilateral meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin should focus on “denuclearization.” But Washington will have to become much more consistent in its rejection of an arms race, including by modifying its support for Taiwan and incorporating China into global arms control leadership. A nuclear arms race with China becomes inevitable only if Washington continues to believe it is.

China is undoubtedly pursuing a military buildup, including investments in nuclear weapons. Between 2020 and 2025, China doubled the number of its nuclear warheads, from 300 to 600—a startling increase, although its arsenal remains small compared with the United States’ approximately 3,700 warheads. In 2021, researchers at the Federation of American Scientists announced that China was constructing 350 fresh nuclear missile silos in three vast sites in Xinjiang and Gansu provinces. Beijing is also pursuing substantial qualitative upgrades to its nuclear weapons, a push it showcased at an October 2025 military parade that unveiled a new sea-released ballistic missile, two new kinds of intercontinental ballistic missiles, a new air-launched hypersonic missile, and a new long-range hypersonic cruise missile.

Then, this July, the Chinese navy tested a submarine-launched long-range ballistic missile that could carry nuclear weapons. This significant upcoming capability will allow China to launch long-range nuclear strikes that can reach the United States from protected waters near its own coastline rather than having to sail out into the Pacific. A recent editorial in a leading Chinese foreign affairs newspaper took the candid yet disturbing step of explicitly linking China’s rapid nuclear buildup to its desire to exert sovereignty over Taiwan. “The great cause of national reunification,” it asserted, “must rest on a solid, realistic foundation. That foundation is, first and foremost, hard power.” Although such overt nuclear saber rattling remains rare, the link between Beijing’s nuclear forces and the Taiwan concern stretches back over three decades and is also supported by the scholar Tong Zhao’s detailed analysis of China’s nuclear buildup in Foreign Affairs in May.

As China builds up its military, the perception that it is on a collision course with the United States over Taiwan—one that inevitably includes the risk of nuclear escalation—has become widespread in Washington. Taiwan, of course, appears to be an obvious flash point. The United States has long committed itself informally to defending the island while China seeks to unify with it, by force if necessary. In October, Army General Ronald Clark, the head of the U.S. Pacific Command, affirmed that his forces are actively readying for a Chinese invasion of Taiwan that could come as early as 2027.

It has been revealed that the Biden administration and both Trump administrations made some attempts to engage China over arms control and nuclear risk reduction. Trump proposed trilateral arms control talks that would include Russia, whereas the Biden administration pursued bilateral talks with China on strategic stability and nuclear risk reduction. But both presidents gave up after China consistently rejected engaging in sustained talks on nuclear matters. Beijing’s stance is that it has a small nuclear arsenal compared with the United States and Russia and that it is key to first establish trust and mutual reassurance about core interests.

Beyond China’s resistance to arms control, theories about power that are trendy in Washington reinforce the collision course mentality. Numerous realist scholars argue that a U.S.-Chinese rivalry and even a great-power war may be structurally difficult to avoid. The political scientist Graham Allison captured this pessimism in his influential 2017 book, Destined for War, which argued that a so-called Thucydides trap—when a rapidly rising power challenges the position of the dominant power, yielding war—would doom the United States and China to conflict.

Recent findings suggest that china hawks, such as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, increasingly advocate an aggressive focus on “preparing for World War III” with China as a way to avoid it. In a July New York Times interview, Colby argued that the United States must “deny” China “the ability to seize and hold the key territory” of Taiwan, by enhancing U.S. deterrence with a massive military buildup. The next month, speaking at a military conference, Colby specified that such a buildup ought to put a greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons and the ability to fight a so-called limited nuclear war. The enemy, Colby noted, has “got to believe there’s some sense in which we would use” nuclear weapons. Toward this end, the United States is building a new intercontinental ballistic missile, a new air-rolled out cruise missile, and new nuclear-armed submarines and bombers, and accelerating the ambitious Golden Dome homeland missile defense project. Unlike earlier U.S. missile defenses, which were designed to intercept limited strikes by so called rogue states such as Iran and North Korea, the Golden Dome is intended to defend against massive Chinese or Russian attacks. But the prospect of losing its ability to retaliate against a U.S. first strike only gives Beijing more incentive to expand its nuclear arsenal.

Recent findings suggest that such a nuclear-heavy approach only prevents a war with China if nuclear deterrence succeeds. That puts a lot of eggs in the deterrence basket. And recent wars suggest that nuclear deterrence is becoming less effective. Russia’s nuclear threats have not coerced Ukraine into halting its strikes deep into Russian territory. Iran has proved willing to launch strikes against nuclear-armed Israel as well as U.S. bases and allies in the Middle East. What is most ominous, in May 2025, India and Pakistan crossed previous redlines and attacked each other’s homelands, something that mutual nuclear deterrence was supposed to prevent. Even if neither the United States nor China want nuclear war, a China determined to unify with Taiwan may not be intimidated by U.S. nuclear threats.

A recent study by Brown University’s Costs of War program found that the United States has already spent more than $3.4 trillion on its militarized rivalry with China over the last decade. Sustaining or ramping up this spending—which encompasses upcoming warships, aircraft, long-range missiles, drones, base upgrades, forward deployments, large military exercises, research and development, and new nuclear weapons—is infeasible in an era of ballooning national debt and expanding domestic needs.

One of the tragedies of an arms race is that neither party may actually want to pursue one. Despite its current arms buildup, Beijing has a long record of moderation in military and nuclear matters. For many decades, it has maintained a minimal nuclear deterrent and a no-first-use policy, and it did not use major military force to achieve strategic goals. Although it has long had access to the relevant technologies, China appears not to have produced or deployed tactical nuclear weapons. Chinese diplomats played a substantial role in coaxing Iran to accept the Obama administration’s 2015 nuclear deal and supported the UN’s relatively stringent sanctions on North Korea. And in the fall of 2022, according to then Secretary of State Antony Blinken and reporting by the Financial Times, China likely intervened diplomatically with the Kremlin to help stop Russia from using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. More broadly, China has embraced international law when it comes to war, playing a constructive role, for example, in removing chemical weapons from Syria in 2013.

It has been revealed that beijing’s inclination toward restraint has not disappeared completely, even as it upgrades its military. In November 2023, U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi agreed to renew lines of communication between their countries’ militaries that had been severed after U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan the previous year. A year later, the two leaders affirmed that humans, not AI, must control the decision to use nuclear weapons. And in late 2025, Beijing released a white paper emphatically reiterating its support for nuclear arms control and has moved toward more transparency by publishing more information, including in English, about its military upgrades.

Sources indicate that chinese leaders clearly do not want a war over Taiwan. Publicly, they repeatedly emphasize that their goal is “peaceful unification” and “winning without fighting,” invoking the Chinese strategist Sun-tzu. Beijing’s longtime “one country, two systems” policy toward Taiwan—which would bring the island under Chinese sovereignty while allowing it substantial autonomy—leaves room for a negotiated solution. Last year, in an notable analysis of China’s strategic ambitions, the scholars David Kang, Jackie Wong, and Zenobia Chan examined 12,000 articles and hundreds of speeches by Xi to argue that Beijing prioritizes regime stability and internal development over displacing the United States as a global military hegemon. Although China’s major, unannounced exercises around Taiwan earlier this month may constitute an exception, overall, Chinese military exercises near Taiwan over the last five years are consistent with this interpretation: many have reacted to perceived provocations, illustrate only medium-scale capabilities, and have generally had a performative quality, accompanied by extensive press coverage.

There is still an opening for the United States and China to de-escalate. To achieve strategic stability, the two countries will need to make a concerted effort to defuse their security dilemma—the dynamic in which each side perceives the other’s defensive measures as aggressive. First, U.S. and Chinese leaders need to revive superpower summitry. Biden held only three face-to-face meetings with Xi on the sidelines of regional economic meetings. Although the May 2026 Beijing summit between Trump and Xi yielded no major breakthroughs, the meeting did improve the two leaders’ personal relationship; today, U.S.-Chinese tensions are lower than they were between 2021 and 2025. This progress suggests the great value of holding a regular, annual, multiday bilateral summit with a significant focus on nuclear arms control. Such meetings would give expert working groups time to methodically develop measures to reduce the risk of conflict. Just as important, the summits need to be long enough to leave room for unscripted conversations. At their first summit, in Geneva in November 1985, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev famously broke away from anxious bureaucrats and advisers for an impromptu walk—an encounter that helped establish a more constructive relationship.

Recent findings suggest that the United States must also take concrete steps to reduce the chance of escalation in the Taiwan Strait. Above all, it should adhere more consistently to its “one China” policy—its position that Beijing is the sole legal government of China. More consistency would include limiting U.S. legislators’ trips to the island and downgrading U.S.-Taiwanese defense relations by, for example, holding meetings less frequently and at lower diplomatic levels. Washington should remind key allies such as Japan to proceed cautiously in terms of their rhetoric and military deployments. Such a restraint-oriented strategy would make it clear to Taiwan that independence is off the table, encouraging it to take a more accommodating approach that would lower the temperature with Beijing. If Washington were to agree to common-sense limitations on arms sales to Taiwan—such as refusing to sell Taiwan the surface-to-surface ballistic Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), which can reach across the strait to the Chinese mainland—Beijing would likely reciprocate by scaling back its military exercises and related military deployments around the island. There are real incentives for Beijing to de-escalate. Doing so could improve relations with neighbors such as Japan, free up focus for domestic priorities, lower military spending, and limit the chance of war.

In a recent development, the Pentagon needs to demonstrate Washington’s intent to avoid war over Taiwan by gradually decreasing U.S. warship transits through the Taiwan Strait. Even more important, Washington should also substantially reduce U.S. military deployments in the Luzon Strait between Taiwan and the Philippines and around Japan’s Ryukyu Islands. Such deployments only exacerbate the security dilemma.

Exhibiting restraint does not mean the United States would be giving Taiwan away. The United States can continue to provide Taiwan with defensive arms (such as missile interceptors, artillery, drones, and mines) and harden U.S. bases in the region to provide stabilizing deterrence. But even if U.S. leaders publicly abjure direct military intervention to defend Taiwan—a rational step that would lower the risk of nuclear war—China will prefer negotiating with Taipei on the island’s autonomy over a bloody military showdown with Taiwanese forces. For their part, Taiwan’s leaders will likely accommodate themselves to limited self-governance under Chinese overall sovereignty. In the end, China’s main goal is to get Taiwan out of the U.S. sphere of influence. Chinese leaders’ major fear is not so much Taiwanese autonomy as the prospect of the island serving as a U.S. forward base—in Chinese parlance, “using Taiwan to contain China.”.

Another vital step would be to seek a multilateral pledge by all nuclear-armed states to employ nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack. Such a policy would reduce the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. China has long embraced such a no-first-use policy, but U.S. leaders have traditionally opposed it, believing that it might expose U.S. allies to conventional attack. The U.S. nuclear deterrent for allies, however, increasingly lacks credibility because the costs of starting a nuclear war would vastly outweigh the benefits. And after the collapse of traditional nuclear arms control, a mutual no-first-use policy offers a promising area of common ground between the United States and China. It would reinforce the existing no-first-use policies of China and India and implicitly acknowledge their leadership in the area of nuclear restraint, a virtue when newer nuclear states are chafing under the old Cold War superpowers’ dominance of arms control. This approach could even entice Beijing into a wider, more comprehensive process of bilateral or multilateral nuclear arms control.

Beyond these three major initiatives, the United States and China should sign an agreement to notify each other about their ballistic missile tests. Washington could also consider giving Beijing a larger role in nonproliferation efforts, for instance by affording China leadership roles in negotiations and inspection regimes in future nonproliferation arrangements. The U.S. arms control agenda with China should focus not only on offensive nuclear systems but also on missile defenses and tactical nuclear weapons, as well as AI technologies. And it would help if the United States evolved its own nuclear posture in the direction of restraint by reducing its warheads, warfighting capabilities, and alert posture.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the United States needs to get serious about reining in an arms race with China before its perception that one is apace becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. The two countries have a mutual interest in restraint. If Washington continues to overlook Beijing’s incentives to compromise—and the real signs that it is willing to do so—an arms race that, as of now, is mostly putative will become a reality. And a catastrophic war that could have been avoided could indeed become inevitable.

#99636. Jensen Huang Is Back

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, collapsed negotiations at this year’s U.N. climate summit, and Ukraine’s naval drone attack.

Nvidia, the semiconductor giant at the center of the global artificial intelligence race, announced on Monday that it had reinstated its CEO, Jensen Huang, just 11 days after he was forced to resign following multiple alleged extramarital affairs.

Recent findings suggest that welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, collapsed negotiations at this year’s U.N. climate summit, and Ukraine’s naval drone attack.

Nvidia, the semiconductor giant at the center of the global artificial intelligence race, announced on Monday that it had reinstated its CEO, Jensen Huang, just 11 days after he was forced to resign following multiple alleged extramarital affairs.

Monday’s announcement marks a dramatic development in a saga that has roiled markets, seen the powerful organization’s value plunge, and fueled uncertainty about the future of the AI boom. Plummeting stock prices had wiped some $2.6 trillion from Nvidia’s market value, and amid mounting scrutiny, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission reportedly rolled out a probe into the company’s accounting practices.

Huang’s alleged affairs were made particularly scandalous—and geopolitically noteworthy—by the fact that one of those affairs was with a woman whom U.S. intelligence agencies suspect of being a Chinese spy. That revelation raised major national security concerns for a company whose most advanced AI chips remained banned from China.

Industry observers note that yet all those concerns now appear to have been cast aside at the behest of Huang’s most powerful backer: U.S. President Donald Trump. Trump has never wavered from Huang’s corner, calling him a “very high-quality person” and an “amazing guy” even after the Nvidia CEO resigned. Now, it appears that the U.S. president decided to put his thumb on the scale to bring Huang back.

On Monday, Nvidia’s stock price rose by 33 percent in the wake of the company’s announcement.

In a recent development, the Nvidia board stated it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

Huang mentioned in a statement shared by the board that he was “honored” to return to Nvidia and would do so with “renewed commitment.” The board, meanwhile, said its previously unveiled independent investigation into Huang’s possible Chinese espionage exposure would proceed as planned and that Huang had pledged to cooperate with it.

Trump, who posted on Truth Social Sunday night that he hoped the Nvidia board would reinstate Huang, also hinted on Monday that such a decision was coming, even before it was officially confirmed.

In a recent development, “He’s back where he should be,” Trump noted in a phone interview with PBS NewsHour minutes before the Nvidia announcement. “Well, he will be soon, hopefully,” he added. Trump also told CNBC after the announcement that he had spoken directly to Nvidia’s board and provided them with assurances on the national security threat. “I convinced them,” he said. “I made the deal.” Afterward, Trump called Huang and asked him to “work hard,” he told CNBC.

Some U.S. lawmakers from Trump’s own party appear to be less convinced. “Jensen Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy. Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang,” Republican Rep. Don Bacon wrote in a post on X.

Texas Sen. John Cornyn was more pointed in his own X post. “No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn wrote. (Both Cornyn and Bacon are leaving Congress at the end of this year.).

Utah Sen. John Curtis also slammed the decision, declaring in a post on X that Huang “was right to step down when the affair came to light.” Curtis also wrote, “I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?”.

Trump dismissed those concerns in his CNBC interview, agreeing when CNBC asked whether Republicans would “come around” on Huang’s reinstatement. As for the national security concerns, Trump dismissed new reporting that the Chinese woman whom Huang had a romantic relationship with, Alice Huang, was in contact with China’s Ministry of State Security—the country’s main intelligence agency—during their affair. “Who isn’t in contact?” Trump asked. “China speaks to everybody,” he mentioned, adding, “They speak to me.”.

Trump mentioned he had spoken to Chinese President Xi Jinping “at length” about Jensen Huang during the two leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, China, last week. The U.S. president also claimed that keeping Huang out of Nvidia would risk the CEO defecting to China. “I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen: ‘Hey, how would you like to come to China?’” Trump said. “He’s got a little blood in him, you know,” the U.S. president added, alluding to Huang’s Taiwanese heritage.

After the interview, Trump made his backing of Huang far more explicit with another post on Truth Social. The post featured an AI-generated recasting of a photo of Trump raising his fist after an assassination attempt in 2024; instead of Trump, the AI-generated version depicted Huang with an Nvidia flag in the background, raising his fist with a red bra in hand. “Sex sells,” Trump told CNBC.

Sources indicate that wednesday, Nov. 25: An EU-Western Balkans summit kicks off in Brussels.

Recent findings suggest that saturday, Nov. 28: Taiwan holds local elections.

Sunday, Nov. 29: Spain holds snap parliamentary elections.

Sources indicate that deep divisions. Negotiations at this year’s U.N. climate summit, also known as COP31, collapsed on Sunday as countries clashed over a proposed deal and ultimately failed to reach consensus. It marks the first time that the climate talks have failed over a final deal in about 17 years, and it comes in a year that has seen record-shattering heat and other climate extremes.

According to recent reports, the proposed deal had omitted any mention of fossil fuels, the primary driver of climate change. That exclusion sparked an uproar and prompted Pacific island nations and the European Union, among others, to reject it.

The proposed agreement “failed to meet the moment,” stated Irish Environment Minister Darragh O’Brien, who was speaking on behalf of the European Union. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required.”.

Maritime strikes. Ukrainian forces deployed seven naval drones in a weekend attack against two Russian vessels located off the coast of Libya, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated in a post on X on Monday. The strikes sank the Russian corvette Merkury, which is one of Moscow’s newest ships, Zelensky said.

Drones also struck a Russian-owned cargo ship in the Baltic Sea on Saturday; the vessel later floated into Finnish waters. Finnish authorities believe that Ukraine perpetrated the attack, but Kyiv has not taken responsibility for it. “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo mentioned in a post on X, though he added that “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”.

In a recent development, under pressure. South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday amid controversy over newly announced anti-cheating measures. After news emerged of a cheating scandal in a separate exam, South Korean officials unveiled a raft of rigid anti-AI cheating measures just days before the country’s annual college entrance exam, known as the Suneung.

Recent findings suggest that the Suneung is a famously grueling eight-hour test that can be vital in shaping students’ career outcomes. Yet the last-minute announcement of the latest rules, which included blaring emergency cellphone alerts, sparked confusion among test-takers. Ultimately, some 111 people were caught cheating, according to officials.

“I believe I am not free from criticism or blame from the public for failing to prepare adequately in advance,” the education minister noted in a statement reported by local media.

It has been revealed that on a stage in Ottawa over the weekend, Trump joked around with two Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carneys—or did he? The Canadian leader actually recruited two comedians to assist him with a roast at an annual dinner with journalists, enlisting impersonators both of himself and his U.S. counterpart. “I am pressing the emergency comedy button,” Carney joked.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., discusses controversies surrounding the Smithsonian Institution and President Donald Trump calling on the museum to replace a sculpture with a statue of George Washington on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’.

Photos taken by a commuter on Washington, D.C.'s Metro system appear to show a White House advisor’s laptop displaying a draft plan to overhaul the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, ProPublica reported.

Last month, a commuter riding the Orange Line from Northern Virginia noticed a man in a suit working on a laptop displaying a document titled "Smithsonian Institution Renewal Blueprint." The commuter photographed the screen and sent the images to ProPublica.

The multipoint draft proposed firing museum Director Anthea Hartig, creating new museum-wide exhibit guidelines that omit the Smithsonian’s diversity style guide, reviewing its traveling-exhibition strategy — including ending "The Bias Inside Us" — and reassessing grants to what the draft called "woke third parties," including the American Alliance of Museums. A separate handwritten note that was also pictured proposed a policy against "X-rated" exhibitions. ProPublica said it likely referred to an exhibit the White House criticized for displaying a two-piece chrome-and-rubber harness designed for sadomasochism.

INSIDE THE BEHEMOTH SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM NETWORK DRAWING FIRE FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION.

Sources indicate that the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 12, 2025. Photos taken on a D.C. Metro train appear to show a White House advisor's laptop displaying a draft blueprint to overhaul the museum's leadership, exhibits and K-12 curriculum. (Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

The draft renewal plan pictured on the staffer's laptop surfaced amid a broader Trump administration effort to reshape how the Smithsonian presents American history. The White House released a 162-page report on July 4 accusing the National Museum of American History of "ideological capture." Two congressional hearings followed, and a July executive order directed officials to post signs outside the museum informing visitors of the report’s findings about "ideological capture," though ProPublica reported the signs had not yet gone up as of publication.

Industry observers note that fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment on the photographed document and whether any of its proposals are under consideration, but did not receive a response by publication. The photographed document does not establish whether the proposals were approved or put into effect.

TRUMP GIVES SMITHSONIAN DAYS TO REPLACE 'STRANGE MODERNIST SCULPTURE' WITH FOUNDING FATHER.

It has been revealed that proPublica reported that it identified the White House staffer as Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy advisor with the White House Domestic Policy Council — which produced the July report — after spotting the initials "B.S." or "S.B." on the laptop screen and following a man matching his description from the Metro to a White House employee checkpoint. ProPublica reported that Bock did not respond to its messages and that the Smithsonian declined to comment.

Sources indicate that proPublica reported that the proposals on Bock’s laptop envisioned a permanent exhibit celebrating Western civilization, a display on prominent American families, a large George Washington statue at the museum entrance and new museum-wide interpretive guidelines written without reference to the Smithsonian’s diversity style guide. A separate handwritten note photographed alongside the laptop also floated a potential new D-Day exhibit.

According to recent reports, the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C.. A July White House report accused the museum of "ideological capture," and a draft renewal proposal photographed on a White House advisor's laptop proposed replacing its diversity guidelines and adding a George Washington statue at the entrance. (Kevin Carter).

In addition to the proposed exhibit changes, the draft called for the firing of National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig and about a dozen senior administrators and curators. That proposal came as Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch, who leads the broader institution, was preparing to retire at year’s end. ProPublica reported that White House criticism of the Smithsonian helped prompt Bunch’s departure.

According to recent reports, TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED.

The draft plan also called for overhauling the museum’s online curriculum for K-12 students, including dropping a module on immigration and creating newly introduced material focused on the Founders, according to ProPublica, which noted the document floated possible titles for the new curriculum, including "Architects of Liberty" and "Profiles in Liberty.".

Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch poses for a portrait at the Smithsonian Castle on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., on May 28, 2026. Bunch is preparing to retire at the end of the year amid White House criticism of the institution, according to ProPublica. (Al Drago/The Washington Post via Getty Images).

The administration’s push to reshape how the Smithsonian presents American history began picking up steam in March 2025, when Trump signed an executive order directing Vice President JD Vance, through his role on the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, to help remove what the order called "improper ideology" from the institution. The Smithsonian, which encompasses 21 museums and D.C.'s National Zoo, is governed by a 17-member Board of Regents that consists of the vice president, the chief justice of the Supreme Court, members of Congress and private citizens. It receives more than $1 billion in federal funding annually.

The White House’s July report cited, among other examples, a museum exhibit that raised the possibility Benjamin Franklin had used enslaved people in his household as subjects in electrical experiments. It also criticized staff training based on a social-action toolkit that the report stated linked museums to White supremacy and other forms of oppression.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

It has been revealed that the report said the museum should not erase slavery, Jim Crow or other national failures. Its broader charge was that the museum was not giving visitors a coherent account of how the country developed, including both its achievements and its wrongs.

The criticism from the Trump administration came amid a longer-running debate over how the museum should tell the nation’s story, which has stretched back to at least 2001.

According to recent reports, proPublica reported that in response to earlier criticism, the Smithsonian convened a blue-ribbon commission in 2001, whose 2002 report urged the museum to present a more unified account of American history. The outlet also reported that after George Floyd’s murder in 2020, Bunch and other leaders began an institution-wide reassessment of the Smithsonian’s priorities and how it tells the nation’s story.

Why Israel Is Losing America

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Notable Ally.
  • Sources indicate that american politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ANDREW P. MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress. He was Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Israeli-Palestinian Affairs in the Biden administration and Director for Egypt and Israel Military Issues on the National Security Council in the Obama administration.

Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Notable Ally.

Sources indicate that american politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel. On November 3, as Americans headed to the polls, U.S. President Donald Trump made the surprising announcement that the United States would stop sending aid to Israel, valued at around $4 billion annually, by the end of the year. That night, Democrats, many of whom are increasingly outspoken in their criticism of Israeli actions, swept the House and Senate.

Sources indicate that as I wrote in Foreign Affairs a year ago, the “exceptional relationship” between the United States and Israel, in which Israel is treated differently than any other U.S. ally or partner, is coming to an end. No other country receives the tremendous latitude and unconditional backing that the United States extends to Israel. In addition to directly hurting Palestinians, the United States’ support for Israel incentivizes reckless Israeli behavior and dubious strategic thinking. The consequences of the blank check are clear. Over the past three years, tens of thousands of Gazans have been killed, progress toward peace and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip has stalled, the annexation of the West Bank proceeds at an unprecedented rate, and the United States is stuck in an unpopular war in the Middle East with seemingly no end. Israel, for its part, is no safer than on October 6, 2023, and unquestionably more isolated.

Industry observers note that things are about to change. For better or worse, the United States will recalibrate its relationship with Israel over the coming years and a newly introduced paradigm for the bilateral relationship will emerge—one in which Israel is expected to comply with U.S. and international law, the two countries refrain from interfering in each other’s domestic politics, and the United States limits its support when Israeli goals conflict with its own.

It has been revealed that this change is inevitable, and there is little that Israel and its supporters can do to stop it. But Israel can help keep the United States onside by making itself a reliable partner. As it begins what could be a drawn-out government formation process after last month’s elections, Israel can opt to change direction and plot a course that will not further alienate its closest ally.

Industry observers note that whoever leads the next Israeli government can begin rebuilding trust with the United States before a fresh U.S. president takes office, in 2029. It won’t be easy. Just as Americans have grown critical of Israel over the past three years, Israelis have shifted further to the right. Israel’s next leaders will need the courage to curb the country’s expansionist policies and resurrect the much-maligned two-state solution. But if they fail to overhaul their approach to Palestinians and the wider region, Israel risks losing its biggest champion and defender—perhaps for good.

According to recent reports, trump, who seems to delight in bullying U.S. allies and partners, has maintained the United States’ long-standing exceptional approach to Israel. He joined Israel in launching strikes on Iran in June 2025 and a larger war in February 2026, embarking for the first time on a truly joint military operation with the Jewish state. Like other presidents before him, Trump has provided Israel with bombs, missiles, and aircraft, largely with no strings attached. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also interfered in each other’s political systems to an unprecedented degree by endorsing candidates.

Industry observers note that time and again, Trump has deferred to Israel even when such support has run against American interests. The 2026 war on Iran is the most blatant example. Netanyahu persuaded Trump to give up nuclear talks with Iran and join a war that has failed in its objectives and upended energy markets. Even where the Trump administration has staked out U.S. priorities, it has largely refrained from trying to compel Israel to adhere to them. Israel, for example, has obstructed Trump’s peace initiative for Gaza, which is meant to restore governance to the Palestinians, disarm Hamas, and lead to a permanent Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel has undermined the plan by expanding its military footprint in Gaza beyond the agreed demarcation lines and denying entry to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), an interim technocratic body that is intended to govern the territory under Trump’s plan and is right now marooned in Egypt. But the Trump administration has barely sounded a single note of disapproval, reinforcing Netanyahu’s long-standing view that he can defy the United States at little cost.

Sources indicate that moreover, it remains to be seen whether Trump will follow through on his pledge to cut military aid to Israel. The timing of his statement suggests it could have been an electoral stunt, and he stated himself that the announcement would deprive the left of a talking point. One possibility is that the United States continues gifting Israel weapons to the tune of billions, just under a different guise. The National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027, which passed the House this summer and could pass the Senate before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress this coming January, contains a provision that would expand the Pentagon’s financial and material assistance to Israel.

Trump has made no effort to bring U.S. military assistance or transfers to Israel in line with what it provides to other countries. For decades, the United States has been reluctant to subject arms sales to Israel to U.S. regulations or condition them on Israeli behavior. All recent presidents, for example, have effectively exempted Israel from so-called Leahy laws, which prohibit U.S. assistance to foreign military units credibly implicated in human-rights violations. Despite rampant settler terrorism in the West Bank, in many cases facilitated by the Israeli military, the Trump administration has not indicated that it would declare any Israeli units ineligible to receive U.S. weapons.

Trump has also intervened in Israeli politics more than any other U.S. leader. He has hectored Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu so that the prime minister can escape the consequences of an ongoing corruption trial. Ahead of October’s election in Israel, Trump offered Netanyahu a “complete and total endorsement” in his bid for another term. Such blatant interference in Israel’s domestic politics not only undermines the rule of law and integrity of Israeli elections but also serves to normalize Netanyahu’s repeated interventions in U.S. domestic politics. True to form, the Israeli prime minister has praised Trump as “by far the greatest friend Israel has ever had or will have in the White House” just two weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, effectively endorsing Republican candidates for Congress. As in other areas of the relationship, Trump has made what is already an unhealthy dynamic worse.

According to recent reports, unconditional support from the United States has hurt Israel in a crucial way: it indulges the worst instincts of Israeli leaders and does nothing to dissuade them from their embrace of a near-perpetual state of war. After Hamas’s attack three years ago, Israel has bombed Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and even Qatar. Although Israel has dealt blows to its adversaries, there is no evidence that these wars have made Israel any safer. Iran and its proxies have been weakened, but in the course of fighting, Tehran has discovered the extent of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the global economy and appears even more interested in developing a nuclear weapon. In Lebanon, Hezbollah still poses a threat and is devising new ways of striking Israeli territory. Although confined to a smaller portion of Gaza, Hamas is reconstituting its capabilities and quashing any internal Palestinian challenge to its rule. And in the West Bank, runaway settler violence, the proliferation of illegal Israeli outposts, and the growing threat of terrorism or even a Palestinian uprising have pushed the territory to the breaking point.

Recent findings suggest that israel has also drifted ever closer to pariah status, isolated internationally thanks to its aggressive tactics. Even the country’s closest historical allies have imposed punitive measures that would have been unthinkable just five years ago. Canada, France, and the United Kingdom, for example, announced wide-ranging sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank in September. Such policies are no longer only the purview of traditional critics of Israel, such as Indonesia and Ireland.

In a recent development, israel’s reputation within the United States has also tanked. According to Pew polling, 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022. So far, Trump has stopped Congress from restricting support for Israel—both through threatening vetoes and applying pressure on congressional Republicans—but he cannot hold back the tide of American public opinion indefinitely. Once it breaks, Israelis will have to face more than criticism from its closest ally and security guarantor. With Democrats soon to be in control of both the House and the Senate, Congress will likely pass bills that sanction settlement building and condition military aid on adherence to U.S. and international law.

In a recent development, without changes in U.S. and Israeli policy, the two countries could see their relationship rupture as continued support for Israel becomes politically untenable in the United States. To rehabilitate itself in the eyes of Americans—and therefore ensure long-term cooperation with the United States—Israel will need to change course. It must abandon Netanyahu’s bludgeoning approach to both the Palestinians and the wider region.

Recent findings suggest that it is no exaggeration to say that the future of the U.S.-Israeli relationship rests on what type of government Israel forms in the next few months. Netanyahu’s exclusion from the next government represents the best hope for preserving bilateral relations with the United States. Netanyahu has proved unwilling to stay out of U.S. politics or modify draconian security policies that have run afoul of the American public. Unfortunately, most of Netanyahu’s rivals for prime minister share his hawkish position on the Palestinians and the Middle East. Were they in power, they seem likely to resist fundamental revisions to Israeli policy that could safeguard the bilateral relationship.

Israel’s next leaders need to journey outside their comfort zone. They will have to come to terms with newly introduced realities: that tensions between the United States and Israel are now deep-rooted and that they can’t rely on the adamantine support of the Republican party any longer. To win back Americans, the Israeli government will have to rigorously follow through on its commitments under Trump’s strategy for Gaza, daring Hamas to follow suit. In addition to flooding Gaza with humanitarian aid, Israel should let the NCAG enter the territory to offer an alternative to Hamas’s rule and nihilistic agenda. Enabling the deployment of newly trained Palestinian security forces and the formation of the International Stabilization Force, a peacekeeping mission, would also help show that, whatever unfolds in Gaza, Israel is operating in good faith. Israeli forces should immediately return to the demarcation lines traced in Trump’s Gaza peace plan and pull back even further in concert with Hamas’s progress in fulfilling the terms of the plan until Israel has completely withdrawn from Gaza.

Israel must also rein in violent settlers in the West Bank and hold them accountable through the courts. The Israeli security services can identify the leaders and primary instigators behind the violence and should arrest them and bring them to justice. Given that settlers have killed and injured American citizens in these attacks, continued inaction by Israeli authorities is a recipe for more friction with the United States, especially if a Democratic government comes to power in Washington.

Industry observers note that israel must also halt its creeping annexation of the West Bank. Over the past three years, the Netanyahu government has increased its military presence in the West Bank, deprived the Palestinian Authority of funds, asserted Israeli government control over larger swaths of Palestinian land, approved a slew of new Israeli settlements, and retroactively legalized illicit outposts. In sum, these actions aim to render a Palestinian state impossible. Although reversing these measures would not arrest the expansion of existing settlements and Israeli infrastructure throughout the West Bank, they would be received positively in the United States.

In a recent development, israeli leaders also need to break the taboo around Palestinian statehood. Only a couple of decades ago, the idea of a Palestinian state was conceivable to most Israelis. Today, Israeli politicians, with precious few exceptions, cannot bring themselves to endorse a two-state solution. It will take time and no small degree of political resolve, but Israeli leaders must convince the public to accept the necessity and the virtues of a Palestinian state existing side by side with Israel. An Israel that can view Palestinians as neighbors entitled to the same rights would provide a very different image to the world than a messianic government bent on expelling whole populations.

These steps will not satisfy all American critics of Israel. Anti-Israeli attitudes cannot be erased in a matter of months. Where anti-Israeli opinion intersects with anti-Semitism—evident in incidents such as a recent boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia organized by the group Philly Bike on Your Left—the task is even more difficult and will necessitate a different set of policies that transcend Israel, including the formation of diverse domestic and international coalitions to identify and condemn anti-Semitic acts. Yet a far less belligerent Israel and one newly committed to the resolution of the unanswered question of Palestinian self-determination would start to shift U.S. public opinion back in the country’s favor.

Sources indicate that if Israel fails to change course, it will find itself less secure and more isolated internationally. Put simply, an Israel without American support will struggle to survive.

Trump pardons turkeys but Hill influence isn’t all gravy after midterm roasting

💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson are all smiles at the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardon at the White House.
  • President Donald Trump on Tuesday celebrated what he called one of the “immense powers” of his office, pardoning two turkeys ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
  • Joined by first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., set to lose power in January after he hands the gavel to a Democratic successor, Trump for the sixth time spared the long necks of two American turkeys — this time “Feathers” and “Freedom.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson are all smiles at the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardon at the White House. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images).

President Donald Trump on Tuesday celebrated what he called one of the “immense powers” of his office, pardoning two turkeys ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. But lawmakers say his influence on Capitol Hill has already changed since Republicans’ midterm losses.

Joined by first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., set to lose power in January after he hands the gavel to a Democratic successor, Trump for the sixth time spared the long necks of two American turkeys — this time “Feathers” and “Freedom.”.

“In a few moments, under the immense powers vested in me by the Constitution of the United States of America, I will grant a full, absolute and unconditional pardon — meaning they will live forever — to two magnificent Thanksgiving turkeys, special turkeys,” Trump said, suggesting he could extend his power to spare the birds from the holiday dining table to somehow grant them immortality.

While voters punished his party’s candidates for doing too little to address high prices and his decision to join Israel in going to war with Iran, Trump on Tuesday remained focused on another area of largely unchallenged authority — his White House projects. He began the event by touting the yearly event, for the first time, being held on the helipad he had built on the White House’s South Lawn. Later, he announced aims for another new location next year.

It has been revealed that “I'm told that per the long-running tradition, these exquisite animals stayed overnight at the nearby Willard Hotel. Unfortunately, for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodation to host such distinguished guests,” he mentioned of the turkeys. “I'm pleased to announce that next year we'll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built. It's going to host a lot of people and a couple of turkeys next year. We're going to do it inside.”.

Trump also highlighted that the two bright, white turkeys were raised in West Virginia — which he carried more than 40 points when he was on the ballot. The turkeys, now spared, will spend their remaining years in Texas, a state where Democrats scored two of their most high profile wins in the House and Senate races — something Trump left unmentioned.

Sources indicate that the pre-holiday vibes were lighthearted on Tuesday, with the president slated to later travel to South Florida for a Thanksgiving weekend of turkey and time at one of his golf clubs. But when he returns, lawmakers will continue assessing how much sway he still has on Capitol Hill as he begins what, for his predecessors, were their lame-duck eras.

One Republican Senate ally acknowledged his influence with lawmakers already has changed.

“I think it's going to be policy-to-policy on that,” remarked Senate Republican Conference Vice Chair James Lankford.

“But he's the president of the United States all the way to the very end. So he still has his veto pen,” the Oklahoman added. “He still has the ability to be able to direct agencies to engage. We're passing legislation. It takes three to tango: House, Senate, and the White House.”.

It has been revealed that senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz of Texas stated Trump’s influence, once the Democrat-controlled House and Senate are seated on Jan. 3, “will, obviously, be different.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I don't think the incoming Democrat majorities are interested in passing productive legislation and passing pro-jobs legislation,” stated Cruz, a potential 2028 GOP presidential candidate. “I think, instead, they're just going to attack the president all day long.”.

Still, Cruz predicted “the president will continue to lead.”.

Trump on Monday showed how he likely intends to use his lame-duck influence on and off Capitol Hill when he successfully pushed for the reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. During an interview with CNBC’s Eamon Javers, Trump made an admission that would be stunning from any other sitting American president about a private organization, saying he had been “speaking to the board directly and indirectly.”.

Sources indicate that in a Monday statement, Nvidia said its board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

In a recent development, such unprecedented moves are a big reason why Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., last week said he expects Trump to be Trump — despite overseeing a midterms campaign he insisted be about himself and his unpopular second-term record.

“Any president is going to have a lot of influence because they get to run the executive branch,” mentioned Scott, a former Sunshine State chief executive. “And they have the biggest pulpit in the world. So he's going to continue to have a lot of influence.”.

Still, some Republican lawmakers have criticized Trump and his team for what they call recent stumbles.

In a recent development, sen. Jim Banks of Indiana last week told reporters he had “a lot of questions” about how Trump and his administration handled upgrades to the country’s air traffic control system that prompted a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13.

According to recent reports, “Somebody needs to be held accountable for what happened,” he noted, raising concerns about the president demanding $50 billion in additional taxpayer monies to build a new system. “I’m not fully convinced that throwing out more money is going to solve the fundamental problems.”.

Trump also has taken ample friendly fire on social media from GOP members over his interference in the Huang scandal.

North Carolina GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan took to X to say the Nvidia founder’s reinstatement was “a mistake.”.

It has been revealed that “For the past two years, I have privately stated there is no way Jensen Huang can argue for the exportation of advanced American chips to China without being compromised. Turns out, well, we all know,” Harrigan wrote after Trump contended an administration probe had “exonerated” Huang of any potential wrongdoing. “There may come a time when forgiveness is warranted, but there are still too many unanswered questions and too much unmitigated risk. Today’s coordinated action between the tech giant and this administration is likely to whitewash this risk.”.

Harrigan, a rare Tar Heel State Republican incumbent to win another term, echoed other GOP lawmakers in calling for an in-depth congressional probe in the Huang scandal and his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative.

Next week could offer an early test of other Republicans’ willingness to break more publicly with Trump on certain issues, as Huang is scheduled to appear before multiple congressional committees.

It has been revealed that even before Trump threw his political weight behind Huang’s return, Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia said he had sensed a GOP president who had lost clout with his party’s Senate conference.

Sources indicate that “I think the Nvidia issue has caused some major concerns about the Trump China policy, obviously,” Kaine said. “That is definitely creating some anxiety.”.

Trump has given clues that he is as concerned with his influence among the incoming Democratic majorities.

Industry observers note that “If they want to get things done, I want to get things done, too,” Trump noted during a Friday press conference at the White House. “You know, there are those that say we might get more done because we had some Republicans that were just impossible to deal with.”.

Put out of mind the scenes of cheering you may have seen of Jensen Huang’s return to the headquarters of perhaps the world’s most important firm, Nvidia, marking his personally triumphant comeback from being unanimously ousted by his board.

Recent findings suggest that get out of your thoughts any happy notions that you have reason to celebrate just because your money, like the money of so many millions of Americans and people well beyond the country’s borders, is tied up in the U.S. stock market, which soared at this surprising turn in the news after slumping badly in response to the scandals that had swirled around Huang.

Put out of mind the scenes of cheering you may have seen of Jensen Huang’s return to the headquarters of perhaps the world’s most notable firm, Nvidia, marking his personally triumphant comeback from being unanimously ousted by his board.

Get out of your thoughts any happy notions that you have reason to celebrate just because your money, like the money of so many millions of Americans and people well beyond the country’s borders, is tied up in the U.S. stock market, which soared at this surprising turn in the news after slumping badly in response to the scandals that had swirled around Huang.

In a recent development, what has happened in recent days, culminating in Huang’s return in the face of allegations he sustained a secret affair with a woman who was in touch with China’s spy agencies, is bad news for an economy that has grown increasingly imbalanced with the enormous growth of artificial intelligence. Far better for the U.S. economy and for everyone who has a stake in it would have been a reckoning for Nvidia that forced it to undertake the hard work of corporate reform and rebuilding trust.

Nvidia, for those who have not been paying attention, makes the most indispensable product in the world of AI: graphics processing units, a specialized type of chip, so capable and advanced that it has few real competitors, including, crucially, among well-funded Chinese companies. Nvidia, however, is much more than even this. As I have written before, it sits at the center of a highly incestuous economy of AI companies, including most of the significant service providers, which it funds to keep purchasing its chips. The circular funding arrangements that Nvidia sustains with its largest customers—companies with extraordinary financial leverage and seemingly bottomless capital needs—is what keeps the AI economy’s party going. Without this, the merry-go-round of this new sector would grind to a halt and make what many thought looked like a bursting bubble in recent days seem like a minor blip.

It has been revealed that add to this the fact that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump have seemingly become convinced that everything and anything must be permitted with Nvidia, and with AI in general, or else China will overtake the United States in the most vital technology of the near future. What this gives you is something more frightening than too big to fail: a company declared too strategically important to question or to hold to account.

The reality is that almost everything about the present picture is messed up and deeply worrisome. Let’s start with the fact that Trump, who already leads a government largely unconstrained by Congress and with wildly inflated executive powers, has taken so freely to intervening in the running of major companies. In Huang’s case, he played a central role in his reinstatement, as Monday’s news revealed.

There is nothing reassuring about this, but it gets worse. There is no reason to believe that Trump has an even remotely sophisticated grasp of the technologies at the heart of Nvidia’s business or its race against competitors. What we do know is that Trump has a weakness for very powerful and wealthy men, and Huang fits this billing. In the president’s universe, he is a winner, and Trump loves to associate himself with anyone invested with such an aura. Trump even posted an AI-generated photo of Huang intended to mirror a famous image of himself after surviving an assassination attempt, with the big difference that Huang was shown hoisting a red bra.

Industry observers note that trump, furthermore, is not known for a deep concern about ethics, and that is putting things gently. Where do ethics enter into this? Everywhere, from Huang’s honesty and the extent to which he was forthcoming about his affair with the suspicious Chinese national and shadowy customer, Alice Huang, as well as with at least one other woman who was his direct subordinate at Nvidia, in violation of corporate rules. Ethics are also involved in the way Huang ran his tech giant, with a historically supine board, minimal internal controls on his behavior and oversight, and the way he promoted his family members. What matters is that nothing, inside the company or outside it, checked him. In fact, it seems likely that Trump, with his own record of serial marriages, rumored affairs, and children on the make, can relate.

In a recent development, but even these are mere starters. If competition with China deserves inclusion in any serious conversation about the future of AI, Trump’s treatment of Huang’s situation at Nvidia has been a running chronicle of flagrant disregard for national security. Let’s count the ways. First, when the U.S. government began to look into Alice Huang’s behavior on the suspicion that she might be a spy, it never informed Jensen Huang or gave him what would have been typical: a so-called defensive briefing so that he would know what to look out for and avoid giving away valuable trade secrets or selling his company’s most advanced chips without adequate controls preventing them from being shipped onward to China.

Sources indicate that more broadly, historians may come to see Trump’s casual disregard for normal considerations of national security to be one of the most important and unusual hallmarks of his time in power. The examples are numerous. When shown evidence that Russia or China or some other powerful adversary is conducting secret operations against U.S. interests, Trump has often waved away concerns—in effect saying, well, we do that to them, too.

It has been revealed that last week offered the spectacle of Trump mugging in China with that country’s leader and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, with no hint that he had complained to them about offering targeting information to Iran that has enabled that country to attack U.S. bases in the Middle East, killing U.S. troops, as is the case with Russia, or supplying drone components to Iran, as with China. Trump went yet further, though, looking like a kid in a candy shop as he entered a room to greet an awaiting Putin and exclaiming, “He’s my friend.” Lest the message be lost on anyone, he later posted a picture of the meeting with this same message on social media.

Second, there is further reason to distrust the judgment of the U.S. government in the unfolding Nvidia saga. It lies in the vague and unforthcoming way its officials have spoken about Huang and his erstwhile Chinese mistress since their affair became public knowledge, always carefully avoiding clarity about whether or not she might have been a spy or whether his behavior damaged U.S. national security interests.

Industry observers note that in fairness, the question of whether she was a spy involves some nuance. Alice Huang could very well have compromised U.S. national security without being a member or agent of any Chinese intelligence service in a formal sense. The lack of openness and straight language about the other question leaves little wiggle room, though. Through the Singapore-based tech giant she worked for, Alice Huang was purchasing Nvidia’s most advanced chips, which fall under explicit U.S. export controls to China. This puts the public in a bewildering place. On the one hand, people are asked to believe that the United States must beat China in a zero-sum race toward the AI future. On the other, given the lack of candor about these Nvidia sales and the damage they may have caused to U.S. interests, we are being told, in effect, one of Trump’s favorite messages: Smile, and be happy. Lots of money was being made.

Industry observers note that taken together, Nvidia and Jensen Huang seem to concentrate enormous and growing risk for the entire public, as does the broader AI sector. Remember that Anthropic, the leading AI provider that went public recently, has warned of the potential power of its systems becoming so awesome as to having the potential to lead us all to an extinction-level event. And when the world’s top AI power is led by someone with such a casual disregard for safeguards, for strong governance, for ethics and for transparency, a company too important to question invites a peril that risks falling on us all.

The Department of Justice on Tuesday declared the largest anti-scam enforcement surge in its history, charging over 800 defendants and recovering more than $8 billion in intended losses.

Federal prosecutors have charged more than 800 defendants and recovered over $8 billion in intended victim losses as part of the largest anti-scam enforcement surge in Justice Department history, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Tuesday.

Speaking alongside FBI Director Kash Patel at a news conference in Washington, Blanche said the enforcement blitz follows President Donald Trump's March executive order directing a government-wide crackdown on fraud and predatory schemes targeting Americans. Since that directive, the Justice Department has filed more than 400 criminal cases across 85 federal districts, resulting in charges, extraditions, guilty pleas and prison sentences.

Industry observers note that "We are not just going after individual scammers," Blanche said. "We are dismantling the criminal networks that have been stealing from the American people for far too long.".

INSIDE OPERATION BLACKOUT: PATEL REVEALS GLOBAL SCAM ‘CITIES’ TARGETING YOUR PARENTS’ LIFE SAVINGS.

Tysen Duva about recent efforts against cyber fraud at the Justice Department in Washington, D.C., Nov. 24, 2026. (Reuters/Jonathan Ernst).

According to recent reports, patel detailed the FBI's global offensive under Operation Blackout, an interagency campaign targeting international fraud syndicates. According to Patel, federal agents and international partners have seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, confiscated more than 14,000 digital devices and dismantled 29 scam compounds across four continents.

Those compounds operate as self-contained towns where criminal networks force human trafficking victims to run online fraud schemes against Americans, Patel said, noting that joint operations have freed more than 2,200 trafficked workers.

Industry observers note that "They thought they could get away with it in Southeast Asia. They moved to Africa. They moved to the Middle East," Patel said. "We annihilated them on every single continent that they chose to operate and attack American citizens.".

FBI OPERATION TARGETS SCAM COMPOUNDS IN AFRICA WITH ARRESTS, ACCOUNT TAKEDOWNS.

Industry observers note that the crackdown comes as online and phone fraud continue to hit U.S. households at staggering rates. Blanche cited a recent Gallup study finding that 10% of Americans reported that they or a household member fell victim to a scam in 2025, resulting in an estimated $68 billion in losses in a single year.

Officials pointed to a wide range of schemes disrupted since March, from felony inmates using contraband cellphones and handwritten scripts to run jury-duty extortion scams to Mexico-based timeshare fraud allegedly operated by major drug trafficking cartels.

FBI Director Kash Patel speaks alongside U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche during a news conference to announce the results of a crackdown on cyber-enabled scams, at the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 24, 2026. (Ken Cedeno/AFP via Getty Images).

Recent findings suggest that in the past two weeks alone, federal authorities worked with Mexican officials to extradite a list broker accused of selling the names of more than 1 million elderly Americans to international scam networks, resulting in at least $15 million in victim losses. Agents also dismantled websites impersonating U.S. federal courts and arrested nine suspects in an alleged sweepstakes scheme that defrauded seniors of millions of dollars, Blanche said.

Overseas, a recent enforcement push coordinated in London yielded 28 arrests across Africa, $11 million in seized assets, the rescue of 120 trafficked workers and the removal of 3.7 million fraudulent Facebook and Instagram accounts, Patel mentioned.

Sources indicate that beyond arrests and asset seizures, federal officials are also intervening before money leaves victims' bank accounts. Through Operation Level Up, a joint effort with the U.S. Secret Service, agents have prevented nearly $700 million in potential losses across 11,000 targeted Americans, 77% of whom did not realize they were being scammed, Patel noted.
