The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.
  • Since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested.
  • Turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.

Ankara’s Risky Bid to Impose Regional Order.

Since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested. The previous Gulf-centered order had Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) trying to stabilize and shape the region using economic statecraft and the normalization of relations with former foes in Iran, Israel, Turkey, and Syria. Three years of war in Gaza, and more recently in Iran and the Gulf, have severely disrupted that order-building project and generated a deep sense of uncertainty about what comes next.

Turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum. Before 2023, Ankara’s influence had been in decline; after years of diplomatic isolation following the Arab uprisings, it had just begun repairing its ties with major regional actors. But in the past few years, Turkey has earned American backing for its policies in Syria and its regional diplomacy, and it has made an effort to secure the home front by pursuing a peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), a militant group that has fought a decades-long insurgency against the Turkish state. Most recently, in August, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey signed the Mecca Defense Alliance, a collective security agreement that institutionalizes Turkey’s regional positioning and pulls the country directly into Saudi Arabia’s war with the Houthis.

Turkey’s post–October 7 strategy has restored the country’s position as a regional heavyweight. But it is not capable of meeting its larger objective: establishing order on its own terms. Turkey, like the region’s other aspiring leaders, lacks the power to impose a new security framework on its own. Its nascent efforts to build one, such as the new Mecca pact, merely make countries outside the bloc feel unsafe, feeding instability. Turkey’s most ambitious plays for regional leadership are therefore likely to prove ineffective or even counterproductive. As long as the Middle East’s highly militarized, zero-sum security dynamics remain, Ankara would be better off concentrating on interests closer to home that it has the power to protect.

Recent findings suggest that this is not the first time that Turkey has tried to shape the broader Middle Eastern order. Ankara saw the Arab uprisings in the early 2010s as a historic window of opportunity. The ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) described the political transformation sweeping the region as “the people’s coming to power,” and the Turkish government expected that eventual elections in the Arab countries rocked by protest would bring into office parties aligned with the Muslim Brotherhood, which was ideologically sympathetic and had practical links to the AKP. The emergence of friendly governments, the thinking went, would increase Turkey’s influence in the region.

It has been revealed that yet these hopes soon receded. Egypt’s Muslim Brotherhood–affiliated president, Mohamed Morsi, was overthrown in 2013, and Turkey’s bet on the opposition movement in Syria failed as Bashar al-Assad clung to power. Turkey was left isolated. A rival axis composed of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE objected to Turkey’s Muslim Brotherhood ties and sought to limit Ankara’s influence. This group contested Turkey’s positions across the Middle East, North Africa, the eastern Mediterranean, and the Horn of Africa, effectively fighting proxy battles with Turkey in conflicts in Libya, Somalia, and Syria.

Then, the attacks on October 7, 2023, ushered in another period of upheaval. Some changes since have played in Turkey’s favor. Chief among them is the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024 at the hands of opposition groups led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham. Turkey had arguably invested more than any other country in pursuit of regime change in Damascus; it assisted opposition groups for years. Yet as the years went by, that objective seemed increasingly out of reach. The region’s other major powers made their peace with the regime’s survival, and even Ankara began considering rapprochement with Assad to avoid being left out in the cold. Assad’s fall changed Turkey’s fortunes overnight, handing it a level of influence in Syria it had not held in more than a decade.

Recent findings suggest that other developments proved more dangerous for Ankara. Israel’s foreign policy became more assertive and revisionist after October 7, and its expansive security objectives began to clash with Turkey’s own. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s sharp criticism of Israeli policies in Gaza strained the relationship, and it deteriorated further when Turkey expanded its foothold in post-Assad Syria and Israel came to view Ankara’s military presence there as a direct threat. As Israel continues to strike sites in Syria—attacks Ankara has condemned—the risk of escalation is only growing. A miscalculation on either side could lead to a direct clash between Israeli and Turkish forces.

The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, meanwhile, has cut both ways for Turkey. While Tehran’s attention has been focused elsewhere, Ankara has welcomed Iran’s retreat from Syria and the chance to push back against its remaining influence in Iraq. Turkey also has no interest in seeing a nuclear-armed Iran upend the regional balance of power. Yet the prospect of chaos across Turkey’s eastern border, should the Iranian regime fall, has bred real anxiety in Ankara, as has the possibility that Iran could become emboldened if the regime emerges from the war intact.

In a recent development, in this complex environment, Ankara has pursued a three-pronged strategy to protect its security interests and, it hopes, capitalize on opportunities the upheaval has created. Since U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to power, Erdogan has drawn Turkey closer to the United States and tried to use his relationship with Washington to advance Ankara’s regional policies. Turkey has also pressed ahead with regional normalization, building on efforts to repair ties with Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and other key Arab countries in the early 2020s, with the aim to forge a broader regional bloc. And, domestically, Ankara launched the “Turkey Without Terror” process, an attempt to resolve the conflict with the PKK inside and outside Turkey, which Turkey’s adversaries have long exploited by arming Kurdish groups or backing them politically.

Some of Ankara’s policies have borne fruit. Consider, for instance, the outreach to Washington. Erdogan’s close relations with Trump helped bring the United States on board with Turkey’s expanded role in Syria. Turkey was one of the four countries Washington brought in to help negotiate the U.S.-proposed October 2025 cease-fire agreement between Israel and Hamas, and as a result, Trump offered and Erdogan accepted a seat on the U.S. president’s so-called Board of Peace for Gaza’s reconstruction. Turkey has played an active part mediating between the United States and Iran during the latest war. And Trump publicly endorsed the Mecca Defense Alliance, calling it “substantial, bold, and vital.” All of this points to a recognition in Washington of Turkey’s regional importance, the U.S. administration’s willingness to support some of Ankara’s priorities, and Turkey’s determination to elevate its own position.

Yet there are undeniable limits to Turkey’s quest for influence. At a February 2026 Board of Peace summit, for instance, Turkey was excluded from participating in a planned international troop deployment and police training in Gaza—a sign that warming relations with Washington were not enough to override Israeli objections to having a Turkish military footprint in the Palestinian territory. In Syria, similarly, the support Turkey has secured from the Trump administration has not stopped Israel from launching military strikes at Syrian targets near Turkish positions. Simply put, Turkey has not been able to use its relationship with the Trump administration to overcome the limit Israeli opposition places on the scope of Turkey’s regional role.

It has been revealed that turkey’s regional normalization efforts have yielded mixed results, too. Restoring diplomatic ties with significant players such as Saudi Arabia is in Turkey’s interest, to be sure. But the alliances Ankara is entering with these countries risk making Turkey and the region less secure, not more. The Mecca pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia could end up hardening rival blocs and elevating regional tensions. Turkey insists that the alliance is directed against no country in particular and has suggested that Egypt, Syria, or even Iran could eventually join. But in the meantime, Iran, Israel, and the Houthis could see it as a threat and try to test or weaken its members’ commitment.

Furthermore, the pact could pull Turkey into other countries’ wars. That possibility is already on the table now that the Turkish parliament has ratified the agreement and the Houthis are escalating their attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Turkish government has insisted that any military support it provided would be confined to deterrence, intelligence sharing, and defense-industrial cooperation. Yet Saudi Arabia is now seeking Pakistan’s and Turkey’s help with air defense and territorial protection, and the three states have agreed to prepare forces for rapid deployment. Sending Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia would still require separate parliamentary approval. If parliament allowed it, even a limited deployment would risk drawing Turkey into a wider regional conflict.

Some kind of regional security framework is necessary. The problem is that no country in the region, including Turkey, has the power to impose a security order on the rest, so whenever someone tries, other countries feel threatened. An informal cooperation framework that is open to all countries in the region—and that asks its members to commit to nonaggression instead of making mutual-defense pledges—might work better. But the assembly and functioning of such a coalition require trust that governments in the region do not have. Breaking the impasse would likely require the United States to play a more constructive role than it has in recent years—not simply endorsing whatever regional arrangement emerges, as Trump did with the Mecca pact, or pressuring countries to normalize relations with Israel without expecting Israel to change its policies in return, as Trump has also done. Instead, Washington, perhaps with the help of Beijing, would need to compel regional rivals such as Iran and Saudi Arabia to take confidence-building measures that would make an inclusive security framework viable in the long run. Without this external push, the narrower security blocs that emerge in the region will only lead to further instability.

Ankara’s strongest cards lie closer to home. The Kurdish peace process has moved slowly since February 2025, when Abdullah Ocalan, the imprisoned leader of the PKK, called on the militant group to disarm. But it has yielded tangible progress. In May 2025, the PKK declared that it would dissolve. In Syria, Kurdish forces are being integrated into the Syrian army, and Mazloum Abdi, the commander of the People’s Defense Units, a Kurdish armed group affiliated with the PKK, was appointed as a presidential adviser in August. Syria’s postconflict transition remains fragile, and the reconciliation between Damascus and Kurdish militants in the northeast may owe as much to American pressure as it does to Turkey’s domestic efforts to make peace with the PKK. But for Turkey, the eventual integration of Syrian Kurdish forces into the Syrian state removes the risk Ankara saw in having an autonomous, armed Kurdish entity on its southern border. And, given the close security and economic ties Ankara has developed with Damascus, as well as the political and legal steps the government can take at home to complete the disbanding of the PKK and to deepen democratic reforms, Turkey has the ability to keep these encouraging developments on track.

It has been revealed that turkey’s regional policies are most successful when the country plays to its strengths—not when it is trying to throw its weight around the region. In the first decade of the twenty-first century, Ankara built real influence by mediating between Syria and Israel and between Palestinian factions, expanding its economic engagement in the Levant, and proposing projects to connect the region’s energy and transportation infrastructure. Military power, meanwhile, has proved most effective when applied for specific purposes, such as to secure the border with Syria. This combination is Turkey’s winning formula: diplomacy and economic outreach to extend its influence, and limited force to protect its core interests. Broad, open-ended commitments, by contrast, risk drawing Turkey into regional conflicts without making it safer.

Industry observers note that today, sticking to a more effective formula does not mean retreating from regional politics. It means setting priorities and planning long-term. Consolidating the Kurdish peace process, keeping Washington invested in Syria’s stabilization, managing the risk of confrontation with Israel in Syria, and maintaining constructive relations with the Kurdistan Regional Government in northern Iraq and the Iraqi government in Baghdad are key to keeping Turkey’s borders secure and are within Turkey’s ability to achieve. Ankara can continue to use its experience in mediation when opportunities to advance peace processes present themselves. It can also promote economic connectivity, both by expanding trade ties and by supporting regional infrastructure projects such as the Iraq-Europe Development Road and a proposed pipeline network connecting the Gulf to Jordan, Syria, and Turkey. It need not shy away from security cooperation with the Gulf, either, if it can engage without making formal commitments. Yet in all these endeavors, Ankara should remember that it has the most clout when it stays out of the region’s conflicts.

According to recent reports, the Middle East’s escalating wars and rival blocs could make a narrower Turkish security policy more difficult to sustain today than it was in the past. Defending Ankara’s interests and playing a constructive role in a volatile neighborhood will require a careful balance. The best way Turkey can contribute to regional stability may be to avoid trying to do too much.

Breaking: Spinning Genocide

  • In a recent development, over the last few years, some of the most vitriolic debates over Gaza have been about language: the meaning of “intifada,” the implications of “from the river to the sea,” and the importance of using the term “genocide.” Many people criticized protestors for what they believed were extreme or dangerous slogans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Over the last few years, some of the most vitriolic debates over Gaza have been about language: the meaning of “intifada,” the implications of “from the river to the sea,” and the importance of using the term “genocide.” Many people criticized protestors for what they believed were extreme or dangerous slogans. Many protestors, in turn, were furious about the shocking chasm between the horrifyingly violent reality they were seeing on social media and the understated, deadening, or deceitful language that political officials and mainstream media were using to describe it.

In a recent development, two new books offer the opportunity to look back at that surreal period with more certainty. The journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed’s Crossing the Red Line is the first reported account of what actually took place inside President Joe Biden’s administration during Israel’s war in Gaza, revealing the truth behind its often deceptive public statements. Assal Rad’s Don’t Say Palestine offers a similar dissection of how the media buttressed the government rather than challenged it, clinging to outdated journalistic notions and biases when the horror unfolding before the world demanded something far different.

In a recent development, over the last few years, some of the most vitriolic debates over Gaza have been about language: the meaning of “intifada,” the implications of “from the river to the sea,” and the importance of using the term “genocide.” Many people criticized protestors for what they believed were extreme or dangerous slogans. Many protestors, in turn, were furious about the shocking chasm between the horrifyingly violent reality they were seeing on social media and the understated, deadening, or deceitful language that political officials and mainstream media were using to describe it.

In a recent development, two latest books offer the opportunity to look back at that surreal period with more certainty. The journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed’s Crossing the Red Line is the first reported account of what actually took place inside President Joe Biden’s administration during Israel’s war in Gaza, revealing the truth behind its often deceptive public statements. Assal Rad’s Don’t Say Palestine offers a similar dissection of how the media buttressed the government rather than challenged it, clinging to outdated journalistic notions and biases when the horror unfolding before the world demanded something far different.

Rad, a scholar of Middle Eastern history, begins her book before Oct. 7, 2023. In 2021, she saw a Newly introduced York Times headline so euphemistic as to be mendacious: “Evictions in Jerusalem Become Focus of Israeli-Palestinian Conflict.” Evictions? “As a historian of the region,” Rad writes, “I was not surprised to see the way the media reflected the official account of their country’s foreign policy positions,” but that didn’t make it less infuriating. Rad posted her marked-up version on social media. It now noted, “Forced expulsions in Jerusalem Become Focus of Palestinian Struggle.”.

Don’t Say Palestine: How the Media Manufactured Consent for Genocide, Assal Rad, Vintage, 256 pp., $20, September 2026.

To Rad, the word “evictions” made ethnic cleansing sound like a real estate dispute or a municipal procedure, and left out the fact that East Jerusalem, where the events were taking place, “is recognized under international law as occupied Palestinian territory.” She knew that this controversy, which was over the Jerusalem neighborhood of Sheikh Jarrah, was representative of the central storyline in the last 150 years of Palestine’s history—a native people dispossessed of their land—and that without the historical context, or the appropriate framing and language, the present-day event made little sense.

Sources indicate that the 2021 riots that ensued when a Jewish settler group claimed these historical Palestinian homes as their own eventually developed into an 11-day war in Gaza. In retrospect, members of the Biden administration should have noticed how the U.S. public responded to this war, in which the Israeli army killed over 250 Palestinians. The officials might have seen that young Americans fresh from the Black Lives Matter movement saw parallels to the Palestinians’ plight, and that global anger at Israel’s brand of asymmetrical violence was growing.

Instead, Biden and team forged ahead, blindly supporting Israel after the Hamas attack on Oct. 7, 2023, with stunningly little awareness of how the American people and the whole world would react. Their obliviousness may have stemmed from a variety of factors: isolation in the Washington bubble, the influence of donors, the belief that Israel was a forever-ally, or a deeper racial bias. What Rad suggests in her clinical, clear-eyed book is that the media played a role in their ignorance as well by parroting the euphemistic, contextless, and factually incorrect language of the U.S. and Israeli governments.

It has been revealed that in the aftermath of Oct. 7, Rad began to rewrite headlines more regularly, particularly targeting major outlets such as the Fresh York Times, the BBC, Reuters, the Guardian, and the Associated Press. She makes a persuasive case for why headlines are important, even more so in the age of social media and the internet. “Headlines matter because people often do not read beyond them,” she writes. Their passive consumption becomes the everyday wallpaper of readers’ realities.

A panel of New York Times headlines annotated by Assal Rad. Assal Rad screenshots via Zeteo.

According to recent reports, many readers will be familiar with Rad’s concerns. Critics of the Upcoming York Times, for example, have long highlighted the newspaper’s usage of passive voice. Headlines like “Strike on Area Where Displaced Gazans Were Camped Kills Up to 25,” or “Lives Ended in Gaza” also studiously avoid naming the perpetrator. After the shocking killing of the 5-year-old child Hind Rajab—who called for help after the Israeli army fired onto her family’s vehicle, initially killing everyone besides her before fatally shooting her and the emergency workers who came to rescue her—major media outlets such as the BBC, CNN, and the New York Times failed to mention Israel or its army in their headlines. As Rad notes throughout the book, similar headlines about atrocities in Ukraine typically name Russia or Putin. Beyond this, Rad points to the use of chillingly anodyne language that is borrowed from the Israeli or U.S. militaries: “targeted strikes” for “indiscriminate bombings,” or “a humanitarian challenge” for what is in reality “a policy of starvation.”.

In the case of Israel’s wars in the Middle East, Rad exposes how the manipulation of the legal and moral term “self-defense” has come to justify more and more violence. The U.S. and Israeli governments have done this before. What’s been different in recent years, however, is that the reality of Israeli actions  has suddenly become ubiquitous and visible. “For the first time,” Rad writes, “millions around the world watched a genocide unfold live on their phones, uncensored, because of the bravery of Palestinian journalists and the reach of social media.” What Israel was doing—blowing up hospitals, collapsing universities, starving already-food-deprived populations, dropping 2,000-pound bombs on cities, men, women, and children—certainly didn’t look like self-defense.

Sources indicate that yet even when a hospital or school was bombed, the U.S. media often hedged along with the Biden government. It claimed that events still need to be investigated, leaving what people saw with their own eyes to hover in factual limbo. Worse, it would repeat officials’ assertions that, say, bombing a hospital and killing hundreds of people might have been legal because the Israeli army was “targeting Hamas,” a widely repeated phrase that came to be imbued with as much exonerating power as “self-defense.”.

Sources indicate that some of these decisions are not easy. Newspapers have a responsibility to break news promptly but never make a single factual error. Israel barred Western journalists from entering Gaza, so in the early weeks of the war newspapers might have been even more cautious before issuing blame for bombings. But ultimately, this led to them to give extraordinary weight to the testimonies of the Israeli army in assessing such ambiguities. Beyond individual incidents, Rad argues that Israel’s war on Gaza should have been framed much earlier as a deliberate campaign of annihilation or genocide, not a war between two equal parties. The laws of war might allow for some morally abhorrent actions by all sides, but those actions look different when they are mere aspects of what was (and remains) a wildly disproportionate campaign.

A photo taken during a controlled tour and subsequently edited under the supervision of the Israeli military shows Israeli soldiers patrolling a road in Rafah in the Gaza Strip on Sept. 13, 2024.Sharon Aronowicz/AFP via Getty Images.

In a recent development, indeed, it is worth asking why the mainstream media believed anything Israel’s radical, far-right, wholly corrupt government or military remarked, whether about specific bombings or larger issues, like the claim it was solely trying to “defeat Hamas.” The tendency to simply relay the arguments of public officials is one of the biggest pitfalls of supposedly objective journalism, especially when it comes to governments that have proven to be autocratic or repressive. I was surprised last year, for example, to see a New York Times headline that said, “Erdogan Calls It an Anticorruption Drive. His Rivals Call It a Political Crackdown.” Erdogan has been a repressive authoritarian leader since 2013; what is the point of putting his propaganda in the headline?

In Don’t Say Palestine, Rad repeatedly highlights these either/or question headlines. One reason for their popularity may be a boring one: They drive reader engagement. In the case of Gaza, however, it’s possible that the media’s noncommittal headlines betray a deeper, more desperate wish.

Industry observers note that as Rad and Ahmed show, Biden’s foreign policy team also seemed desperate to believe in a fantasy version of Israel. Despite the country’s long history of violence against Palestinians, and despite the repeated genocidal statements from high-level Israeli officials, Biden and his team continued to give Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Israeli army the benefit of the doubt. For Biden and those around him, Israel remained inherently good, a delusion that might have come naturally to Americans because they believe it about themselves.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hugs U.S. President Joe Biden upon his arrival at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport in Israel on Oct. 18, 2023.Brendan Smiallowski/AFP via Getty Images.

Ahmed, one of the few reporters to consistently break news and pursue stories about Biden’s foreign policy advisors, offers a painstaking, chronological account of the administration’s gross failures in Crossing the Red Line. One of the most important throughlines of Ahmed’s book is how the Biden foreign policy team subverted the very traditional processes of U.S. government, all to maintain their secretive stranglehold on this conflict.

It has been revealed that crossing the Red Line: Biden, His Advisors, and Israel’s War in Gaza, Akbar Shahid Ahmed, W.W. Norton & Co., 368 pp., $31.99, September 2026.

According to Ahmed, Biden’s team demonstrated a “disdain” for their fellow Democrats and government colleagues, sometimes acting like intelligence officers running a covert war in Latin America while swatting away annoying moral and legal restrictions. “Twice in December [2023], Blinken invoked emergency powers to ignore the standard procedures for U.S. arms deals—which involved consultation with Congress,” Ahmed writes, “so that Washington could rush equipment to the Israelis.” Uzra Zeya, who oversaw human rights work at the State Department, discouraged “split memos” in which some officials could oppose a policy that others had endorsed because those memos would put Blinken on record for whatever he decided. The resulting “consensus memos” instead created what another official called “herd immunity,” in which no one could be blamed for the policy.

Members of the Biden foreign policy team had been to law school and they knew how to twist legal logic. “For [Jake] Sullivan to claim that lack of proven intent to violate international law precluded Israel’s having committed war crimes,” Ahmed writes, “suggested that the administration could never acknowledge that that occurred.” Those violations were most visible and obvious when it came to military strikes on sites protected by international law, like medical facilities, schools, and houses of worship—all places that Israel would bomb and destroy over time. During the first bombing of Gaza’s Al-Ahli Hospital, “Biden not only declared Israel’s innocence immediately,” Rad notes, “he defined a norm in which Israel could not be guilty because its moral superiority made it incapable of such breaches … The Al-Ahli hospital episode became the model for how the Biden administration would approach the Gaza Genocide. Israel would be taken at its word, exonerated from guilt, and allowed to act with total impunity, with the backing and corroboration of the United States to provide credibility for its actions at every turn.”.

Impunity for abetting war crimes weakens U.S. democracy.

A newly introduced book details how the country slayed Washington’s foes.

Recent findings suggest that the conduct of Israel’s bombing campaign was a key element in the International Criminal Court’s case against Prime Minister Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant. Another was starvation. Using starvation as a method of warfare is a war crime; Human Rights Watch declared that Israel was doing this as early as December 2023. Yet Biden officials publicly doubted humanitarian and intelligence officials, rejecting assessments that would have been taken “as gospel” in other times. When representatives from aid groups met with White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk, Ahmed writes, “he surprised them by denying that conditions could worsen.” In a much-talked-about passage, Ahmed writes that both McGurk and Sullivan told others they didn’t think Palestinians were actually starving or looked skinny—something both men deny.

But the reason this allegation isn’t hard to believe in the context of Ahmed’s book is because an ongoing war with bombing campaigns of stunningly high frequency requires humans to constantly make all kinds of macabre logistical choices and decisions. As long time Middle East hand Aaron David Miller told the Fresh Yorker in 2024, Biden did not have the “same depth of feeling and empathy for the Palestinians of Gaza” as he did for Israel. Indeed, the Jerusalem Post revealed this month that during Biden’s last phone call with Netanyahu before leaving the White House, Biden mentioned, “You’re a good man … I admire you. It took a lot of courage to do what you did.”.

Hidaya, a 31-year-old Palestinian mother, carries her sick and malnourished 18-month-old son Mohammed al-Mutawaq inside their tent at the Al-Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, on July 24, 2025.Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP via Getty Images.

Industry observers note that the idea that Israel was actively trying to starve Gaza was softened by much of the media too, despite Israeli officials’ open declarations of this intent. Rad notes that in the Economist, a story on the threat of famine in Gaza didn’t even mention Israel. In headlines, the New York Times asked, “Why Isn’t More Aid Getting to Gazans?” and, “What is a Famine and Who Determines that One Exists?” in March and June 2024, respectively. (Israel has long controlled all food that gets into Gaza as part of its decades-long occupation and blockade.) When Israel’s defense minister Israel Katz stated explicitly that no aid would be allowed into Gaza, major outlets like Reuters posted headlines that uncritically echoed Israel’s official statements like: “Israeli Defense Minister Says No Humanitarian Aid to Enter Gaza as Tool of Pressure on Hamas.” As Rad contends, this effectively legitimized the use of hunger as a weapon of war. One BBC article remarked that over the last two years, Palestinians’ access to food had been “complicated.” “The same article repeatedly stated Israeli denials of any wrongdoing, including the government’s rejection of the [Integrated Food Security Phase Classification] report”—the global gold standard of food security assessments. According to the BBC, Israel denied that Israeli soldiers had shot and killed aid seekers, and Netanyahu denied that starvation was taking place at all.

With the normal channels blocked, the Biden administration went to embarrassing lengths to get food to Palestinians, such as building a pier in the sea and airdropping food packages, all to avoid doing the obvious, which was forcing the Israelis to allow food into the strip. The Americans also clung to and broadcast the idea that a ceasefire represented the only way to end Gaza’s suffering. No matter how many times Netanyahu rejected ceasefire terms or petulantly sabotaged them, and even after Israeli press reported Netanyahu’s obvious self-interest in prolonging the war, Biden and his team insisted it was the only way out of the unfolding disaster.

Starting in April 2024, to avoid the ceasefire he never wanted, Netanyahu began targeting people in other countries. First, there was the bombing of the Iranian consulate in Damascus; then, in July, there was the assassination of Ismail Haniyeh inside Iran; and in September, there was the Israeli pager attack on Hezbollah operatives (as well as innocent bystanders) as they went about their daily lives. In rapid succession, the Israelis then killed Hassan Nasrallah and unleashed an astounding bombing campaign on the city of Beirut, as well as a ground invasion into Southern Lebanon. Today, that region has been razed to the ground. Whole villages have been destroyed, 4,300 people have been killed, and more than 1.2 million displaced.

Recent findings suggest that at every horrific turn in Crossing the Red Line, Ahmed stops to remind us that the same day, week, or month that another horror or humiliation occurred, the Biden administration would decide to send more weapons to Israel anyway. “Regardless of the gut-wrenching cost and their mutual disdain,” Ahmed writes, “Netanyahu and Biden might still take credit for a new Middle East in which Israel held more sway.”.

In a recent development, palestinians bury relatives killed in overnight Israeli strikes on the Fatima Bint Asad school in Jabalia, at a cemetery in the northern Gaza Strip on May 12, 2025. Bashar Taleb/AFP via Getty Images.

Ahmed argues that careerism and groupthink fueled a lot of the behavior of the Biden team. But his reporting also suggests that strengthening Israel—ensuring that it wins everything—was a goal in itself. For decades, U.S. policy was for Israel to be the strongest country in the Middle East, and in 2025, a U.S. government at last achieved that goal. Israel became the region’s undeniable military heavyweight.

Recent findings suggest that thanks to works like Rad’s and Ahmed’s, the human toll of this policy has become clear to most Americans. Increasingly, newspaper headlines have reflected this reality, too. Here’s a recent one from the New York Times: “Israel Has Committed Genocidal Acts in Gaza Since Cease-Fire, U.N. Human Rights Panel Indicates.” For her part, Rad does not deny that many journalists who have written and reported on the war have done excellent work. The value of her critique is more about these Western publications as a whole – how they often fail to fulfill their most vital professional purpose:  holding the powerful to account.

For the Biden team, the failure of accountability has continued even after leaving office. Confronted with evidence of their culpability in this nightmare, former officials now use opaque and passive language, as if the people who ran the most powerful country in the world simply had no control of events, no control over Netanyahu and no control over President Biden, that sad prisoner of a 1970s sepia-toned fever dream about Golda Meir. As a result, they end up implying that they were merely shirking their moral responsibility to please their aging leader, as if they were functionaries in an authoritarian regime.

In a recent development, it’s possible—in the sense that anything is possible—that these officials were ignorant of what kind of country Israel had become in the last 20 years. Ignorance of cultures and history, after all, was a major engine of the Americans’ failed wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Moments in Ahmed’s book manage to surprise even him, such as when veteran Middle East diplomat Barbara Leaf cries, “Come on, the IDF doesn’t participate in settler violence!” Perhaps Biden’s team were also victims of decades of misleading or understated media headlines and that was why they continued to give Israeli leaders the benefit of the doubt—or take them at their word. But there is another term for consistently giving the benefit of the doubt to people who share your skin color over people who don’t. In Crossing the Red Line, Ahmed argues that the war on terror conditioned most “U.S. foreign policy professionals” to be comfortable “with jaw-dropping atrocities and dehumanizing of people in the region.” Rad goes back further, to the entire history of Palestine. “The horrors that have been normalized in Gaza,” she writes, “are the culmination of this long history of racism and injustice.”.

Today, Republicans, some Democrats, and probably much of the U.S. security state is still responsible for supporting Netanyahu’s government as it works to destroy Gaza. It was Americans’ own corrupted consensus and Israeli’s murderous one that came together to wreck the international legal order, all while Western media organs chronicled the downfall of that order in careful, hedging tones. One of the most accurate headlines about Gaza, Rad writes, came from the satirical newspaper the Onion following the October 2025 ceasefire announcement: “Israel Agrees to Go Back to Killing Palestinians on Less Frequent Basis.” The advantage of fact-based, active-voiced headlines is that they don’t only tell what’s happening in the present. They tell what will still be happening in the future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ohio State accounting professor Brian Mittendorf examines the Obama Foundation's financial health, assets and endowment as construction costs hit $1 billion.

Former President Joe Biden has raised a shockingly small amount of funds for his presidential library compared to former President Barack Obama.

The figures are fueling skepticism about how history will remember Biden's single term in the White House.

In a recent development, in 2017, Obama’s first year out of office, the two-term president managed to bring in $232.6 million in donations and contributions to fund the foundation behind his presidential library. By comparison, Biden secured just $1.5 million in 2025 for his presidential library foundation, per tax filings.

This is less than 1% of what his former boss raised in the same amount of time after leaving office.

Even before leaving office, President Donald Trump’s library foundation has already dwarfed that of his predecessor by raising tens of millions of dollars from a variety of sources, including companies that settled lawsuits with him.

In a recent development, OBAMA CENTER ISN'T A TRADITIONAL PRESIDENTIAL LIBRARY. CRITICS SAY IT'S AN ACTIVISM CENTER.

Industry observers note that former US presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden shake hands during the opening of the Barack Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, Illinois, on June 18, 2026. (Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images).

Though the Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation has yet to decide on a construction site, it’s already running a deficit, spending $600,000 more than it raised in 2025. A Biden library official claimed that it wasn’t actively fundraising in 2025 in a statement shared with CBS News.

The lack of enthusiasm for Biden’s legacy has led some to claim that Americans may simply forget about his presidency as the years go on.

According to recent reports, "Presidencies usually fade," Axios’ Zachary Basu wrote of his legacy. "But in just one year, Biden’s has been reduced to a footnote by a successor committed to dismantling every pillar of Washington’s old liberal order.".

Heritage Action press manager Doug Blair told Fox News Digital, "Joe Biden spent half a century in Washington and did nothing to benefit the American people.".

In a recent development, "The anemic fundraising for his presidential library is a fitting bookend for a failed presidency Americans are eager to forget," he added. "Joe Biden left Americans worse off by every conceivable measure and his legacy will be a southern border blown wide open, the disgraceful image of him checking his watch as fallen American troops returned home from Afghanistan, and endless scandals and investigations surrounding him and his corrupt family.'.

BIDEN'S BATTLE WITH ADVANCING CANCER RENEWS FOCUS ON PROSTATE DISEASE.

Allies of the former president point to the fact that Biden presided over the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, influential pieces of domestic legislation and America’s withdrawal from Afghanistan, parts of his legacy that could contribute to historical staying power.

It has been revealed that A January 2025 Gallup poll found that 54% of U.S. adults believed history would remember Biden as a "below-average" or "poor" president.

It has been revealed that former U.S. President Joe Biden attends the dedication ceremony for the opening of the Barack Obama Presidential Center in John Lewis Plaza (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images).

A source close to Biden’s foundation told CBS News that it ramped up its fundraising in 2026, pulling in multiple multi-million-dollar contributions, including two $5 million donations.

Another source told the outlet that some of Biden's close allies are frustrated that Democratic donors aren’t stepping up to support the former president’s library.

Further complicating Biden’s fundraising efforts, and his ability to nurture his public image, is his advanced age and Stage 4 prostate cancer, which has metastasized to his bones.

OBAMA CENTER OPENS AFTER YEARS-LONG SAGA AS LOCALS WARN ‘MONSTROSITY’ COULD PRICE THEM OUT.

Former President Barack Obama and the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, where construction costs are now projected to reach approximately $1 billion, nearly triple the upper end of the original estimate. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images; Talía Sprague/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

While the increase in funds is no doubt encouraging for Biden’s allies, it still puts them far behind Obama, who raised $164.8 million for his foundation in 2018.

Obama ultimately spent nearly $1 billion on his presidential library in Chicago, a sum Biden likely will not be able to reach given his current fundraising levels.

Is China Misreading the Moment?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3227 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations.
  • Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.
  • President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. He served as Director and Deputy Senior Director for China and Taiwan Affairs at the National Security Council from 2021 to 2024.

Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.

Sources indicate that when U.S. President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing. The trade war of 2025 is in abeyance, the two governments have confirmed a relationship of “constructive strategic stability,” and, to the alarm of American allies, Trump and Xi are planning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Beneath the surface, however, the détente is beginning to crack.

It has been revealed that the relationship between Washington and Beijing looks remarkably different from the way it did a little over a year ago, when the two sides agreed to a truce in Busan, South Korea. In April 2025, Washington initiated the trade war by raising tariffs on China past 140 percent, and Beijing responded by restricting rare-earth exports later that month and threatening another cutoff that October. After Trump promptly backed down, the two leaders reached the deal in Busan: Washington would cap tariffs and suspend a specific export control regulation known as the Affiliates Rule in exchange for Beijing’s suspension of newly introduced export controls on minerals and magnets and the resumption of their normal flow to the United States. On that basis, both sides pursued a broad deescalation.

Sources indicate that since then, the Trump administration has been notably accommodating. Washington has kept fresh tariffs at 12.5 percent, well below the 20-percent ceiling Beijing previously agreed to. It has let advanced AI chips flow to China and to Chinese cutouts in Southeast Asia and has not added a Chinese firm to the Entity List in over the year, the longest pause since 2008. It has withheld arms sales from and downgraded defense talks with Taiwan, cut back naval transits of the Taiwan Strait, and raised doubts about U.S. support in the event of a crisis. And it has offered only muted support to such allies as Japan and the Philippines in the face of escalating Chinese coercion. All the while, Trump has praised Xi as a “great leader” and extended rare courtesies, including by welcoming Xi on the tarmac when he arrived in Washington for a state visit in September, the first such greeting of a foreign leader in 60 years.

In a recent development, beijing has appreciated this accommodating approach—and seized the opportunity to act more assertively. It has viewed the competitive pause as temporary, a product of China’s growing strength and Trump’s admiration for Xi, and as a way to buy time to build advantage before the next eruption of tensions. With Washington occupied by its war in Iran and humbled by defeat in the last round of the trade war, Beijing has throttled the supply of minerals and magnets to the United States, taken steps to ensure that its industrial and technological gains remain in China, and increased pressure on its neighbors.

Sources indicate that so far, Beijing has used the time well, advancing its objectives with little serious pushback from Washington. But China risks overreaching in its relationship with the United States. Not only is an incoming Democratic Congress likely to constrain Trump’s conciliatory China policy. There are also growing frustrations over Beijing’s unwillingness to fulfill the terms agreed to in Busan. Pressure on AI chips and export controls are emerging in the wake of revelations about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and his organization’s influence over U.S. export control policy. And new U.S. policies in response to the scandal could provoke a response from Beijing.

Xi and Trump will meet in Shenzhen and again in December in Miami, but with the January expiration of the Busan agreement looming in the background (and with no summits planned for next year), time is running out for the two leaders to extend and strengthen the current truce. If the détente falls apart the next time Washington’s and Beijing’s interests clash, China will be better prepared. It may also, perhaps hubristically, be more willing to escalate.

Industry observers note that although China favors Washington’s current accommodating approach and hopes it will last as long as possible, Beijing is also confident that it is strengthening its hand for a more contentious future. For China’s leaders, the current détente has been less an end goal than a temporary intermission, a means to build leverage ahead of the next round of strategic competition and, ultimately, a decisive long-term advantage.

Prominent Chinese scholars see the calm that followed Busan as tactical rather than strategic. Chen Dongxiao, the president of the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, told the Shanghai news outlet The Paper that the two countries remain in a “tactical truce.” In May, Wu Xinbo of Fudan University told Beijing News, “If we can achieve a relationship of constructive strategic stability over the next three years, it will extend China’s period of strategic stability and win us time and space for development.” Writing in the journal International Review in August, he declared that the current “tactical stability” was “neither sustainable nor solid.” Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese foreign ministry official, was more blunt: “The more time we have, the better prepared we might be towards a final showdown on Taiwan or maybe another trade war.”.

According to recent reports, beijing attributes little of the stabilization to Washington. In his August essay, Wu wrote that it “is not the result of the U.S. side having a change of heart or showing goodwill, but was won by China through arduous striving and struggle.” The United States had no choice; it simply needed the “breathing room.” Wang Yong, the director of Peking University’s American Studies Center, described the trade war as “a tipping point in terms of strength.” The former editor of the Global Times, Hu Xijin, wrote in a Weibo post after the U.S. midterm elections that “the current equilibrium in U.S.-China relations is the result of a contest of strength.” As Wu told The Paper in September, Washington has come to understand that Beijing “needs to be treated equally and with respect” and that China is “bolder about ‘drawing its sword.’” Keeping the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets tight, to Beijing’s mind, might reinforce the current competitive pause rather than undermine it by reminding American leaders of China’s leverage.

In a recent development, another critical factor in the current de-escalation, Chinese analysts argue, is Trump’s personality. Trump’s “distinct and unique decision-making style,” as Chen put it, has single-handedly blunted the more forceful defense of U.S. interests that members of his own administration and legislators in both parties favor. “He is often not entirely swayed by bipartisan opposition and still continues to pursue policies based on his own judgment,” Chen explained in the same interview. Writing in the Singaporean paper Lianhe Zaobao in September, Zhao Minghao of Fudan University more pointedly explained that Trump “admires power and prefers to engage with the leaders of powerful countries,” a stabilizing trait that benefits Beijing’s diplomacy while leaving allies and partners on the sidelines. “Of all modern U.S. presidents, Trump has cared the least about Taiwan,” one Guizhou-based commentator wrote. “He would readily sacrifice the island for his own interests.” An article reposted on the website of Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party’s flagship journal, dwelt on Trump’s decision to greet Xi at the airport when he arrived for his state visit in September. The gesture, it claimed, “reflects the new historical position of China-U.S. relations.”.

But China also worries that Trump’s influence will decline over the next two years and perhaps cease altogether after 2028. Wang Hao, a professor at Fudan University’s Center for American Studies, told Phoenix News that the Democratic Party’s approach will not be “as pragmatic and flexible as the Trump administration’s,” a sentiment echoed across Chinese social media after the Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections.

The awareness that Trump’s approach may not survive beyond his presidency is precisely why Beijing has sought to lock it in through diplomacy. According to the Chinese readout, at the summit in May 2026, Xi declared that the relationship of “constructive strategic stability” he and Trump had agreed to build would provide guidance for U.S.-Chinese relations “over the next three years and beyond.” That duration was not accidental. As the scholar Zheng Yongnian put it at the time, the three-year window was “tailor-made for President Trump,” matching his current term. Beijing hopes it will bind his successor.

If diplomacy fails to secure U.S. deescalation, China hopes leverage will succeed. Over the last year, Beijing has used the time and space created by the détente to strengthen its position in industrial and technological competition with the United States. Beijing has long sought to make the world more dependent on China while reducing its own dependence on the world. But over the last year, that approach has evolved. Beijing has unveiled a raft of measures intended to ensure that its industrial, technological, and scientific know-how do not diffuse beyond China’s borders in order to lock in the country’s advantages.

It has been revealed that to keep foreign firms in China and blunt Western countries’ leverage over the Chinese economy, the State Council issued Orders 834 and 835, which effectively threaten companies that cut ties with Chinese partners or seek to exit the country with the risk of investigation, exclusion from the Chinese market, exit bans on executives, and possible criminal prosecution. To keep talent in China, Beijing has authorized exit bans on citizens considered possible risks to industrial or technological security and, according to Bloomberg, now requires travel approval for top AI and chip specialists and their families. And to keep scientific discoveries in China, the Ministry of State Security has warned researchers that they must clear security reviews before submitting articles to foreign journals. China has also imposed or proposed newly introduced export controls on dozens of technologies, from mining and batteries to AI models and biotechnology in order to protect its industrial capabilities. Beijing has even worked to prevent the transfer of equipment and engineers to India and Southeast Asia, stalled battery ventures with Indian firms, undermined Apple’s effort to move manufacturing to India, and issued a sweeping regulation that subjects Chinese investment abroad to a national security review more expansive than the United States’ own outbound investment review.

Beijing’s rare-earth licensing regime exemplifies China’s leverage-building strategy. To obtain a license, foreign buyers must hand over customer lists, the identities of their end customers, and images of their production lines, all of which gives China insight into Western dependencies and helps it uncover chokepoints it can squeeze. Beijing has threatened to use these powers against countries that seek to protect themselves from the flood of Chinese manufactured goods entering their markets. In July, Beijing showed how precise it can now be in applying pressure when it cut off 14 European firms, including the German arms maker Rheinmetall, from Chinese dual-use exports in retaliation for EU sanctions related to Chinese support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Beijing has paired these measures at home with escalating pressure campaigns in its near abroad, betting that a distracted and chastened Washington will not come to the aid of China’s neighbors. That campaign has been most brazen in the South China Sea, where China has engaged in escalations unseen before the détente. Since Busan, Beijing has essentially abrogated its 2024 understanding with the Philippines, which maintained stability on the question of Second Thomas Shoal. In July, a Chinese coast guard boat rammed a Philippine navy inflatable and its crew clubbed a sailor on the head with a wooden baton, the most violent assault on Philippine personnel in years.

The timing of these incidents has been provocative. In July, when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio were in Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations meetings, the coast guard debuted water-cannon attacks on Philippine vessels near Scarborough Shoal. Then, in September, during Xi’s U.S. state visit, Chinese warships and cutters blocked a Philippine resupply mission outright for the first time in two years. In October, Chinese cutters interfered with a medical evacuation from Second Thomas Shoal, delaying a patient transfer by ten hours. Last month, Beijing’s ambassador in Manila mused that if China chose to use force against the Philippines, “we may easily win.”.

China has also run its broadest coercion campaign against Japan in more than a decade, nominally in response to comments made by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Taiwan. It has included a travel advisory, a seafood ban, a dual-use export ban, and curbs on rare-earth exports that have forced Japanese companies to contemplate shutting down operations. Chinese carrier-based fighters have locked their weapons-targeting radar onto Japanese jets. Beijing has also pursued new gas structures in the East China Sea and set a record 357-day coast guard presence in 2025 around the Japanese-administered Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands), with cutters now chasing Japanese fishing boats into territorial waters. Washington’s support for Tokyo has, so far, been limited.

In a recent development, and around Taiwan, China has made its pressure quieter but more routine. In December 2025, during the People’s Liberation Army’s Justice Mission exercises, China fired live rockets closer to Taiwan than ever before, landing ten of them inside the island’s 24-nautical-mile contiguous zone. As of this summer, Beijing has reduced air incursions, but coast guard activity around Taiwan’s outlying islands has become routinized. And since June, Beijing has run standing “law enforcement patrols” east of Taiwan, asserting jurisdiction over the waters Taipei would need in a blockade.

Outside of Asia, Beijing has sought to take advantage of anger, particularly in the developing world, at the Trump administration’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and the Iran war. Before traveling to Washington, Xi made a point of stopping in several capitals: he toured Bishkek and Cairo, and attended the BRICS summit in New Delhi, stressing that China, not the United States, is now the steadier partner.

Beijing has reason to think this approach is working. It rightly judged that Washington would prioritize keeping the détente alive over responding to its provocations. A year after Busan, China holds a tighter grip on critical supply chains, has set latest precedents in Asia, and faces an adversary in Washington that has grown used to holding back. Beijing likely believes it is better off now than it was when the truce began.

What looks like success now, however, may still prove to be overreach. In addition to rare earths and magnets, several notable questions went unresolved in past U.S.-Chinese summits and are likely to resurface in this week’s summit in Shenzhen, including China’s anticipated purchases of Boeing aircraft and agricultural products, AI safety, and the United States’ suspension of arms sales to Taiwan. But the most important question is what will become of the current trade truce.

The United States has complied with the terms of the Busan agreement, suspending the Affiliates Rule and lowering tariffs, but Beijing has throttled the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets to the United States. U.S. officials say China has delivered only about two-thirds of what it promised, and trade data suggest the shortfall is larger still. The administration believes Beijing’s noncompliance is deliberate. Anecdotal evidence from American business leaders in regular touch with the Ministry of Commerce confirms the administration’s assessment that Beijing seeks to keep a tight leash on rare-earth minerals and will occasionally “yank the chain” on individual companies in response to any perceived slight by Washington.

From the U.S. perspective, the very point of the Busan negotiations was to avoid this situation. Indeed, the U.S. fact sheet at Busan indicated that China agreed to glitch general licenses for a number of rare earths and other critical minerals to American end customers and their suppliers worldwide; case-by-case licenses, which could be delayed by Beijing, would not be required. China has not denied making that commitment, and a few weeks after the summit, the Ministry of Commerce began issuing a upcoming category of general licenses to magnet makers. But Beijing’s licenses have been narrow and firm specific, and American industry continues to face enormous challenges in securing certain rare earths, notably yttrium and scandium.

Beijing’s intention may not be to undermine the Busan agreement but, paradoxically, to strengthen it. In keeping with its belief that strength begets American conciliation, China’s strategy appears to be to occasionally impose shortages to remind Washington of the leverage that Beijing continues to enjoy. But the tactic is beginning to backfire. Shortages of yttrium, used for jet engines and gas turbines, have forced some suppliers to suspend production. Chipmakers are running short of scandium. All of this strengthens the arguments of those who believe Beijing never intended to honor Busan and that the United States should begin to walk away from the agreement. If Washington concludes that China will weaponize rare earths no matter what the United States does, the case for American restraint may fall apart, and with it the détente that has bought Beijing the time it prizes.

Industry observers note that tensions are also mounting in other areas. Each side is increasingly frustrated with the other’s unilateral economic measures and restrictions on technology, particularly those that were not addressed in Busan: for Beijing, U.S. import controls, outbound investment regimes, and licensing backlogs; for Washington, Chinese export controls and State Council directives. A Democratic Congress is less likely to countenance Trump’s China policy and more likely to pursue investigations into China’s espionage and influence efforts and potential malfeasance at the Department of Commerce. The explosive controversy around Huang and Nvidia has the potential to inject fresh tensions into the relationship, particularly on matters related to AI and export controls. The Department of Commerce has already issued a upcoming interim final rule to stop Chinese firms from smuggling chips into China or remotely accessing American AI chips in Southeast Asian data centers. Administration officials insist that closing a loophole China itself claims not to use “should not be something that generates countermeasures.” But Beijing may well retaliate before the rule takes effect in February.

In a recent development, these headwinds make breakthroughs in Shenzhen on purchases, artificial intelligence, nuclear weapons, or Iran less likely. With the truce, extended last week by just two months, set to formally expire on January 10, the summit is one of the last opportunities for Trump and Xi to reach even a modest declaration that they are working to extend the terms set out in Busan and will aim to conclude negotiations in December, when Xi comes to Miami for the G-20 summit.

In a recent development, if China were to continue to throttle rare-earth minerals and magnets, and a January breakdown did come to pass, the two sides might find themselves in another round of escalation. Xi may arrive at the two upcoming summits holding a stronger hand than he did in Busan. But his actions are gradually producing a counterpart with less room—and perhaps less reason—to keep folding.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming era of maritime chokepoint disruption has, in many ways, highlighted the importance of Africa’s Red Sea and Gulf of Aden states. The Houthis’ ability to hold the Bab el-Mandeb at risk, combined with the deepening rivalry between the Abraham and Mecca blocs of the Middle East, have created powerful incentives for a range of extra-regional actors to further expand their partnerships along the Horn of Africa’s coastline. This is particularly clear in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where the United Arab Emirates, Israel, and the United States have grown their diplomatic and military engagement in Puntland and Somaliland, and where the United States has pursued a diplomatic rapprochement with Eritrea.

What does this mean for the Horn of Africa’s littoral states? Although their geographic proximity to what Bruno Macaes called “the strait at the center of the world” has emerged as valuable strategic currency, it is not hard to see how the attempt to coopt Africa’s Red Sea states into one alliance or another could go wrong. The concerns are threefold: that the Horn’s littoral states might become entrapped in conflicts that are not their own; that the intra-Horn rivalries the littoral states are already enmeshed in are made more acute; and that internal governance conditions in the Horn’s states further deteriorate.
