The Only Way to End the Netanyahu Era

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that AYMAN ODEH served in the Knesset from 2015 to 2026.
  • Arab Citizens of Israel Can Bring Change, but They Can’t Do It Alone.
  • Recent findings suggest that as the Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot struggles to assemble a governing coalition following last month’s elections, Israel finds itself in a familiar political predicament.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that AYMAN ODEH served in the Knesset from 2015 to 2026. He is the former leader of the Joint List and the Hadash party.

Arab Citizens of Israel Can Bring Change, but They Can’t Do It Alone.

Recent findings suggest that as the Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot struggles to assemble a governing coalition following last month’s elections, Israel finds itself in a familiar political predicament. The parties opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition command a clear majority in the Knesset, with 67 of its 120 seats. Yet the four Jewish-led parties in Eisenkot’s camp hold just 48 seats, leaving them unable to form a government on their own. The impasse echoes the prolonged political deadlock between 2019 and 2021, when Netanyahu’s supporters and his opponents remained locked in competing parliamentary blocs, and four consecutive elections failed to produce a stable governing majority.

But one thing is different this time. Israel’s Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Raam, are stronger than ever. Powered by extraordinary turnout among Arab citizens of Israel, they won a record 19 seats in the Knesset: 11 for the Joint List and eight for Raam. This political mobilization is crucial in itself, demonstrating Arab voters’ overwhelming desire for change and their recognition of the importance of participating in elections. But its significance goes far beyond the number of seats they have won. Together, the Arab parties now have the potential to be a decisive force in an anti-Netanyahu coalition, providing the parliamentary backing needed to form a government. The proof of this power has already been shown: on November 17, Arab support was crucial in the vote to replace the Likud speaker of the Knesset with a speaker from Eisenkot’s party. Now they have a historic opportunity to put the country on a different path.

As the first and former leader of the Joint List, I know how much is at stake. In 2019, I helped lead a groundbreaking effort to give Arab-led parties a direct voice in the Israeli political system. We took an enormous political risk by endorsing Benny Gantz, then a former chief of staff of the Israeli military and Netanyahu’s principal rival, as a candidate to form a government. We did so despite our profound political and ideological differences with him. Although that effort ultimately fell short, with Gantz choosing to pursue a “unity government” with Netanyahu instead, it established an key precedent: by showing a willingness to work with Jewish political forces with whom they had deep disagreements, parties representing the Arab public had a real chance to prevent a Netanyahu-led far-right government from holding power.

Today, after nearly four years of disastrous leadership by Netanyahu and his far-right allies, that possibility has become far more urgent. It will take political courage on both sides. Eisenkot must be able to offer something to the Arab-led parties, and the Arab-led parties will need to be comfortable offering support to a government that they may not agree with on many concerns. But the remarkable Arab turnout and the sizable Israeli majority that is now against Netanyahu have pointed to a way forward. Not only Israel’s future but also its place in the region and the world may depend on the willingness of its leaders to engage with the country’s Palestinian minority. Ultimately, such a partnership will be essential to building the trust between Jews and Arabs that is a prerequisite to achieving any real progress toward a viable Israeli-Palestinian peace. This is the real choice now facing Israel: whether Israelis are prepared to replace the politics of supremacy and exclusion with a politics of equality.

In a recent development, the factors that drove record numbers of Palestinian citizens of Israel to the polls in October have been years in the making. Although the country’s Arab citizens make up more than 20 percent of the Israeli electorate and have long made vital contributions to Israeli society as doctors, lawyers, engineers, high-tech professionals, and in many other fields, the Israeli right has for decades demonized them as enemies: a fifth column and a threat to the state. In recent years, this hostility has increasingly manifested itself in harassment and open racism at universities and workplaces, in the media, in the parliament, and in everyday life.

Recent findings suggest that yet it would be a mistake to assume that Arab exclusion has been driven only by Netanyahu and the radical right. Zionist parties of the center and the left have also contributed, by keeping a distance from Arab voters or simply ignoring them. The belief that Jewish citizens should ultimately determine the country’s political direction while Arab citizens must remain within whatever limits have been set for them runs deep in Israeli politics. Netanyahu understood early on how to turn this contradiction into a political strategy. Since the 1990s, he has repeatedly used the same formula: inciting his supporters against Arab citizens, delegitimizing Arab representatives in parliament, and convincing Jewish Israelis that a government that relies on Arab political support would somehow be illegitimate.

In a recent development, these tactics proved to be among Netanyahu’s most effective political tools, especially given that Arab-led parties have long been some of his biggest foes. He didn’t need to convince everyone to support his Likud party or its various coalition partners. He only needed to convince enough people, including Jewish Israelis who opposed him, that working with Arab-led parties was dangerous and unacceptable. Netanyahu’s strategy also helped suppress Arab turnout. Since the Arab-led parties had little chance of changing the status quo, Arab voters had little incentive to vote: for many years, a significantly lower proportion of Arab citizens went to the polls than did their Jewish counterparts.

That began to change in 2015 with the creation of the Joint List, which for the first time brought together four parties representing the Arab public on a single electoral ticket and which became the third-largest faction in the Knesset. By embracing a broader vision for our society, grounded in Jewish-Arab solidarity and opposition to the racism of the right, the Joint List demonstrated that Palestinian citizens of Israel could play a latest and more influential role in the country’s political system. Then, under my leadership in 2019, the Joint List decided to back Gantz’s bid to unseat Netanyahu. The decision was highly controversial, both within the Arab electorate and across Israeli society. Many Arab voters were deeply ambivalent about supporting a potential government led by a former army chief whose political positions, particularly on the status of Palestinian citizens of Israel and the occupation, differed sharply from their own. Nevertheless, we were prepared to take that political risk because we understood that defeating Netanyahu was more key.

Industry observers note that in practice, our willingness to cooperate with the Zionist opposition was not, in fact, reciprocated. The Jewish opposition parties wanted our votes but could not bring themselves to accept us as equal political partners. And, ultimately, Gantz decided to form a government with Netanyahu instead. Nevertheless, the experience showed that Jewish-Arab political cooperation could open up latest horizons for a large segment of the public. Since then, every time that Arab-led parties have recommended or supported the effort of a Jewish candidate to form a government, or whenever the Israeli center-left has depended on their support, additional segments of Israeli society have become more open to this kind of cooperation.

It has been revealed that in 2021–22, an Arab party, Raam, joined the short-lived government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. I had serious reservations about the model of partnership that emerged, which seemed to rest on the expectation that Arab political representatives would limit their involvement to civilian and domestic matters, while refraining from addressing political and national questions, particularly the occupation and the Palestinian issue. I reject this distinction. We are part of the Palestinian people, and our identity and political concerns cannot be separated from our citizenship in Israel.

But these kinds of slow and painful steps are how political change often happens in national struggles. It does not always begin with a moral or democratic awakening. Sometimes, it begins with pragmatic necessity. When there is no other option, people begin to reconsider what had once been seen as impossible. In the current election, that dynamic has become even more important. After the unending crisis of the past four years, many Israeli voters, including both Arabs and Jews as well as the leaders of most of the Zionist opposition parties, have concluded that getting rid of the Netanyahu government is more necessary than ever.

In recent past elections, voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel has generally remained between 50 and 60 percent. What explains the unprecedented 20-percentage-point surge in turnout in the October election? Three developments stand out: the war of annihilation in Gaza and the killing of tens of thousands of Palestinians; the daily racism and hostility that Arab citizens now face in the streets, in public spaces, and in virtually every aspect of their lives; and the crime that has spiraled out of control in Arab communities under the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose policies have allowed it to flourish, and the relentless settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank enabled by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. All the grief and frustration accumulated over these years were brought to the ballot box.

But there was another crucial factor as well. In the run-up to the election, Arab citizens, following the nearly even polls between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, could see in black and white just how much the outcome would depend on them. Voting this time would be more than a political choice. It was for many a personal responsibility and a way of taking control of their own future. That is why hundreds of thousands of Palestinian citizens of Israel made their way to the polls, defying years of efforts to silence them and undermine their political agency. Many understood that the future direction of the country might be quite literally in their hands.

Recent findings suggest that I saw elderly people, like my friend Jumah from Jisr al-Zarqa, taking to the streets and campaigning for the Joint List. Many of them had lived through the 1948 nakba, or “catastrophe,” which accompanied Israel’s establishment and involved terrible massacres, the destruction of hundreds of Palestinian villages and towns, and the displacement of around 750,000 Palestinians. I saw young people debating politics in the cafes and restaurants of my beloved Haifa, persuading their friends to vote. I saw women and men from Nazareth, Umm al-Fahm, Sakhnin, Rahat, Akko, Kafr Yasif, Majd al-Krum, and countless other towns and villages united by a shared sense of purpose. I saw political consciousness become a living, collective force. For a moment, the boundaries between generations and communities seemed to disappear.

The result marks a remarkable advance of the process of Arab participation in the Israeli political system that began in 2019. In this election, Arab citizens of Israel turned out in record numbers, dramatically narrowing the historical turnout gap with Jewish voters. And that has made another political reality increasingly clear: Israel’s liberal and centrist camp cannot form a government without the parties that represent the Arab public. If it excludes them, as well as the ultra-Orthodox and the far right, it will not reach the 61 seats needed. This is the demographic reality. Israeli Jews who oppose Netanyahu must decide whom they are willing to build a political future with.

The debate about what Eisenkot should do and whether he should ask for Arab support is now unfolding beyond the Knesset, in people’s homes, cafés, in universities, and on the street. It is a deeply controversial question, and many Israelis disagree strenuously about it. Yet for the Arab-led parties, gaining sufficient importance to be able to provoke these conversations is an achievement. The fact that this debate is even taking place demonstrates how the political process has caused Israelis to consider possibilities that until recently seemed unimaginable.

Recent findings suggest that in the end, Eisenkot may have few other options if he wants to replace Netanyahu, as he has promised. In most cases, political parties support coalitions to advance positive changes and achieve concrete goals. But there are moments when political cooperation is necessary for a different reason: to prevent something far worse. The most immediate and overriding objective today is to bring an end to the far-right Netanyahu government. That is a priority on which both the Zionist opposition and the Arab-led parties can agree.

Beyond this shared basic goal, the Arab-led parties should use their political influence to work on two levels. First, they must seek tangible improvements in their constituents’ lives: combating organized crime in Arab communities, securing budgets, addressing the housing crisis, ending the brutal treatment of Palestinians living under occupation in the West Bank, and pushing for a permanent cease-fire and the reconstruction of Gaza. These are fundamental concerns of human dignity and civilian life. On a broader level, they should continue to push for real progress on Israeli-Palestinian peace that is ultimately based on two states coexisting, side by side.

It has been revealed that I do not expect the current Israeli political establishment to embrace these positions, but that does not mean that the Arab parties should not raise them at every opportunity. At the same time, the Arab parties can use their newfound political clout to build alliances between Jews and Arabs around shared political and strategic goals. The resulting partnerships must be about more than parliamentary arrangements; it must also create the foundations for a different future. That will require Jewish and Arab citizens of Israel to engage with one another on the basis of equality, rather than mere political convenience.

Thus far, Eisenkot has given few indications that he is prepared to go down this path. Since the election, it has been encouraging to see him condemn Netanyahu for fueling what he described as a “racist and violent” campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens. Yet many of the mainstream Zionist parties in Eisenkot’s camp have vowed not to work with the Arab parties. Still, Eisenkot must consider what that would mean. Thirty years from now, people will ask how Jewish supremacy became so normalized that even politicians who called themselves democrats accepted the exclusion of one-fifth of their fellow citizens. They will ask why Israel’s opposition could recognize the danger posed by Netanyahu’s government but not confront the assumptions that made his politics possible.

Sources indicate that there is an irony in the fact that, in a country that seeks to keep political hegemony exclusively in Jewish hands, the Palestinian minority, after decades of struggle for political recognition and equal rights, has emerged as one of the most significant forces shaping the country’s political future. We have come to understand that we must be courageous and cooperate with the Zionist parties of the center and left in order to oust Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, and Smotrich. The question now is: Do these parties, which call themselves democratic and liberal, have the same courage?

Six days later, Huang was back, restored after a unanimous vote by the same board. Nvidia’s shares soared. Many investors celebrated the return of the leather-jacketed founder credited with making the company the engine of the artificial intelligence revolution.

Sources indicate that three years earlier, OpenAI’s board had dismissed Sam Altman, citing a lack of candor with directors. Five days later, Altman returned, and most of the directors responsible for his removal were out.

Sources indicate that in both cases, directors discovered that formal authority to remove a chief executive does not mean the power to do so in practice. The episodes exposed a three-pronged weakness in corporate governance: the challenge of maverick founders, the extraordinary complexity of AI, and the growing dependence of the U.S. economy and national security on a handful of companies at the technological frontier.

Both Altman and Huang have personas, know-how, and market-moving power that made them unfireable. Yet if the boards of the country’s most consequential technology firms cannot exercise ultimate authority over management, these companies are effectively ungovernable. This reveals a major gap in corporate stewardship, underscoring the imperative of robust regulation to ensure that the vulnerabilities of powerful U.S. companies do not become fatal weaknesses for the country’s democracy and society writ large.

Sources indicate that the iconic corporate founder is a hallmark of U.S. business culture. Henry Ford and Andrew Carnegie shaped society-altering industries around their personalities and distinctive working styles. Steve Jobs provides the most celebrated historic example of this type of figure in tech. Forced out of Apple in 1985, Jobs returned in 1997 when the tech giant was in steep decline. His track record of inventiveness helped win back employees, customers, investors, and developers. He also persuaded Bill Gates to invest $150 million in Apple and commit to developing Microsoft software for Macintosh computers, building an ecosystem whose fortunes were intertwined with his own and that has dominated the market for decades.

Recent findings suggest that these bold founders may have as much in common with an artist or creator than they do with fellow CEOs. A great architect or film director works with large teams but puts an unmistakable stamp on their work. Although a studio or tradition can continue after its originator dies or departs, investors, collaborators, and audiences do not always stay on.

It has been revealed that this analogy helps explain why succession at frontier technology companies is so fraught. Investors bet on a founder’s judgment about technologies whose commercial potential is unproven. Engineers are inspired by a particular visionary. Customers and business partners invest in the future that the founder promises. As these forces rally, they reify perceptions of an individual’s genius, which attracts still more talent and capital. Confidence becomes self-perpetuating.

Such devotion is measurable. Huang topped Glassdoor’s 2026 ranking of CEOs with a 99 percent approval rating among employee reviewers. Thousands of employees reportedly signed a letter seeking his reinstatement this month. His reportedly cruel behavior toward certain employees seemingly did little to puncture that aura.

OpenAI’s 2023 crisis demonstrated the power of such fealty. After its board fired Altman, more than 95 percent of the company’s employees signed a letter threatening to resign unless he came back. Microsoft, OpenAI’s largest commercial partner, rolled out a red carpet to Altman, promising to allow him to rebuild his team there. Faced with losing the workforce that was OpenAI’s principal asset, the board folded. The employees, investors, and commercial partners whose confidence had helped make Altman successful overpowered those charged with supervising him.

These examples do not prove that founders are irreplaceable. Apple’s revenues more than doubled during the early years of John Sculley’s post-Jobs tenure in the 1980s; more recently, the company has thrived under Tim Cook since Jobs’s death. When Uber’s Travis Kalanick was forced out in 2017, investors worried about losing the transportation innovator’s aggressive founder. His successor, Dara Khosrowshahi, now presides over a company that generated $193 billion in gross bookings and $10 billion in free cash flow in 2025.

Board members are a little like grandparents. They admire and care about the baby, comforted that the parent—the CEO—does the daily grind. When the parent disappears, the board is left holding a crying, demanding infant. Sedate quarterly meetings suddenly turn into frantic round-the-clock Zooms. Having lost the one person who they trusted to raise the child, boards want nothing more than to once again pass the progeny into capable hands.

Industry observers note that when it comes to AI companies, the problem is magnified by the extraordinary gap between a CEO’s knowledge of frontier technologies and what even accomplished directors can understand. Nvidia’s 10-person board includes Melissa Lora, the former president of Taco Bell; Stephen Neal, a distinguished trial lawyer; and Dawn Hudson, a former Pepsi-Cola and National Football League marketing executive. Three of the 10 have served on the board for more than 28 years each. Just one is under the age of 60. While several board members have technology backgrounds, the emergence of Nvidia’s chips and financing as lynchpins of AI competition has transformed the demands on a group of directors who were chosen at least in part because Huang trusted them not to get in his way. Alongside bleeding-edge technologies, the board is now dealing with matters of foreign espionage, regulatory capture, securities fraud, and export controls. It’s not hard to imagine Nvidia’s directors feeling out of their depth.

In a recent development, the governance challenges created by Nvidia’s technological complexity are compounded by the firm’s centrality to the U.S. economy and national security. A 2026 investment analysis estimated that 42 AI-related stocks accounted for 60 percent of the S&P 500’s gains in 2025. By September 2026, Nvidia alone represented approximately 8.4 percent of the index. Huang’s reinstatement on Monday propelled a broader market rally, underscoring how closely U.S. financial fortunes have become tied to confidence in the AI industry. The national-security dependence is at least as consequential. AI is increasingly incorporated into military intelligence, surveillance, cyber operations, logistics, and command-and-control systems. Access to advanced computing is at the heart of competitive tensions with China.

Recent findings suggest that these dependencies help explain U.S. President Donald Trump’s extraordinary intervention in Nvidia’s leadership deliberations. According to Semafor, the president called into a Nvidia board meeting to press for Huang’s return, suggesting that China might recruit him if Nvidia failed to take him back. Though no investigation has been completed and the allegations of Chinese plotting to compromise Huang are alarming, Trump personally vouched that his return would pose no national security risk. It is hard to know who possesses greater leverage in the Trump-Huang relationship—the president who controls regulatory decisions or the corporate titan whose technology is essential to domestic prosperity and national security.

Reliance on individual technology entrepreneurs for vital national functions can compromise public interests. In October, Ukrainian forces experienced serious disruptions to Starshield satellite communications, impairing military operations. Elon Musk subsequently acknowledged that his company, SpaceX, had restricted certain uses of the service, though responsibility for the disruptions remains contested. Society depends on interconnected technological systems that are vulnerable to malfunction and compromise; the power vested in a handful of tech moguls who control these networks is staggering.

In a recent development, U.S. institutions have failed to reckon with this amalgamation of power. Congress remains divided over how to regulate AI. Federal agencies possess fragmented authority over specific risks and no mandate from the White House to address them. Companies develop capabilities faster than public institutions can assess them. CEOs with immense technical resources and public influence end up guiding the officials responsible for overseeing them.

The consequences of this glaring void will reverberate internationally. U.S. corporate leadership is predicated on the perception that U.S. companies operate within a system of enforceable laws, strong oversight, and credible government institutions. This distinguishes U.S. technology from Chinese alternatives, whose governance remains vulnerable to direct state intervention. But if U.S. boards cannot meaningfully restrain powerful executives, and the president can intervene in their internal deliberations, those differentiators collapse. Governments considering whose AI infrastructure to trust will ask whether U.S. companies offer genuine institutional safeguards.

In a recent development, the obvious response is to strengthen corporate oversight. Some mechanisms already exist. Nvidia has an independent board, audit and governance committees, and a confidential reporting hotline. It has now added a specialized national security committee and is upgrading its compliance function. OpenAI maintains a safety and security committee overseeing its operations. But all these arrangements depend on directors whose authority may be subsumed by founder loyalty, commercial pressure, and technological complexity.

Industry observers note that other highly regulated industries offer more robust, proven oversight models. Under Federal Reserve rules, large bank holding companies must maintain independent risk committees, including directors with relevant expertise; chief risk officers report directly to those committees as well as management. Britain requires senior executives at financial firms to be approved by regulators, makes it clear what each is responsible for, and can hold them personally accountable if they fail to take reasonable steps to prevent wrongdoing. U.S. pharmaceutical regulation provides another precedent. Federal rules give drug manufacturers’ quality-control arms the authority to approve or reject products and manufacturing procedures, so that decisions do not lie simply with a CEO’s commercial preferences.

These models suggest an approach to governing companies whose technologies pose exceptional public risks. Congress should establish an independent federal supervisory authority for designated frontier AI companies, including critical infrastructure providers and developers of exceptionally capable models. Its jurisdiction should depend on the risks and systemic importance of technology companies, rather than their size or public-firm status. Now that corporate interests have captured the U.S. executive branch, legislative oversight is essential.

Industry observers note that such an institution would need permanent technical staff with expertise in advanced computing, model capabilities, cybersecurity, and intelligence threats. It would require secure access to proprietary information, the power to inspect governance systems, and the authority to compel corrective action. Its independence from day-to-day political intervention would be essential.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, regulated companies should have dedicated board-level risk committees staffed by directors with technical and national-security competence. Those committees should retain their own expert advisors and receive regular reports from both the CEO and independent risk, safety, and compliance officers. Boards should be required to document how they evaluate consequential decisions, oversee potential conflicts of interest, and prepare for abrupt leadership transitions.

Recent findings suggest that A further priority is genuine protection for whistleblowers. Nvidia’s formal policies prohibit retaliation, yet recent reporting suggests that employees fear speaking openly. In technology companies, confidentiality is increasingly difficult to preserve. Employers can potentially reconstruct a source’s identity from records of device use, badge access, communications, and document activity, even when a reporter or investigator promises anonymity. One shudders to think what this might mean for Nvidia employees who recently spoke out about mistreatment or alleged misdeeds, believing that Huang’s tenure was over for good.

A modern whistleblower regime should offer secure channels outside the organization, enforceable restrictions on attempts to identify confidential sources, and meaningful penalties for retaliation. An independent regulator should interview employees and business partners without requiring them to expose themselves to management. Such protections are particularly key during investigations involving a powerful founder.

Industry observers note that it may be tempting to conclude that Nvidia’s crisis ended happily once Huang returned and the market rallied. The OpenAI episode invited a similar reaction, especially as the company continued its rapid expansion after Altman’s reinstatement. But neither recovery resolves the institutional weakness that allowed directors’ decisions to be reversed under pressure.

U.S. technological leadership cannot depend on a system in which the most influential executives are effectively irreplaceable. A company that is too massive to lose its founder may also be too powerful to govern itself. As AI becomes embedded in the economy, national security, and public life, the United States needs oversight institutions capable of withstanding the demands of employees, investors, politicians, and even the most celebrated innovators. The long-term credibility of U.S. technological leadership will depend on it.

According to recent reports, suzanne Nossel is a columnist at Foreign Policy, the Lester Crown senior fellow for U.S. foreign policy and international order at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, and a senior advisor to the Starling Institute. She is the author of Dare to Speak: Defending Free Speech for All. X: @SuzanneNossel.

Avoiding Colombia’s Escalation Trap

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3358 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ELIZABETH DICKINSON is Deputy Director for Latin America at International Crisis Group.
  • How a U.S.-Backed Offensive Could Help Bogotá Reclaim Its Conflict Zones.
  • In a recent development, on September 21, José Luis Pérez Villanueva, better known as “El Cholo”—the second-in-command and financial architect of the criminal group Autodefensas Conquistadores de la Sierra Nevada—was killed during a Colombian police operation on the rural outskirts of Santa Marta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ELIZABETH DICKINSON is Deputy Director for Latin America at International Crisis Group.

How a U.S.-Backed Offensive Could Help Bogotá Reclaim Its Conflict Zones.

In a recent development, on September 21, José Luis Pérez Villanueva, better known as “El Cholo”—the second-in-command and financial architect of the criminal group Autodefensas Conquistadores de la Sierra Nevada—was killed during a Colombian police operation on the rural outskirts of Santa Marta. Within hours, militants from that organization launched a dramatic campaign of terror. The group, known colloquially as Los Pachenca, demanded that businesses across the city shutter. Some 90 percent of shops did, as videos circulated of gunmen shooting up storefronts that stayed open.

For two decades, Los Pachenca has been the unquestioned criminal authority in the beachfront city and the adjacent Sierra Nevada mountain range, charging extortion payments from businesses and residents and controlling the flow of drugs out of the Port of Santa Marta, en route to Europe and beyond. But the level of control the group exhibited during the strike was particularly jarring, given that Santa Marta is the vacation home of many of the country’s elite and a common destination for international visitors. Colombia’s government responded by militarizing the city, sending in hundreds of soldiers and police officers, who rolled into town on the main highway with tanks and air support. Many shops still stayed closed until the morning of September 25, when the group declared that it was ending the strike. For locals, Los Pachenca’s reaction was a message about who remains in charge.

Calm has since returned to Santa Marta, but the incident may be indicative of risks to come. Colombia’s newly elected president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has promised a steep military escalation against illegal groups, which have grown precipitously in recent years. As he does so, armed and criminal organizations will undoubtedly respond. Often, their target will not be the state. Instead, they will likely direct their violence against the civilian populations, whom they have spent years coopting and coercing. That is because armed and criminal groups across the country have learned that their true leverage is their ability to govern local communities—and to intimidate and punish them into silence. Even when they do attack state forces, their use of weapons such as improvised explosives and makeshift drones means that bystanders often suffer. In one recent incident in the Pacific coast department of Valle del Cauca, four drone attacks released by an armed group in a single day left five civilians injured.

These dangers are particularly acute as de la Espriella’s pledge of a zero-tolerance crackdown against armed and criminal groups has won enthusiastic support from Washington. Both countries want massive and visible victories against these outfits. They triumphantly revealed a new era of cooperation when the president took office in August, including a promise of upgraded military ties. (The United States has not yet publicly pledged new weapons, but it is already providing greater intelligence and logistical assistance on some operations.) After two years of tensions and threats between President Donald Trump and leftist former President Gustavo Petro, the political realignment means that Colombia is once again the United States’ closest defense ally in South America. This is likely to continue, despite major Democratic wins in the U.S. Congress, as the relationship’s focus on security has a long history of bipartisan support.

In a recent development, this week, during U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Bogotá, the de la Espriella administration signaled that it would seek congressional approval for joint military operations with the United States in Colombia. This cooperation will likely yield initial results. The Colombian government has said that it aims to ramp up attacks against armed and criminal groups and to go after leaders who enjoyed protection as counterparts in peace talks during the past administration.

Yet Colombia’s true challenge is not how to carry out attacks but what to do afterward. Surgical strikes, which see the military enter and exit quickly, leave civilians more vulnerable in the aftermath, as armed groups retaliate against alleged informants and tighten their grip in areas they control. Bogotá must ensure that every operation includes contingencies to anticipate criminal groups’ reactions and build on successful offensives by weakening their grasp on communities. The government will need to strengthen the police’s ability to patrol contested areas, a costly but necessary process that the United States and other partners should support.

The stakes are high. Bogotá has a chance to leverage its increased military pressure to open the door for the state, rewriting the story of who governs conflict areas. If the government misses this opportunity to consolidate state control, however, Colombia risks entering an escalatory spiral in which civilians pay a mounting price for a campaign intended to protect them.

Industry observers note that armed and criminal groups have spent the last decade expanding their reach across Colombia. According to the local think tank Pares, the number of municipalities with an armed group presence rose from 212 in 2018 to 518 last year—or about half of all municipalities. This deterioration reversed dramatic and hard-won improvements in security. After the historically violent decades of the 1990s and 2000s, military pressure and negotiations yielded a 2016 peace agreement demobilizing the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), once the country’s dominant rebel group. Colombia’s countryside breathed a sigh of relief as the FARC pulled out of areas where it had been in control, which represented a quarter of the country’s land.

It has been revealed that the FARC’s exit, however, did not pave the way for Colombia’s highly centralized and bureaucratic state to claim control of those vast geographies. Instead, old armed groups such as the National Liberation Army and newer ones such as the Gaitanista Army of Colombia (also known as the Gulf Clan) saw a chance to expand their access to trafficking routes, coca crops, illegal mines, and, ultimately, vulnerable rural populations. Kidnapping for extortion and mass displacement began to resurface, shattering optimism that progress would move in one direction. Over the last four years, membership in illegal groups has nearly doubled, to some 27,000 fighters today.

As a candidate, de la Espriella successfully harnessed public frustration by promising mano dura, or iron-fisted tactics, including aerial attacks and increased incarceration, facilitated by the construction of mega-prisons. He blamed his predecessor’s administration for accelerating insecurity. The first leftist to be elected president in modern Colombia, Petro had entered office in 2022 vowing to de-emphasize the military’s role and instead hold peace talks with various armed organizations. But not every group participated, and many of the ones that did sought to take advantage of cease-fires to cement their control over communities. Midway through his term, Petro pivoted back toward deploying the armed forces. But much of the harm was already done.

In a recent development, colombia’s new president has been in office only a little more than 100 days, but the shift is marked. De la Espriella carried out three bombing raids in his first weeks. He has extradited dozens of individuals to the United States, including senior leaders, and the administration has killed or captured many others. The president is doggedly pushing to restart aerial fumigation of coca crops, which the state carried out in the early 2000s to try to reduce the number of hectares under cultivation; the practice has since been heavily restricted by court rulings over concerns about health and environmental consequences. Both in private and in public, military leaders laud the government’s new support for their operations.

Industry observers note that the Trump administration has also welcomed these developments, which align with a regional trend favoring Washington’s approach on counternarcotics. For Colombia, the newly introduced era of security cooperation with the United States represents a return to the status quo ante of the last quarter century, which was briefly disrupted by the Petro administration. U.S.-Colombian military ties were forged through antidrug efforts and deepened in 1999 with Initiative Colombia, a decadelong $10 billion aid package that funded, among other things, the expansion and professionalization of the security forces and fumigation. The Colombian police and military are deeply integrated with their American counterparts. They use U.S.- and NATO-compatible systems, travel by the hundreds to the United States each year for instruction, and receive American intelligence. In nearly every operation, at least one step (and often far more) in the logistical chain is either coordinated with Washington or relies on U.S. support. That relationship never fully stopped under Petro, but the two sides were notably wary of each other. Now bilateral trust appears to be restored.

According to recent reports, even before the elections, de la Espriella impressed U.S. officials by outlining his aims to reclaim security momentum for the state. The Colombian president is now acting on several explicit U.S. priorities, including extraditions and legislation to designate numerous groups as terrorist organizations. Meanwhile, Bogotá’s coca eradication targets are even more ambitious than Washington’s. At a personal level, relations are strong, too. Two of Colombia’s top military officials previously served as envoys to U.S. Southern Command.

Industry observers note that bogotá says that it intends to deliver results for Washington’s antidrug goals and has explicitly asked for additional support in the form of funding, aircraft, surveillance technologies, and maintenance. Although Colombia’s military remains among the best trained in the region, its logistical needs are critical. Only 13 of Colombia’s 53 Black Hawk helicopters are in working order, and defense spending has shrunk as a share of the national government’s budget, from 22.4 percent in 2003 to just 14.7 percent in 2025, with a growing proportion of those funds spent on salaries and pensions.

How much the United States will provide remains to be seen. In August, U.S. Southern Command’s General Francis Donovan discussed ways to shore up the deteriorating air fleet during a visit to Bogotá. The United States has also redeployed surveillance drones from Africa to Colombia and Ecuador, where they are already aiding intelligence collection. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio was reluctant to pledge specific aid while in Colombia in September, and most of this assistance is likely to be in kind or to stay in the hands of the U.S. military and contractors, with little entering the Colombian budget. Much of it appears to be focused on short-term offensive wins.

It has been revealed that colombia has returned to tactics such as aerial bombardment because they arguably worked against the FARC. Founded as a Marxist rebellion in the 1960s, the group behaved like a conventional army, dressed in uniforms, and sought out combat with the state. This meant that the Colombian military could bomb encampments and that capturing leaders left the organization at times rudderless. Slowly chipping away at the FARC’s hierarchy and control helped push the group to finally negotiate its disarmament, beginning in 2012.

But today, those same strategies are yielding diminishing returns. The current generation of armed and criminal groups has little interest in confronting the state. Instead, they behave like businesses, seeking to safeguard access to natural resources, supply chains, and trafficking routes. They live within the civilian population and rarely wear uniforms. Leaders are easily replaced and hierarchies are fluid. Critically, Colombia’s armed groups have learned that wars with the military are costly but that controlling local populations—through intimidation and violence, but also by offering economic incentives, jobs, and services—is comparatively cheap. The battlefield has evolved from a conventional conflict to a contest over who can govern territories and the people living there.

It has been revealed that santa Marta offers an example of how this fresh model of warfare works. On most days, an outsider in the city would never perceive the presence of Los Pachenca. The group’s members do not patrol or identify themselves. Yet residents know them well from the weekly or monthly extortion payments they are forced to make. Local companies and government officials essentially view the group as an inescapable reality. Pushing back carries a violent price, but paying a protection tax, taking a bribe, or facilitating illegal commerce keeps business running smoothly.

Recent findings suggest that the criminal governance of rural areas is even more suffocating. Groups that emerged from splinters of the former FARC, known as dissidents, often force local residents to hold identity cards, issued so that militants have a full census of who lives in the area and can detect possible enemy fighters. In the Amazon region, these groups keep a land registry more complete than that of the state so that they know exactly whom and how much to extort.

With this intense surveillance over society, armed and criminal groups frequently deploy the civilian population as human shields against military offensives and police patrols. The most egregious example is the widespread use of forcibly recruited children as bodyguards for senior commanders. De la Espriella’s initial bombardments, which killed at least six children, were even temporarily halted by a court over concerns about minors. Senior officers admit that these types of casualties are inevitable around high-value targets, and that the groups know that the military is far less likely to proceed if it means killing children.

Industry observers note that armed and criminal groups will also try to use the military operations to their political advantage. When children are killed in bombardments, for example, FARC dissidents spin the local narrative into a story about how the state cares little for rural populations. The argument sticks because there is rarely a credible state presence that can serve and protect these same communities and earn their trust.

There are more immediate consequences, as well. In the aftermath of bombardments and high-level captures, armed and criminal groups often undertake what amounts to a purge of the population, killing or exiling anyone they believe to have collaborated with the state. And when the state takes out a leader, intra-group violence frequently ensues as former associates compete to take his place. Many residents shelter inside to avoid being caught up in the fighting, leaving children without school and parents without income. If new splinter groups emerge, the combat for control over neighborhoods can place even more civilians in the crossfire. This fallout widens the gap between immediate tactical results and long-term security gains. Taking out a senior leader wins applause, but conditions may well worsen on the ground.

De la Espriella’s administration has rightly identified winning territorial control, permanently dislodging criminal groups, and restoring state governance as its ultimate goals. The dilemma it now faces—exacerbated by U.S. support that focuses on attention-grabbing wins—is how to both achieve short-term results and ensure that these do not unleash new waves of violence, retaliation against civilians, and, in turn, criminal consolidation.

Recent findings suggest that the challenge is twofold. First, the military needs to anticipate groups’ violent reactions and to safeguard the population. In the case of Santa Marta, for example, the government could have increased police presence in the city in the hours after El Cholo was killed. Before the next bombardment or high-level capture, the state should ensure that a ground team of soldiers or military police is ready to hold the ground, protect the community, and prevent the armed group from swiftly stepping back in to reclaim territory.

The second challenge—establishing lasting territorial control—is trickier. A permanent rural security presence might offer the best chance for Colombia’s government to change the direction of the conflict. The country’s military leadership controls only the tip of the spear, not the rest of the state. Time and again, governments “send only the military to the hardest areas,” a retired senior officer told Crisis Group. Moreover, soldiers are operating under heavy pressure for quick wins, which are measured in the number of combatants and especially high-value targets that are killed or captured. There is a real risk that by focusing largely on these statistics, the state will overlook more comprehensive policies necessary to achieve durable security.

It has been revealed that pressure to deliver fast results has in the past incentivized unacceptable practices. In the early 2000s, intense political demands for combat kills fueled elaborate schemes in which soldiers murdered thousands of civilians and counted them as guerrilla fatalities, a scandal known as “false positives.” These crimes deeply compromised public trust in the security forces, and the military has worked for years to build a culture and procedures that ensure they do not happen again. Today, the country’s senior military leadership is likely the first and best brake on any attempts to use excessive force. Commanders say that they are cognizant of the need to guard against rules being slowly stretched until they are broken. “We need a stronger security approach, but it also worries us when we hear there is pressure for ‘results,’” one officer mentioned. But U.S. rhetoric and behavior, including its decision to sink what it claims are drug-smuggling boats on the high seas, compound these risks.

Success, then, may demand a strategy that is ultimately anchored in a much stronger and larger police force, fit for the job of safeguarding civilians rather than merely carrying out offensive strikes. Military operations can generate a window of opportunity by shuffling dynamics on the ground or removing certain dangerous players. Yet those reconfigurations will turn out in the state’s favor only if the resulting vacuum is eventually filled by reliable law enforcement. Take, for example, an operation that temporarily dislodges a group from a rural hamlet. If the military acts alone, it will likely enter and leave in a matter of days or even hours, allowing the armed group to quickly return. If, however, the offensive is followed up with permanent police patrols, access to the justice system, and social interventions, criminals will have a harder time regaining control.

This, of course, is easier said than done, given the government’s resource constraints. To create effective and permanent patrols, police departments operating in the countryside need more officers and equipment to maintain a presence in the most remote communities. Colombia has roughly 180,000 uniformed police officers, a figure that, per capita, puts it on the lower end of OECD countries, many of which are far more urbanized and therefore easier to patrol. In Colombia’s conflict-affected areas, outgunned officers must often stay inside their local stations for their own safety, limiting their ability to build trust and channels of communication with the population. Other state institutions, such as the justice system, say that they cannot establish a durable foothold in villages without guarantees of protection in the medium term—exactly what rural policing should strive to provide. The U.S. State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs has funded the building and equipping of rural police stations in the past; it should expand this work. International partners with long-standing expertise in rural policing, such as Canada and France, could provide critical support, as well.

In cities, the challenge is different. In Santa Marta, for example, the state is present, but it is weak and vulnerable to the pressure and cooptation of the same groups that it must confront. The police need both more officers and better working conditions—including salaries, benefits, access to education, and social support for families—that could help them resist bribes. Regular vetting and counterintelligence checks can help ensure that police are fighting on the side of the state and not its adversaries.

Recent findings suggest that expanding the police will be an expensive, long-term undertaking. In the interim, Colombia could prioritize more personnel for critical areas and ensure that officers have a strong grounding in community policing, allowing them to understand the most pressing risks facing civilians. That means regular outreach to communities to build trust and make certain that officers are seen as having a stake in local well-being. The United States, meanwhile, must continue to help Bogotá strengthen its police and courts with direct financial and technical assistance.

In a recent development, colombia, backed by renewed U.S. support, cannot afford to repeat past mistakes or ignore how the conflict has changed. Bogotá must therefore strategy for and capitalize on military pressure to do something no government in Colombia’s history has done: govern well in conflict areas.

Solar lease holdouts still see value in privately-owned residential projects

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects.
  • A residential solar project in Upcoming York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions.
  • After 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects. The ITC is a historic renewable energy subsidy that provides a 30% tax credit against the total cost of an eligible project, and it is currently available to the commercial and utility-scale solar segments.

A residential solar project in Upcoming York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions. Credit: Nickels Energy Solutions.

After 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned. However, a loophole in the tax credit language has allowed leased or “third party-owned” (TPO) solar projects to still receive the ITC (25D) on residential solar projects. In this scenario, it matters who owns the solar project, not necessarily where it’s built. The project can be subsidized because it is owned by a commercial manufacturer, and not the homeowner.

Some residential solar installers are still strictly pursuing and installing privately-owned solar projects. Nickels Energy Solutions (NES), a residential solar contractor working in Central New York believes a privately-owned PV system is still the better deal for the customer.

“We don’t have the same offers as some of the bigger companies,” mentioned Kevin Nickels, VP of sales with NES. “If you can offer leases, it’s like the ‘haves and have-nots.’ I don’t have that loophole or that trick up my sleeve, so it forces me to get the project sold, while I’m as sharp as I can be with margins to make it somewhat competitive.”.

According to recent reports, TPO solar transactions are typically arranged at a lower up-front cost than a wholly owned solar project. Lease contract lengths vary by provider, and financiers have surety in these transactions because the projects will be built with products from an approved vendor list (AVL). Products on an AVL can qualify for a domestic content subsidy, another tax credit in addition to the ITC, because they are manufactured using a certain percentage of domestic components.

These are premium products vetted for AVLs. But it can also mean that installers are paying premium prices for components in building TPO solar projects.

Nickels believes that, while a privately owned residential solar project will cost more at the start, the combination of expensive components and interest rates for financing over a lease term — with factors like rate increases — can cost a customer more in the long run.

“I don’t think all leases are bad,” he mentioned. “I just don’t think it’s what’s best for the industry or the homeowner.”.

Selling residential solar in 2026.

Sources indicate that rudy Wright, owner of Wright-Way Solar of Tyler, Texas, has shifted the organization’s focus from building new projects to servicing existing systems. As the ITC exited the residential solar market, so did many of the lenders financing these projects. Without lending options, Wright-Way’s installation output has slowed down, and those clients who can afford solar are paying with cash or using a home equity loan to cover the cost.

Despite that, Wright mentioned he isn’t very interested in building leased solar projects.

Wright-Way Solar built a solar plus storage project at a Ranch in Texas featuring arrays that are facing east, west and south. Credit: Wright-Way Solar.

In a recent development, “I do think it cost me some of those entry level clients, but every time I analyzed the financing end of it, I felt like I was benefitting my company and the industry more than the customer,” Wright remarked. “I haven’t seen the angle where bringing a pre-purchase agreement or bringing a lease agreement has enough ironclad return for the customer.”.

Industry observers note that tyler is a unique market for solar because many of Wright-Way’s customers are trying to make their properties more resilient, and less reliant on the grid, by installing solar and storage, and not just seeking cost savings for their energy use. Wright has installed solar plus storage systems on Texan ranches at a scale close a small commercial project.

That promise of resilience is still enough reason for some people to commission a solar project in Texas, where the state’s independent electrical grid operator has faltered and experienced dangerous outages in recent years.

“Folks realize money in the bank doesn’t do you any good if the power goes out,” Wright remarked.

NES is still building a steady pipeline of residential solar projects in Latest York. Nickels stated that has been possible in part because many of its clients are upper-middle class; but New York also maintains an incentive program for solar projects, NY-Sun, which includes a 25% state tax credit for residential systems.

Recent findings suggest that “The OBBBA caught a lot of states flat-footed,” Nickels stated. “Without federal support, it puts a lot of pressure on what the state is offering.”.

Recent findings suggest that some states’ solar subsidy programs have stepped in where federal support has diminished since the OBBBA was passed. The North Carolina Clean Energy Technology Center maintains the Database of State Incentives for Renewables & Efficiency, which analyzes which states currently have policies and incentives supporting clean energy developments. Every state has policy enabling solar projects, but not necessarily cost incentives for individual projects.

In a recent development, while traditional residential solar projects have lost a significant subsidy, the reality is that energy costs have risen in response to new grid demands from hyperscale data centers and oil scarcity from the United States’ war in Iran. Sure, a privately owned residential solar project won’t receive the ITC, but it can still stabilize energy costs without them.

“We lost a major incentive, but the rate increase is proportional,” Nickels stated.

As Russia batters Ukraine’s cities with missile strikes, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has delayed sending scores of Patriot air defense missiles to the embattled country, including those held by European nations, according to a Financial Times report.

It has been revealed that in total, the U.S. has held up around 60 Patriot air defense missiles, including more advanced PAC-3 missiles as well as around 20 PAC-2 missiles. The missiles include those that are already held in European stockpiles but require U.S. sign-off before their transfer.

Recent findings suggest that the missile transfers were originally set to occur in September, October, and November in batches of around 10 missiles each. A further delivery is set for December. Ukraine began sounding the alarm publicly in October.

Patriot air defense missiles are Ukraine’s primary defense against Russian ballistic missiles, which Russia has used in an accelerating campaign to make Ukraine’s major cities unlivable.

Since September, Russia has attacked Ukraine’s energy infrastructure more than 350 times, frequently resulting in days with no regular supply of power or water, a growing concern as winter approaches. The Pentagon is separately delaying approving a plan to allow Ukraine to produce its own Patriot missiles domestically.

In a recent development, the slowed deliveries follow interruptions in recent weeks to the functioning of Starshield, a version of the Starlink satellite internet service that Ukraine relies on for battlefield communication. Ukraine uses Starshield in its mid-range strike drones, as well as in systems used to defend against jet-powered Russian attack drones. Starshield is owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Musk and the Trump administration have traded blame over who is responsible for the throttling of Ukraine’s Starshield access.

Even as Russia scores wins in its missile campaign against Ukraine, however, recently leaked data and Ukraine’s own strikes illustrate the high price Moscow is paying.

Russia has lost at least 490,000 soldiers, according to data derived from a leaked Russian government database and analyzed by independent Russian news outlet Meduza. Even that may be an underestimate—a further 230,000 are listed as missing in action, many of whom are likely dead but not yet officially recorded as such. That means that as many as 720,000 may have died in Ukraine. The losses place the war in Ukraine as the deadliest conflict for Russia since World War II.

Recent findings suggest that russia primarily sends volunteers to fight in Ukraine and pays large bonuses as an incentive. While Russia has so far been able to find enough volunteers to staff its army, the losses are an economic and social strain on the country. Data compiled by Janis Kluge, an expert on Russian recruitment, shows a slowdown in recruiting for October as compared to last year.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s long-range strike capacity continues to develop. On Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Ukraine was behind a strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland. Ukrainian drone also recently attacked a Russian warship docked at a port in Libya. Ukraine on Tuesday separately rolled out yet another mass wave of strikes on Russia, with Russia stating that it shot down 699 drones.

Deadly airstrikes. Israeli forces have “eliminated” Naim Abu Nahal, the head of Hamas’s internal security apparatus, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz confirmed in a joint statement posted on X on Tuesday. Nahal took on the role in September, after Israeli forces seized his predecessor in a Gaza ground operation and took him to Israel. “No terrorist will succeed in evading the long arm of the State of Israel,” the statement added.

Recent findings suggest that the Israeli military also launched two airstrikes that killed six other people in Gaza on Tuesday, including a teenage boy and two police officers, who were killed at a police station, according to Palestinian health officials and first responders. Gaza’s police force slammed what it called “an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos,” the BBC reported; Israeli forces stated they struck “military operatives.”.

It has been revealed that corruption probe. A top Chinese Communist Party official once considered a possible successor to Chinese leader Xi Jinping is being investigated “for suspected severe violations of discipline and laws,” Xinhua reported on Tuesday, in the latest example of ongoing purges of China’s leadership.

The official, Chen Jining, is the head of the Communist Party in Shanghai, China’s most populous city and a key economic center. He is also a member of China’s Politburo, an elite group of 24 officials that help lead the country. He had been seen as likely to rise within the ranks of China’s government, having previously served as mayor of Beijing.

The move is part of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign that has seen hundreds of top officials, including many within the military, convicted. Since 2025, three other members of the Politburo have also faced corruption charges, and in the last two months, corruption charges were announced against both Beijing’s deputy mayor and the former mayor of major city Chongqing.

Xi’s consolidation of power comes ahead of a likely fourth term as president beginning next year, meaning that he will hold power until at least 2032.

It has been revealed that money up front. Japan will pay its full contribution to the International Criminal ​Court (ICC) ahead of schedule following an appeal by the court after the United States sanctioned it, according to Prime Minister Sanae ‌Takaichi.

According to recent reports, japan is one of the largest contributors to the court, accounting for around 15 percent of its funding. The early payment will give the court a larger financial cushion after U.S. sanctions take effect in April 2027.

The Trump administration launched a campaign against the ICC in July, starting with pressuring other nations to withdraw from it. That effort has been largely unsuccessful, with only four countries—Tajikistan, Chad, Venezuela, and Naoero—leaving the court. In October, the United States sanctioned the ICC itself, which U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called a “rogue court.”.

Sources indicate that the United States has long been concerned about the ICC’s ability to prosecute U.S. soldiers. However, the Trump administration’s pressure on the ICC represents the sharpest attack yet on the body.

In a recent development, sunset today will see the appearance of a supermoon, during which the celestial body will be about 30 percent brighter and nearly 20 percent larger than normal. In North America, a full moon that falls after Nov. 7 is known as a “beaver” moon, as it usually occurs around when beavers are building their dams and stocking up on food. If you happen to miss this month’s supermoon, though, don’t worry: There are three more coming in a row in December, January, and February, according to NASA. Happy moongazing!

These factors, combined with Solana’s low fees and high throughput, position it well for consumer and high-frequency use cases that could accelerate demand in a recovery.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • How Fighting Weakens Washington’s Reputation—and Backing Down May Strengthen It.
